provisions.heading: On June 10, 2026, the Senate Armed Services Committee voted
provisions.text:
18–9 to advance the NDAA for Fiscal Year 2027 to the Senate floor.
The committee passed this bill in response to an increasingly
dangerous threat environment and a rapidly evolving battlefield
landscape. Recognizing those trends, the committee approved a
substantial increase in our national security investment—the larg-
est defense dollar figure in American history.
There is one goal behind this heightened funding: maintaining
American deterrence in the most complex threat environment since
World War II. The dictators ruling China, Russia, North Korea,
and Iran have formed an axis of aggressors. They share both ambi-
tions and weapons. Together, they hope to weaken American lead-
ership and fracture the free world. Often, they pursue those aims
with weapons only this century could have produced. Ships and air-
craft remain vital tools of conflict. But the wars of today are often
fought remotely, with soldiers far from the front line piloting
drones, launching space-based weapons, firing hypersonic strike
weapons, wielding artificial intelligence technologies, or spinning
internet-based cognitive warfare schemes.
America must keep pace. The alternative is to invite aggression.
On those points, the Congress, the White House, and the Depart-
ment of Defense agree. In this NDAA, the committee acted on
those convictions.
The defense industrial base has begun humming, spurred by
Federal investment, the geopolitical threats at hand, and the in-
domitable drive of America’s innovators and entrepreneurs. This
NDAA authorizes increased defense spending—a necessary action,
and one still cheaper than failing to deter war. These funds will
shore up our traditional platforms and adopt emerging tech-
nologies. But the bill also enacts reforms to ensure those dollars
are spent wisely. The committee built on last year’s acquisition re-
forms to further trim bureaucratic excess and streamline Pentagon
budgeting.
The result is an NDAA tailored to 21st century conflict but writ-
ten to shield Americans from it. As always, the surest guarantee
of peace is remaining fully prepared for war.

provisions.heading: BUDGET AUTHORITY IMPLICATION
provisions.text:
The administration’s budget request for national defense discre-
tionary programs within the jurisdiction of the Senate Committee
on Armed Services for fiscal year 2027 was $1,098.8 billion for base
Department of Defense (DOD) programs and $41.4 billion for na-
tional security programs in the Department of Energy (DOE).
The committee recommends an overall discretionary authoriza-
tion of $1,140.1 billion in fiscal year 2027, including $1,099.0 bil-
lion for base DOD programs, $41.1 billion for national security pro-
grams in the DOE, and $11.9 billion for defense-related activities
outside the jurisdiction of the NDAA.

sion D of this bill summarizes the direct discretionary authoriza-
tions in the committee recommendation and the equivalent budget
authority levels for fiscal year 2027 defense programs. The table
summarizes the committee’s recommended discretionary authoriza-

provisions.heading: War II-era aircraft
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the profound contributions of Amer-
ican naval aviators during World War II and the lasting impor-
tance of preserving the aircraft they flew. As the number of sur-
viving veterans of that conflict continues to decline, the aircraft
that remain in the Department of the Navy’s possession serve as
tangible, irreplaceable links to a defining era in American and
world history.
The committee emphasizes that these aircraft are national assets
and must be treated with the respect appropriate to their historical
value. These aircraft are not only critical to honoring those who
served but also to inspiring future generations with the legacy of
service and sacrifice.
The committee is concerned that many of these historically sig-
nificant aircraft, particularly those produced prior to December 31,
1945, are currently housed on external display and/or are aban-
doned as wartime crash wreckages still under Department of the
Navy ownership and control. These aircraft are at increasing risk
of irreversible degradation due to environmental exposure. Without
urgent action to relocate these aircraft into indoor, climate-con-
trolled environments, their long-term preservation may no longer
be viable.
Therefore, the committee recommends a provision that would di-
rect the Secretary of the Navy to preserve these aircraft.
The committee also directs the Secretary of the Navy to provide
a briefing, not later than April 1, 2027, to the Committees on
Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives on
the Department of the Navy’s plan to relocate, preserve, and sus-
tain its World War II-era aircraft currently on external display,
while also seeking policy reforms that will allow properly qualified
American museum entities to recover abandoned World War II-era
crash wreckages that are not deemed to be wartime aircrew graves.
The briefing should address the following:
(1) A plan to initiate the phased relocation of historic air-
craft produced prior to December 31, 1945, from external to in-
door display facilities, with priority given to F4F and FM1/2
Wildcats, F6F Hellcats, F4U/ FG–1 Corsairs, SBD Dauntlesses,
SB2C Helldivers, PBJs (B–25s), P2Bs (B–29s), JD–1s (A–26s), E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

craft crash wreckages that are known aircrew grave sites. It
includes World War II-era crash wreckages on land, in lakes,
and in the world’s oceans. This generally reflects a policy long
instituted by the Department of the Navy. The Congress has
an established track record of empowering such recoveries for
historic preservation purposes;

for future generations. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: Command Post capability
provisions.text:
The committee recommends a provision that would limit the obli-
gation or expenditure of fiscal year 2027 travel funds for the Office
of the Secretary of the Air Force until the Secretary of the Air
Force submits the report required by section 154 of the National
Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Public Law 119–
60).
The committee also directs the Secretary of the Air Force to brief
the congressional defense committees, not later than March 31,
2027, on an assessment of the feasibility and affordability of a busi-
ness jet solution to host associated Looking Glass-Next aircrew and
required hardware and software, as well as platform dependencies
such as capability and capacity of additional seating, power, cool-
ing, internal aircraft and offboard line-of-sight and beyond line-of-
sight communications, and information technology and security in-
frastructure.
Sec. 137—Mobility capabilities strategic plan
The committee recommends a provision that would direct the
Secretary of the Air Force, in coordination with the Commander,
U.S. Transportation Command and in consultation with the com-
manders of the geographic combatant commands, to submit to the
congressional defense committees, not later than January 1, 2027,
a comprehensive strategic plan, and a briefing on the plan, for the
development, acquisition, modernization, and integration of Depart-
ment of Defense total force mobility capabilities through fiscal year
2047.
The committee believes a comprehensive mobility capabilities
strategic plan is needed to ensure that the Department of Defense
can project and sustain forces in an increasingly contested and dis-
persed environment. Adversaries are developing capabilities to dis-
rupt logistics networks and challenge U.S. mobility and access,
while operational demands continue to grow in scale and com-
plexity. The committee is concerned that current planning does not
fully reflect the innovation, integration, and use of emerging tech-
nologies and commercial partnerships required to meet these chal-
lenges. Accordingly, the committee encourages the Department of
the Air Force to adopt a more forward-looking and analytically rig-
orous approach to ensure a long-term, integrated strategy that
aligns requirements, investments, and modernization efforts across
the Joint Force through 2047 and maintains resilient and effective
mobility capabilities.

provisions.heading: Items of Special Interest
provisions.text:
Air Force combat search and rescue forces
The committee is concerned about combat search and resecure
(CSAR) force structure in the Air Force. In recent years, the Air
Force truncated the buy of HH–60Ws and has since transferred 26
HH–60Ws from units responsible for CSAR operations to the Air
Force District Washington (AFDW) to replace H–1 helicopters.
AFDW uses these helicopters to support contingency response,
homeland operations, and ceremonial honors in the National Cap-
ital Region.
The committee believes that these actions have left CSAR forces
unnecessarily short of the forces needed to support CSAR oper-
ations in a major contingency. Therefore, the committee directs the
Secretary of the Air Force to conduct a study of CSAR require-
ments and capabilities, including HH–60Ws and HC–130Js, and
provide a report and briefing on that study to the congressional de-
fense committees, not later than March 31, 2027.
Furthermore, the committee directs the Secretary to avoid mak-
ing any changes in CSAR force structure until the study is com-
pleted and he or she has provided the results of that study to the
Congress.
Anti-ship air-launched missiles
The committee notes Anti-Access/Area Denial (A2/AD) environ-
ments present the need for new, more capable weapons such as the

provisions.heading: Offensive Anti-Surface Warfare Increment II (OASuW Inc II)/
provisions.text:
Hypersonic Air Launched OASuW (HALO) program. HALO is in-
tended to be a carrier-suitable, higher-speed, longer-range, air-
launched weapon that will significantly increase the Navy’s capac-
ities for long-range fires in A2/AD environments. The Navy had in-
tended to accelerate the fielding of HALO to support early oper-
ational capability in fiscal year 2029.
However, in early fiscal year 2025, the Department of the Navy
notified the committee of its intent to cancel the solicitation for the
OASuW Inc II/HALO engineering and manufacturing development
(EMD) effort, citing insufficient funds. In March 2025, the Navy
discontinued work on the HALO approach to transition to EMD
and directed a restructuring program to emphasize technology mat-
uration in May 2025. The committee is concerned that development
for OASuW Inc II/HALO is languishing, even though the require-
ment for such capability remains valid.
Additionally, the committee is also aware of promising opportuni-
ties associated with the Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector.
The weapon is intended as a smaller, shorter-range, lower-cost ca-
pability to augment the existing Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile
(LRASM). However, the committee further notes that the Depart-
ment has expressed an intent to significantly increase production
rates of LRASM over the next 5 years.
Carrier aviation faces unique constraints on sortie numbers,
range, and onboard stores of munitions. These limitations make op- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

(3) The intended acquisition pathway for these programs.
Arctic wargaming and operational simulation capability
The committee recognizes the growing strategic importance of
the Arctic region and the increasing operational challenges posed
by extreme cold weather environments, contested logistics, limited
infrastructure, and expanding military activity by strategic com-
petitors. The committee believes that the Department of Defense
must continue to improve its ability to plan, train, and operate in
Arctic and high-latitude environments across all domains.
The committee notes the importance of advanced wargaming and
operational simulation capabilities to support planning and pre-
paredness for Arctic operations, including multi-domain operations,
contested logistics, maritime security, and crisis response scenarios.
The committee further believes that such capabilities can support
improved coordination among the combatant commands, the mili-
tary services, the Coast Guard, interagency partners, and allied
and partner nations operating in the Arctic region.
The committee encourages the Secretary of Defense to continue
developing and expanding Arctic-focused wargaming and simula-
tion capabilities to support operational planning, experimentation,
and exercises in extreme cold weather and high-latitude environ-
ments. In doing so, the committee encourages the Department to
prioritize: (1) Simulation and modeling of multi-domain operations
in Arctic environments; (2) Testing and analysis of contested logis-
tics networks in remote and austere regions with limited infra-
structure; (3) Development of operational concepts and response
protocols for maritime security, environmental incidents, and crisis
response in the Arctic; (4) Use of high-fidelity virtual models of
Arctic terrain, maritime chokepoints, and gray zone scenarios; and
(5) Deployment of mobile or expeditionary simulation capabilities
that can support units operating in remote locations where perma-
nent infrastructure is limited.
The committee directs the Secretary of Defense to provide a
briefing, not later than February 3, 2027, to the congressional de-
fense committees on the Department’s efforts to develop and ex-
pand Arctic-focused wargaming and operational simulation capa-
bilities. The briefing shall include: (1) An update on current and
planned initiatives; (2) A list of participating organizations; (3) A
description of how the capabilities integrate with combatant com-
mand planning and exercises; (4) Details on coordination with al- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: Portfolio Acquisition Executive Command and Control and Counter

Command-and-Control will use to demonstrate the value of the De-

The committee strongly encourages the Army to accelerate
CMFF program resourcing. Army prioritization of CMFF will ben-
efit efforts across the Department including the Army Next Gen-
eration Command and Control initiative, the Marine Corps ground
electronic warfare (EW) and communication programs, and Navy
surface fleet EW initiatives. Failure to effectively resource and ac-
celerate this early MOSA program will slow industry adoption and
prevent the services from realizing the benefits of the evolving
CMOSS standard that hundreds of companies have adopted.
The committee directs the Secretary of the Army to provide a
briefing, not later than April 1, 2027, to the congressional defense
committees on the schedule to accelerate CMFF along with a de-
tailed list of vehicles and platforms that will host CMFF.
Army investment in autonomous surface vessels
The committee recognizes the potential of integrating commercial
autonomous surface vessel technologies into the Army watercraft
fleet for logistics support.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of the Army to
provide a report, not later than March 1, 2027, to the Committees
on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives,
on its efforts related to autonomous surface vessel technology. The
report shall include:
(1) An overview of current and planned Army investments in
autonomous surface vessel programs, including a detailed
breakdown of efforts to leverage commercially available plat-
forms and technologies;
(2) An assessment of:
(a) how those investments address gaps identified in
operational plans for contested and uncontested environ-
ments; and
(b) the suitability of vessels being procured for needs in
the Indo-Pacific theater, such as sea state survivability, E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

(3) Plans to test and evaluate available platforms, including
under contractor-owned, contractor-operated arrangements;
(4) A description of collaboration with other services on au-
tonomous surface vessel development activities; and
(5) A 5-year roadmap for expanding investment in commer-

Army Mobile Tactical Cannon modernization and artillery
automation
The committee remains concerned that current towed and semi-
automated artillery systems place significant physical and cognitive
burdens on cannon crews, particularly during sustained high-inten-
sity and large-scale combat operations. The committee notes that
manual loading, ammunition handling, and resupply of 155mm ar-
tillery systems contribute to crew fatigue, reduce sustained rates of
fire, increase logistical strain, and extend the amount of time artil-
lery units remain stationary and vulnerable to counter-battery fires
and unmanned aerial system threats.

provisions.heading: The committee believes the Army’s Mobile Tactical Cannon
provisions.text:
(MTC) modernization efforts present an important opportunity to
improve survivability, lethality, mobility, and soldier effectiveness
through the integration of advanced automation technologies. The
committee further believes that increased automation across the
full kill chain and sustainment cycle can reduce soldier workload,
improve operational tempo, support ‘‘shoot-and-move’’ tactics, and
enable smaller crew sizes while sustaining or increasing combat ef-
fectiveness.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Secretary of the Army
to prioritize highly automated solutions in the development and ac-
quisition of future MTC systems. In evaluating modernization ap-
proaches, the committee encourages the Army to consider systems
that incorporate: (1) Automated ammunition handling and cham-
bering systems designed to increase the rate of fire while reducing
manual lifting and repetitive physical strain on soldiers; (2) Digital
fire-control systems that reduce manual data entry requirements
and support automated laying and targeting functions; and (3) Au-
tonomous or semi-autonomous ammunition resupply and transfer
mechanisms capable of improving survivability and reducing resup-
ply timelines between ammunition carriers and firing platforms.
Furthermore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Army to
provide a briefing, not later than March 1, 2027, to the Committees
on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives
on the MTC acquisition and modernization strategy. The briefing
shall include: (1) A comparison of estimated soldier physical work-
load requirements between current artillery systems and proposed
automated solutions; (2) An explanation of how automation, crew
reduction, and soldier workload reduction are being evaluated with-
in ongoing self-propelled howitzer modernization efforts; (3) A de-
scription of plans to integrate automated or autonomous ammuni-
tion resupply capabilities into future artillery formations; and (4) E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Army rifle-mounted aiming laser strategy
The committee supports the Department of the Army’s efforts to
improve soldier lethality through modernization of its inventory of
legacy close combat weapons, ammunition, and individual aiming
and fire control systems. The Army is currently pursuing several
development programs to modernize its inventory of infantry weap-
ons, ammunition, and aiming systems like the AN/PEQ–15. How-
ever, the committee is concerned that the Army has not yet devel-
oped a strategy for replacing their aging rifle-mounted aiming and
illumination lasers and notes numerous commercially available al-
ternatives.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Army to
provide a report, not later than March 31, 2027, to the Committees
on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives
on the assessment of commercially available rifle-mounted aiming
lasers to replace current legacy systems.
Army small unmanned aerial systems munitions
The committee is concerned that the Army lacks a clear roadmap
for mass production of small unmanned aerial systems (sUAS) mu-
nitions, despite adequate funding.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Army to
provide a briefing, not later than April 1, 2027, to the Committees
on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives
on weapons systems delivered through sUAS. The briefing shall de-
scribe: (1) The quantity of droppable or kinetic weapon systems de-
livered through sUAS required for the Army; (2) The current num-
ber of qualified weapons suitable to support the sUAS lethality
needs of the Army; (3) A roadmap with fielding options to fulfill
lethality needs; and (4) The status of funding provided for such mu-
nitions systems included in the fiscal year 2028 president’s budget
request and across the future years defense program.
Army small Unmanned Aircraft Systems scaling and deploy-
ment strategy
The committee recognizes the increasing operational importance
of small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS) at the tactical level,
particularly for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, force pro-
tection, offensive capabilities, and combined arms maneuvers. The
war in Ukraine underscores the decisive advantage conferred by
rapidly deployable, attritable, and networked sUAS capabilities in
contested environments. The committee is concerned that the
Army’s current approach to procuring, scaling, and fielding sUAS
to tactical units remains fragmented and insufficient to meet
emerging operational requirements. While the Army has made
progress through experimentation and limited fielding, the com-
mittee lacks a comprehensive understanding of how these efforts
are being integrated into a sustained, large-scale deployment of
sUAS as a core element of tactical unit capability. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

(ENVG–B) program. The committee understands that while SBMC
is in development, ENVG–B is being fielded today and provides su-

The committee is also concerned with the threat from adversary

ued reliance on large inventories of legacy aviator night vision im-
aging systems despite efforts to produce replacement capabilities.
The committee understands that the commercial industry is pro-
ducing advanced light-weight night vision systems that meet Fed-
eral Aviation Administration flight certification requirements and
are in use by select U.S. law enforcement and military units. These
systems meet or exceed Army requirements for image intensifica-
tion, field of view, weight, and compatibility.
The committee directs the Secretary of the Army to provide a
briefing, not later than March 31, 2027, to the Committees on
Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives
that includes:
(1) A summary of night vision systems currently in use
across Army aviation force structure, including performance
specifications and inventory quantities for each system;
(2) A description of operational improvements sought to cur-
rent capabilities to include image intensification and increased
panoramic field of view;
(3) An assessment of the impact of the weight of the current
night vision system on aviator neck strain and injuries;
(4) An assessment of commercial, off-the-shelf night vision
systems that meet or exceed Army requirements as suitable re-
placements for existing aviation night vision systems; and
(5) An analysis of fielding such commercial, off-the-shelf so-
lution(s) to replace legacy aviator night vision imaging systems
in lieu of continuing existing advanced development efforts, in-
cluding a comparison of fielding timeline and cost.
B–21 force structure and production strategy
The committee is concerned that the current program of record
for the B–21 Raider may be insufficient to meet the requirements
of the 2026 National Defense Strategy. The committee notes that
the program of record for 100 aircraft has remained unchanged
since 2015, despite significant changes in the security environment,
including the expansion of China’s nuclear forces. The committee
further recognizes that a range of senior national security leaders,
including the Chair of the 2023 Strategic Posture Commission and
former commanders of U.S. Strategic Command, have called for an
expansion of the B–21 fleet. The committee also notes that Con-
gress has provided funding to expand B–21 production capacity.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force,
in coordination with the Commander, U.S. Strategic Command and
the Direct Reporting Program Manager for the Critical Major
Weapon Systems Programs, to submit a report and provide a brief-
ing to the congressional defense committees, not later than March
1, 2027, on the force structure and production strategy for the B–
21 aircraft. The report shall include:
(1) An assessment of the number of B–21 aircraft required
to meet the nuclear and conventional mission requirements of
the 2026 National Defense Strategy, including the analytical
basis and assumptions used to determine such requirement; E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: Briefing on Marine Aviation Plan
provisions.text:
The committee understands that the U.S. Marine Corps has spe-
cific force structure modernization goals, but the committee needs
more information and more frequent communication on legislative
barriers, such as policy and military construction, that inhibit the
implementation of the Marine Aviation Plan.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Navy to
provide a briefing to the congressional defense committees, not
later than February 1, 2027, regarding the Marine Corps Marine
Aviation Plan, including the implications for Marine Corps aircraft
force structures, recapitalization, training, and the sustainment of
the active and reserve components of the Marine Corps.
Briefings on Air Force sustainment funding and spare parts
availability
The committee remains concerned that current Air Force aircraft
sustainment funding levels and spare parts availability may be in-
sufficient to meet evolving global mission requirements. Current
spare parts funding levels for the Air Force are estimated to sup-
port approximately 80 to 85 percent of weapon system sustainment
requirements, contributing to grounded aircraft, cannibalization of
parts, and reduced mission-capable rates across multiple fleets of
the Air Force.
It is the committee’s belief that the Secretary of the Air Force
should improve the mission capable rates of Air Force aircraft by
addressing spare parts shortages, depot repair backlogs,
sustainment supply chain risks, and limitations on organic repair
capability.
To ensure a clear understanding of these challenges, the com-
mittee directs the Secretary of the Air Force to submit a report to
the congressional defense committees, not later than March 31,
2027, detailing aircraft sustainment metrics for the below-specified
platforms over the previous 5 fiscal years. This report should in-
clude an analysis of enacted sustainment and spare parts funding
compared to requested levels, an assessment of industry’s capacity
to meet these requirements, and an evaluation of the resulting mis-
sion risks for each platform.
To ensure rigorous oversight of the Air Force’s readiness efforts,
the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force to provide E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Cargo projectile munition production
The committee understands that cargo projectile munitions re-
main a critical instrument of war on the modern battlefield. In par-
ticular, the committee is aware that area effect cargo carrying pro-
jectiles, such as the Dual-Purpose Improved Conventional Muni-
tion, have proved to be a valuable tool in the arsenal of partner na-
tions like Ukraine. Further, the committee notes that urgent re-
quirements for area effects cargo carrying projectiles have depleted
U.S. arsenals, necessitating new production.
The committee directs the Secretary of the Army to provide a re-
port, not later than February 26, 2027, to the Committees on
Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives on
the Department of the Army’s plans to procure cargo projectile mu-
nitions. The report shall include:
(1) An analysis of the strategic and operational impact of
Ukraine’s employment of United States-supplied cargo projec-
tiles, including cluster munitions, on Russia’s ability to pros-
ecute military operations in Ukraine since the February 2022
full-scale invasion;
(2) An analysis of the impact of this expenditure of cluster
munitions on United States and allied stockpiles of cluster mu-
nitions and cargo projectiles more broadly;
(3) An analysis of current defense industrial base cargo mu-
nition production capacity, including within the defense or-
ganic industrial base, including the capability to surge produc-
tion;
(4) Minimum sustaining production rates for cargo projectiles
within the defense organic industrial base;
(5) Projected cargo munition procurement under the future
years defense program; and
(6) Analysis of the workforce requirements needed to sustain
projected production rates.
CH–47 lightweight ballistic protection system upgrades
The committee recognizes the importance of modernizing the
CH–47 fleet with the latest advances in lightweight ballistic protec-
tion. Next-generation systems can reduce armor weight by up to 25
percent, which would enable the Army to meet current and future
operational requirements while increasing payload capacity and ex-
tending range.

provisions.heading: Collaborative Combat Aircraft
provisions.text:
The committee notes the progress of the Air Force’s Collaborative
Combat Aircraft (CCA) Increment 1 and supports transition to full-
rate production. The committee encourages the Navy and Marine
Corps to leverage Air Force designs, technologies, and collaboration
models to accelerate the development of their own CCA capabili-
ties; however, the committee notes that the Navy and Marine
Corps have provided comparatively limited updates on their CCA
efforts relative to the Air Force and expects improved visibility
going forward.
The committee supports keeping costs low without sacrificing ca-
pability and expects future CCA increments to provide sufficient
range, speed, and power to enable autonomous self-deployment
from the United States and effective operation in contested envi-
ronments. The committee further notes the importance of main-
taining a diverse set of propulsion options across CCA variants to
support mission diversity, resilience, and supply chain risk reduc-
tion.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force
and the Secretary of the Navy to provide a briefing to the congres-
sional defense committees, not later than March 31, 2027, on the
impact of cost considerations on CCA requirements. The briefing
shall address effects on platform characteristics and fleet-wide
costs, including propulsion choices, and identify technology ap-
proaches, including commercial and modified off-the-shelf solutions,
to reduce attrition and improve operational flexibility. The briefing
shall also include the Navy’s and Marine Corps’ incorporated devel-
opment strategies and technology leveraged from the Air Force
CCA program, opportunities to update the tri-service agreement to
align capabilities and resources, and the potential to field CCA as
complementary to, or in place of, existing programs of record.
The committee also supports expanding exports to allies and
partners through Foreign Military Sales and Direct Commercial
Sales and encourages the Department of Defense to facilitate
exportability as expeditiously as possible.
Commercially available extra-large unmanned underwater
vehicles fielding acceleration
The committee supports the Navy and the Defense Innovation
Unit’s (DIU) efforts to competitively demonstrate commercially
available extra-large unmanned underwater vehicles (XLUUVs) ca-
pable of deploying large payloads across extended ranges in con-
tested environments. Open competitions conducted by the Navy
and the DIU in 2025 have identified commercial XLUUV platforms
capable of providing scalable, cost-effective solutions to address E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Complementary radar solutions for low, slow, small, un-

The committee believes that certain commercial radar solutions
may be effective as complementary radar solutions for low, slow,
small unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) integrated defeat systems
(LIDS).
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Army, in
coordination with the Joint Interagency Task Force 401, to conduct
an evaluation of commercially available radars capable of enhanc-
ing the Army’s LIDS effort. In conducting the evaluation, the Army
should assess:
(1) The ability of complementary, commercial hybrid, and/or
passive, distributed radar solutions to operate from fixed sites,
mobile platforms, elevated platforms, unmanned ground vehi-
cles, and/or tethered to UAS;
(2) The ability of complementary solutions to easily hand off
tracks to Ku Band radars integrated into modern Army com-
mand and control systems to cue kinetic and/or non-kinetic
interceptors;
(3) The technical maturity, reliability, maintainability, cyber-

(4) The extent to which the capability supports repairability,

Comptroller General review of Army light tactical wheeled
vehicle program management
The committee recognizes that the Army is pivoting its tactical
vehicle strategy toward lighter, unarmored systems like the Infan-
try Squad Vehicle (ISV) to better suit Indo-Pacific operations. Evi-
dence suggests that key performance parameters for reliability and
survivability may have been de-scoped to justify production despite
documented test failures. Furthermore, the heavy use of commer-
cial-off-the-shelf components may leave the Army without the tech-
nical data needed for long-term maintenance, creating a ‘‘vendor
lock’’ scenario. By utilizing accelerated acquisition authorities, the
service is bypassing traditional oversight and suppressing dura-
bility benchmarks to meet aggressive 2030 fielding timelines.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Comptroller General of
the United States to review the Army’s Light Tactical Vehicle pro-
gram management, addressing the following: (1) The extent to
which the Army’s decision to move the ISV to full-rate production
in 2023–25 involved formal waivers of reliability and other stand-
ards; (2) How plans to procure Tactical Wheeled Vehicles are struc-
tured to secure sufficient intellectual property for maintenance of
commercial-off-the-shelf platforms like the ISV; (3) The projected
effects of the Army’s decision to cease Joint Light Tactical Vehicle
(JLTV) procurement on estimated sustainment costs and the long-
term viability of the tactical wheeled vehicle industrial base; (4)
The effect of the Army’s JLTV decision, as the Joint Program Exec-
utive Office, on other services’ JLTV acquisition efforts; and (5) The
extent to which the use of middle tier of acquisition or other rapid-
fielding authorities for the ISV and future ‘‘Mobile Brigade Combat
Team’’ platforms achieve Office of the Secretary of Defense-level
testing approvals or involve waiving durability benchmarks. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: Aerial Systems
provisions.text:
The committee notes the increased role of unmanned aircraft sys-
tems (UAS) on the battlefield, especially in current conflicts in
Ukraine and Iran. In August 2025, the Secretary of Defense des-
ignated the Secretary of the Army as the Executive Agent for
Counter-small UAS (C–sUAS) and directed the Army to establish
Joint Interagency Task Force (JIATF) 401 to align authorities and
resources. At that time, the Secretary of Defense emphasized the
need to focus on speed in outpacing threats and ensuring air sov-
ereignty and directed the completion of specific activities to better
assure the success of this organization. Additionally, the Congress
modified section 199(g) of title 10, United States Code, to require
the Task Force Director to report annually to the congressional de-
fense committees on their progress.
The committee is supportive of the Department of Defense’s ef-
forts and is committed to ensuring that funds are used to develop
C–sUAS capabilities that protect warfighters. To that end, the com-
mittee seeks to better understand how the Army has addressed the
Secretary of Defense’s requirements for JIATF 401 and is using
this task force to acquire needed C–sUAS capabilities.
The committee directs the Comptroller General of the United
States to review the Army’s efforts to establish the task force and
use it to develop and acquire C–sUAS capabilities or procure com-
mercially available solutions. This assessment should: (1) Assess
whether the Army has completed the tasks directed in the Sec-
retary of Defense’s August 2025 memo; (2) Assess the Army’s proc-
esses for identifying current and future requirements for C–sUAS
capabilities; (3) Evaluate the extent to which the Army’s efforts to
acquire C–sUAS technologies are consistent with relevant leading
practices pertaining to product development and risk management;
and (4) Assess improved communication across the Joint Force on
C–sUAS capabilities.
The committee further directs the Comptroller General to pro-
vide a briefing to the Senate Armed Services Committee, not later
than April 16, 2027, on the preliminary findings of the assessment,
with additional work to follow at a mutually agreed upon time and
in a mutually agreed upon format.
Comptroller General review of Soldier Borne Mission Com-
mand systems
The committee notes the critical role that battlefield awareness
and integrated systems play in soldiers’ decision-making. As the
Army works to deliver a single platform to improve sensing and sit-

grated soldier-borne solution for the tactical community. The com-
mittee remains committed, however, to provide oversight of the
new acquisition pathway being pursued by the Army to deliver on
the Soldier Borne Mission Command (SBMC) initiative given the E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: Conversions to Air National Guard Contingency Response

Groups
The committee understands that the Air National Guard is con-
verting several units to Contingency Response Groups (CRG). The
committee is interested in the progress associated with these con-
versions, including the necessary funding for manning and equip-
ment to support conversions. Therefore, the committee directs the
Secretary of the Air Force to provide a briefing to the Senate
Armed Services Committee, not later than February 1, 2027, that
includes the following:
(1) A list of the units identified for conversion;
(2) The planned timeline for conversion of each unit;
(3) Current manning of each unit identified for conversion;
(4) Manning necessary for each newly established CRG and
planned timeline for reaching required CRG manning levels;
(5) Equipment necessary for the new CRGs, existing equip-
ment gaps for each converting unit, and plan, including
timeline, for fully equipping each unit;
(6) Funding necessary for the conversion for each unit,
whether funding has yet been allocated for each conversion
and reasoning why funding has not yet been allocated or has
been diverted from the conversion; and
(7) Risks to the mission should the deadlines for conversion
not be met, including impacts on recent operations such as Op-
eration Epic Fury. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Counter small uncrewed aerial systems at southern border
The committee notes with concern reports of increased uncrewed
aircraft system (UAS) activity along the southern land border of
the United States, including their potential use for reconnaissance
and smuggling by transnational criminal organizations. The com-
mittee commends recent Department of Defense efforts to address
domestic UAS incursions but remains concerned that forces oper-
ating along the southern border are not yet widely equipped with
counter-UAS systems that can effectively mitigate threats within
the Homeland.
Therefore, the committee encourages Joint Interagency Task
Force 401 and Joint Task Force—Southern Border to prioritize col-
laboration on the rapid delivery of cost-effective, low-collateral-ef-
fects interceptors capable of safe kinetic mitigation of UAS along
the southern land border within the United States. The committee
further notes that operational challenges exist in this threat envi-
ronment including the need to account for safety risks in miti-
gating drones over civilian inhabited areas, including the risk of
falling debris from disabled UAS.
Counter—unmanned aircraft systems low-altitude detection
capabilities
The committee is concerned with the increasing use of small,
low-altitude unmanned aircraft systems to conduct surveillance,
disrupt operations, or threaten military installations and other De-
partment of Defense facilities. Effective counter—unmanned air-
craft system operations require persistent detection and tracking of
small, slow-moving airborne objects operating in complex, low-alti-
tude environments.
The Department has long employed avian radar systems to miti-
gate bird-aircraft strike hazards at military airfields. The com-
mittee believes that commercially available avian radar tech-
nologies incorporate detection, tracking, and classification capabili-
ties that may be adaptable for counter—unmanned aircraft system
missions. The committee understands that such systems are al-
ready deployed at military and civilian facilities and believes that
they may offer a cost-effective, non-kinetic, dual-use option to com-
plement existing counter—unmanned aircraft system sensor archi-
tectures.
Therefore, the committee encourages the Secretary of Defense,
acting through the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and
Engineering and the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition
and Sustainment, and in coordination with the military depart-
ments, to assess the operational utility of adapting existing avian
radar technologies for counter—unmanned aircraft system detec-
tion and tracking at fixed installations, including opportunities for
limited pilot efforts and integration with existing command and
control systems, as appropriate.
DDG 51 multiyear procurement

in December 2025 laid out a new path forward for large surface
combatants with the transition from the design of the current next
generation destroyer, DDG(X). That plan also includes a new guid- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

need to continue to build DDG–51 Flight III destroyers well into

The current DDG–51 multiyear procurement (MYP) contract
ends in fiscal year 2027. The committee supports the need for a
new MYP contract beginning in fiscal year 2028 and directs the

Department of Defense approach to countering cellular-en-
abled unmanned aerial systems
The committee recognizes the growing threat posed by commer-
cially available unmanned aerial systems (UAS) that leverage cel-
lular networks, including 4G LTE and 5G, for command and con-
trol and data transmission. These systems can operate beyond line-
of-sight, evade traditional radio frequency-based countermeasures,
and blend into civilian telecommunications traffic, complicating de-
tection, attribution, and mitigation efforts.
The committee believes that the Department of Defense must
adopt a proactive, layered, and technology-driven approach to coun-
tering cellular-enabled UAS threats, prioritizing capabilities that
operate across the full spectrum of detection, identification, and
mitigation, while ensuring coordination with civil authorities and
minimizing disruption to lawful civilian communications.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to
provide a briefing, not later than April 16, 2027, to the Committees
on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Repr

provisions.heading: Drone Center of Excellence in Army National Guard
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the significant role drones play in cur-
rent military operations and is concerned that the Army does not
have a plan to expand the capability into the Army National
Guard. The committee believes that a Drone Center of Excellence
(COE) within the Army National Guard at a National Guard train-
ing site would not only build capability and readiness in the Guard
but expand the Army’s ability to contribute to the Joint Force.
The committee directs the Secretary of the Army to provide a re-
port, not later than April 16, 2027, to the Committees on Armed
Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives on the ad-
visability and feasibility of establishing a Drone Center of Excel-
lence within the Army National Guard at a National Guard train-
ing site. The Secretary shall consider the following functions of said
COE when making his determination: (1) Certification of operators
of unmanned aerial systems during annual training periods; (2) De-
velopment of doctrine, tactics, techniques, and procedures for the
operation of such systems; (3) Experimentation on integrating arti-
ficial intelligence applications for target recognition and real-time
situational awareness into the operation of such systems; and (4)
Conduct of force-on-force unmanned aerial systems exercises, in-
cluding brigade-level ‘‘drone wars’’ experimentation integrated with
infantry, armor, and joint formations.
Enabling integration of additional capabilities into Inte-
grated Battle Command System
The proliferation of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and one-
way attack unmanned aerial systems, combined with the prospect
of raid-sized and prolonged attacks, places a premium on inte-
grated air and missile defense architectures that maximize
battlespace awareness, improve shot doctrine, and preserve ad-
vanced interceptor inventories. The Army’s Integrated Battle Com-
mand System (IBCS) is the Army’s primary effort to realize an
any-sensor, best-interceptor architecture that can integrate addi-
tional sensors and effectors, expand the defended area, and im-
prove magazine depth by matching the most appropriate inter-
ceptor to each threat.
The Army’s current approach to integrating sensors and effectors
into the IBCS focuses on ‘‘1–N’’ integration. Instead, the Army
should consider a more agile and scalable approach that enables
the concurrent integration of multiple sensors and effectors
through open architecture, leveraging software-driven development,
and close collaboration with industry partners. The committee en-
courages the Army to accelerate the integration of joint and allied
sensors and effectors.
The committee directs the Secretary of the Army to provide a
briefing, not later than February 26, 2027, to the Committees on
Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives, on
efforts to accelerate the integration of the IBCS. The briefing shall
include: (1) An update on progress on integrating the IBCS; (2) A
description of barriers, including cost, to expanding integration ef-
forts; (3) A discussion on operational lessons incorporated from re-
cent conflicts into integration efforts; (4) A description of how the
Army is leveraging the IBCS to improve shot doctrine, conserve ad- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

vanced interceptors, and sustain magazine depth during protracted
operations; and (5) How the service intends to expand the number
of allies and partners that are acquiring and deploying the IBCS
to strengthen missile defense integration across theaters of oper-

Evaluation of wing-in-ground effect craft
The Department of Defense requires a range of flexible, surviv-
able, and rapidly deployable mobility platforms to support distrib-
uted operations, contested logistics, and maritime maneuvers
across multiple theaters.
The committee understands that the Marine Corps has under-
taken development, prototyping, and operational evaluation activi-
ties related to wing-in-ground effect craft as part of broader efforts
to support logistics for Stand-In Forces and Marine Littoral Regi-
ments. The committee views these efforts as a valuable contribu-
tion to the Department’s broader understanding of the potential
military utility of wing-in-ground craft in making a contribution to
solving the contested logistics problems facing the Department.
The committee directs the Secretary of the Navy to submit a re-
port to the congressional defense committees, not later than March
1, 2027, on the Department’s assessment of wing-in-ground effect
craft. The report should include the following:
(1) An overview of the Department’s plans for experimen-
tation, testing, and evaluation activities related to wing-in-
ground effect craft across the military departments and com-
batant commands;
(2) An assessment of potential operational roles for such
platforms in support of joint missions, including distributed
maritime operations, logistics support, special operations, and
maritime interdiction;
(3) A description of how the Department may be considering
the integration of wing-in-ground effect craft into joint and
service-level concepts of operations;
(4) An assessment of potential advantages associated with
wing-in-ground effect craft, including survivability,
sustainment, basing, interoperability, and command and con-
trol considerations;
(5) A projection of the resources that would be required to
support further experimentation, concept development, and po-
tential integration of wing-in-ground effect craft into joint oper-
ations; and
(6) A discussion of any policy, acquisition, or regulatory bar-
riers that could affect development, testing, or operational em-
ployment of wing-in-ground effect craft.

The committee recognizes the importance of the National Guard’s
FireGuard program in equipping State National Guard units to de-
tect wildfires, notify authorities, and develop products for dissemi-
nation to

provisions.heading: Artillery Rocket System Integration
provisions.text:
The committee notes that the Ground-Launched Small Diameter
Bomb (GLSDB) program represents an innovative and cost-effec-
tive capability developed by industry at significant private expense,
including the establishment of dedicated production infrastructure
without initial government investment. The program demonstrates
a strong approach to diversifying and strengthening the defense in-
dustrial base by combining established prime contractors with new
market entrants, creating a more resilient and competitive supply
chain that complements efforts such as the Guided Multiple
Launch Rocket System—Extended Range.
The committee further recognizes the significant export potential
of this capability, which can enhance allied interoperability and
strengthen partner nation deterrence at lower cost and with rapid
fielding potential.
Additionally, the committee highlights the successful integration
of GLSDB with the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, sup-
ported through reconciliation and developmental funding, and
notes the expectation for continued rapid progress toward oper-
ational deployment. This effort underscores the value of leveraging
existing platforms with advanced munitions to deliver affordable,
scalable, and near-term combat capability for the Joint Force and
allied partners.
Increasing and diversifying munitions inventories
The committee supports the Department of Defense’s efforts to
increase production capacity for critical munitions. However, the
committee is concerned that the Department’s proposals largely
focus on expanding output along existing, traditional production
lines and do not sufficiently broaden the industrial base or diver-
sify the inventory with affordable, mass producible munitions. A
more balanced mix of munitions combining exquisite capabilities
with affordable, mass-produced systems is needed to reset the eco-
nomics of ‘‘cost-per-kill’’ and ensure sufficient magazine depth for
sustained operations. In support of these initiatives, the National
Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Public Law 119–
60) provided the Department with multiyear procurement author- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

ity for multiple lower cost weapons programs to generate a con-
sistent demand signal for lower-cost munitions providers.
However, the committee believes the Department needs to have
additional lower cost munitions to complement exquisite capabili-
ties, diversify munitions inventory, and mitigate risks associated
with insufficient capacity to effectively sustain long-range fires in
a protracted conflict. The Department, in coordination with the
services, should increase capacity by providing a multi-year de-
mand signal through multiple complementary affordable, mass pro-
ducible munitions programs of record, and the accelerated identi-
fication and scaling of production-ready capabilities. Additionally,
the committee believes that the Department should consider afford-
ability and manufacturability in developing the Department’s mu-
nitions requirements.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to pro-
vide a briefing to the congressional defense committees, not later
than January 1, 2027, on munitions programs. The briefing shall,
at a minimum, address the following:
(1) The total munitions requirements over the future years
defense program for all munitions, including the quantities
needed to meet urgent, high-volume surge capacity in the
event of conflict;
(2) The planned total munitions inventory over the future
years defense program for all programmed munitions;
(3) An identification of production-ready lower cost muni-
tions that could be capable of closing identified inventory gaps
that the Department has assessed for affordability and capa-
bility of scaling production quantities; and
(4) A detailed strategy for implementing a mixture of exquisite
and affordable munitions to fill munitions requirements.

provisions.heading: Long Range Fires acquisition strategy
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the high importance of next generation
artillery rounds, such as the M1128 and XM1113, to deliver in-
creased range to the warfighter. The committee also understands
the need to expeditiously scale production of these rounds to re-
plenish depleted artillery war stocks. Additionally, the committee
understands the complexity of the supply chain to deliver critical
rounds to the warfighter.
The committee directs the Secretary of the Army to provide a re-
port, not later than March 31, 2027, to the Committees on Armed
Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives on the
Army acquisition strategy for the procurement of M1128 and
XM1113 artillery rounds.
Navy destroyer production
The committee notes that the Navy plans to begin advance pro-
curement of a battleship program in fiscal year 2027, called the
BBG(X). This effort is to design and build a ship that would carry
a high capacity of offensive missiles in addition to Standard Missile
air defense weapons.
For several years, the Navy has been designing a follow-on to the
Arleigh Burke-class destroyers (DDG–51). The program is called
the DDG(X) program. The goal of this effort is to provide major up- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

grades to the current destroyer design and continue to build de-
stroyers to replace the early DDG–51 destroyers that are approach-
ing the end of their useful service lives. These ships will begin re-
tiring at a rate of three to five per year starting in the mid-2030s.
Initial estimates of the unit cost of the BBG(X) are between
$12.0 billion and $13.0 billion. At that price point, the Navy cannot
afford to replace retiring DDG–51s with BBG(X) battleships on a
one-for-one basis.
Therefore, the committee believes that:
(1) The Navy needs to continue work on the DDG(X) pro-
gram so it will have options for replacing the early DDG–51s
when their useful service lives have expired;
(2) Work on the DDG(X) program needs to continue along
roughly the same schedule as was envisioned last year; and
(3) Design and construction of the BBG(X) should not sup-
plant the important work that needs to continue on the
DDG(X).
Networked autonomous kinetic capability against small un-
manned aerial systems
The committee recognizes that recent conflicts have dem-
onstrated the rapid proliferation, increased lethality, and evolving
sophistication of Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aircraft systems
(UAS) to include First-Person-View drones and coordinated swarm-
ing tactics capable of targeting across the battlefield. The com-
mittee notes that these threats have proven increasingly resilient
against current countermeasures and have exposed significant
vulnerabilities across the force.
The committee notes that many existing Department of Defense
counter-UAS investments have focused on high-cost, low-density
air defense solutions that are not suitable for broad deployment
across formations. The committee is concerned that efforts to adapt
legacy remote weapon stations for counter-UAS missions have not
produced scalable or sufficiently autonomous capabilities needed to
protect maneuver and sustainment formations in contested envi-
ronments.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Secretary of the Army
to establish requirements for a networked, autonomous kinetic
counter-UAS capability designed to protect ground combat, support,
and on-the-move formations against Group 1 and Group 2 UAS
threats. Such capabilities should seek to minimize soldier cognitive
burden, leverage common-service weapons and existing platform
architectures where feasible, enable autonomous and robotic oper-
ations, and provide a cost-effective solution suitable for large-scale
deployment across tactical formations.
The committee directs the Secretary of the Army to provide a
briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and
the House of Representatives, not later than February 26, 2027, on
the assessment of current capability gaps, integration challenges,
and operational requirements associated with fielding scalable au-
tonomous counter-UAS protection systems for maneuver and
sustainment formations. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Non-kinetic effectors for point defense
The committee appreciates the Department of Defense’s focus on
counter-unmanned aerial systems (UAS) technology evaluation and
investment in preparing for emerging threats. However, repeated
reports of drone incursions at critical Air Force installations in the
Homeland and abroad causes the committee to be concerned that
the Air Force’s investments in counter-UAS technologies for air
base air defense systems (ABADS) are insufficient.
Of particular note is the Air Force’s lack of plans to employ non-
kinetic effectors for point defense. The committee encourages the
Air Force to accelerate the evaluation and potential deployment of
non-kinetic effectors, such as high power microwave systems, to de-
fend critical points against UAS threats.
The committee directs the Chief of Staff of the Air Force, in co-
ordination with the Commander of Air Combat Command, to de-
liver a briefing to the congressional defense committees, not later
than March 1, 2027, that includes:
(1) A summary of existing non-kinetic solutions for critical
point defense under the ABADS architecture and plans for the
evaluation of emerging technologies, such as high power micro-
wave systems;
(2) An analysis of options for accelerating the adoption of
non-kinetic effectors for critical point defense, as well as associ-
ated resourcing requirements;
(3) A review of interagency barriers impeding the rapid de-
ployment of non-kinetic effectors in domestic airspace, includ-
ing efforts to alleviate such barriers alongside interagency
stakeholders; and
(4) Any further matters deemed necessary by the Chief of
Staff.
This report should be unclassified but may include a classified
annex.

System swarms
The committee recognizes the Department of Defense’s efforts to
develop low-cost Counter-small Unmanned Aerial Systems (C–

that defending personnel and infrastructure in high-collateral
areas requires cost-effective, non-kinetic technology with multi-tar-

committee observes that aerial non-kinetic effectors with high-pow-

nical maturity but have received only incremental funding since
2019. The committee believes that transitioning such capabilities
from prototypes to a program of record is essential to achieving

The committee directs the Secretary of Defense to provide a
briefing, not later than February 26, 2027, to the Committees on
Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives on

procurement of low-collateral, non-kinetic solutions for C–sUAS

The committee recognizes the significant contributions of
Watervliet Army Arsenal as a historic and critical component of the
organic industrial base, particularly in its longstanding role as the
only organic capability at scale for large- and medium-caliber can-

quirement for Watervliet Arsenal to remain the premier govern-
ment-owned, government-operated capability for the technical ex-
pertise and skilled labor that it currently provides, in addition to
the other services it provides in support of national defense and
combat readiness. The committee underscores that continued long-
term modernization efforts at Watervliet Arsenal and the Army’s

The committee is concerned that the Army does not have a suffi-

lenges in its organic industrial base—personnel shortages, aging
infrastructure, obsolete machinery, antiquated processes, incon-
sistent delivery schedules, and defective tubes due to poor raw ma-

Any changes in quality assurance processes related to raw material

Over-the-horizon targeting and operational authorities
The committee notes the increasing importance of over-the-hori-
zon targeting (OTH–T) capabilities to enable Joint Force operations
in contested and denied environments. OTH–T capabilities are es-
sential to providing timely, accurate, and resilient targeting data to
support long-range precision fires, maritime strikes, and integrated
deterrence objectives.
The committee is concerned by reports of potential disruptions to
existing OTH–T architectures, including uncertainties related to
the delineation and integration of activities conducted pursuant to
title 10, United States Code, and title 50, United States Code. The
committee recognizes that effective OTH–T often depends on close
coordination between military operational forces and intelligence
community elements. However, ambiguity in roles, responsibilities,
resourcing, and oversight mechanisms may create seams that could
degrade operational readiness and combat effectiveness.
The committee directs the Secretary of Defense to ensure that
OTH–T capabilities required for operational plans remain fielded,
interoperable, and resilient during any transition to future systems
or programs of record.
To that end, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in
coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, to provide
a briefing to the congressional defense and intelligence committees,
not later than July 1, 2027, on:
(1) The current architecture supporting OTH–T for combat-
ant commanders, including dependencies on title 50 authorities
or intelligence community capabilities;
(2) Any identified or projected gaps or disruptions to OTH–
T capability over the future years defense program;
(3) Current research, development, test, and evaluation ef-
forts to improve OTH–T capabilities;
(4) The Department of Defense’s plan to transition critical
OTH–T capabilities into enduring programs of record, where
appropriate;
(5) Governance mechanisms to clarify title 10 and title 50
roles and responsibilities for OTH–T-related activities; and
(6) Steps being taken to ensure uninterrupted operational
support to combatant commanders during capability transi-
tions.
Rapid integration of weapons onto fighter aircraft
The committee recognizes the growing need to rapidly integrate
advanced weapons and capabilities onto fielded aircraft to respond
to evolving threats and sustain combat power in high-intensity con-
flict. The committee notes that current delays associated with the
integration of new weapons, software, and subsystems onto legacy
aircraft platforms due to limited government software engineering
capacity and proprietary operational flight program (OFP) architec-
tures. These delays result in slowing the fielding of critical capa-
bilities to U.S. and allied warfighters. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Such approaches could enable more rapid integration of weapons

provisions.heading: Lighting System
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the importance of the Expeditionary
Airfield Lighting System (EALS) in supporting Agile Combat Em-
ployment and operations from austere and dispersed airfields, such
as those in U.S. Indo-Pacific Command. While the current EALS
configuration provides energy-efficient lighting capable of battery
and solar operation, it continues to rely on wired command and E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

The committee is concerned that, even when configured for
standalone self-power battery and solar operation, the system con-
tinues to rely on wired command and control cabling and also lacks
remote health and status monitoring capability. The committee is
concerned that continued reliance on wired systems reduces deploy-
ment agility, increases logistics burden and constrains rapid recon-
figuration of expeditionary airfields. Similarly, the lack of remote
health and status monitoring increases the risk of degradation and
reduced readiness when deployed. The committee understands that
the Department of the Air Force has identified this capability gap
as a formal deficiency within the program.
The committee understands that industry has developed, and the
Air Force has validated, a secure wireless control and monitoring
capability to address this deficiency. The committee strongly en-
courages the Air Force to pursue the incorporation of this capa-
bility into the EALS system.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force
to provide a briefing to the congressional defense committees, not
later than January 1, 2027, on the opportunities that exist to ad-
dress the reliance on wired command and control cabling and lack
of remote health and status monitoring capabilities. The briefing
should include, but not be limited to, the following:
(1) A transition and acquisition strategy for incorporating
said wireless control and monitoring capability into future
EALS procurements, including key decision points and con-
tracting approach; and

upgrade kits or other retrofit approaches to enable the incorpo-

Sec. 211—Improving the requirement for an alternative test

The committee recommends a provision that would amend sec-

Year 2026 (Public Law 119–60) to clarify that Software Acquisition
Pathways under section 3603 of title 10, United States Code, are

Sec. 212—Development, test, evaluation, demonstration, and
transition to production of alternative low-cost weapon
systems
The committee recommends a provision that would direct the
Secretary of Defense to initiate and pursue accelerated acquisition
programs for alternative low-cost systems in eight critical cat-
egories: (1) Alternative low-cost hypersonic strike systems; (2) Al-
ternative low-cost cruise missiles; (3) Alternative shoulder-launched
missiles; (4) Alternative extended range munitions; (5) Alternative
mid-range integrated air and missile defense (IAMD) interceptors;
(6) Alternative exoatmospheric interceptors; (7) Alternative short-
range IAMD interceptors; and (8) Alternative medium-range air-to-
air missiles.
The committee is concerned by the high expenditure of precision-
guided munitions and interceptors during recent operations. These
expenditures rapidly depleted stocks of weapons that cost millions
of dollars per unit and have production lead times measured in
years, often exceeding 3 years from contract award to the delivery
of additional inventory.
Many of these systems were originally designed and developed
decades ago to meet the most demanding high-end threat require-
ments against peer adversaries. While they have performed very ef-
fectively, they were not optimized for manufacturability, rapid
scalability, or cost-effective mass production. As a result, the
United States now faces challenges in rapidly replenishing inven-

continue to play a critical role against the most sophisticated
threats. However, the Department also needs complementary, al-
ternative, and low-cost weapon systems that can fulfill the majority
of mission requirements in many scenarios, provide survivability
and attrition tolerance for the high-end inventory, create necessary
magazine depth for sustained operations, and enable rapid replen-

of commercial supply chains and components, modular designs, and

provisions.heading: Defense Experimental Program to Stimulate Competitive
provisions.text:
Research
The committee notes that in the section 4201 table for Research,
Development, Test, and Evaluation, Defense-wide, there is an in-
crease to PE 61110D8Z, Basic Research Initiatives, of $40.0 million
for the Defense Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Re-
search (DEPSCoR) program.
The committee continues to be supportive of the DEPSCoR pro-
gram, which helps build and expand the national innovation base
for research and education by funding research activities in science
and engineering areas responsive to the needs of national defense.
The committee welcomes the fact that DEPSCoR was included as
part of the budget request for fiscal year 2027 but notes that the
amount was well below levels requested by the Congress for the
past several years. The program is intended to increase the number
of university researchers and improve the capabilities of institu-
tions of higher education in eligible jurisdictions to perform com-
petitive research relevant to the Department of Defense (DOD).
The committee also views DEPSCoR as a component in any effort
by the DOD to identify, shape, and foster innovation ecosystems
that support DOD research and technology needs. Along with other
funding programs and authorities available to the Department,
DEPSCoR should be considered as a means to expand and diversify
the innovation ecosystem for the DOD.

to restore funding reductions to these lines and increase support
for microelectronics development; standards development; and vali-

Defense (DOD), especially in areas of advanced packaging and for
microelectronics materials other than traditional silicon-based sys-
tems, such as gallium nitride, silicon germanium, and silicon car-
bide.
The committee notes its disappointment at the DOD’s short-
sighted decision to reduce these programs by $392.4 million and
$81.6 million, respectively. The committee believes such reductions
threaten the ability of the Department to fully capitalize on the
foundational investments made as part of the Chips and Science
Act to help reinvigorate the domestic industrial base for microelec-
tronics, and to continue to invest in the new and novel devices and
packaging techniques the DOD needs to compete with adversaries
in the future information environment. The needs of the DOD are
unique compared to commercial microelectronics, and while the De-
partment can ride the wave of such investments, it also needs par-
allel and complementary investment to deal with challenges like
radiation hardening, new and novel materials, and innovative de-
sign and packaging approaches. The committee believes that addi-
tional prototyping activities that can be demonstrated through the
Microelectronics Commons program will help transition more capa-
bilities into the hands of the warfighter and may have spillover
benefits for the domestic commercial microelectronics sector.
Further, the committee notes that the Department still has sig-

assurance techniques as a complement to existing security ap-
proaches. The committee also notes that with the recent update of
the charter for the Joint Federated Assurance Center, there are in-
creasing opportunities to leverage those capabilities within the
Government, as well as with key industry partners. Additional re-
sources will assist with that expansion of activities.
The committee also encourages the DOD to leverage these addi-
tional activities to support the development of resilience in the sup-
ply chain for microelectronics, like diversifying the printed circuit
board supply chain, and to demonstrate new interconnect tech-
nologies to increase device throughput and performance. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

by Army watercraft conducting logistics, maneuver, and

unmanned systems, and indirect fires.
The committee believes the Army should possess an indigenous
unmanned surface vessel (USV) capability to escort and support
Army watercraft, providing enhanced force protection, early warn-

The committee commends the Army’s use of competitive experi-

(2) An assessment of existing and emerging autonomy tech-
nologies, including commercially available solutions from U.S.
industry, relevant to escort, sensing, and force protection mis-
sions;
(3) A summary of ongoing experimentation and prototyping

Briefing on use of high-power nuclear fission for space oper-
ations

provisions.heading: Joint Emergent Technology Supplying On-Orbit Nuclear Power
provisions.text:
(JETSON) program and recognizes high-power nuclear fission as a
critical component of sustained U.S. preeminence in space. The
committee notes prior investment in early-stage demonstration pro-
grams, including the Kilopower Reactor Using Stirling Technology
program. However, the committee is concerned that the Depart-
ment of Defense has not yet established clear operational require-
ments, validated mission needs, or developed an execution pathway
to transition these technologies into operational in-space nuclear
fission power capabilities.
As the Department’s reliance on maneuverable and power-inten-
sive systems increases, enduring and resilient power generation
will be essential to support missile intercept, offensive and defen-
sive space control, long-duration mobility, high-duty-cycle sensing,
secure communications, and autonomous operations. The com-
mittee believes that without defined operational requirements, a
coordinated acquisition strategy, and a funded plan for maturation
and testing, the Department will be unable to field nuclear fission
power systems necessary to sustain U.S. military advantage in
space.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force,
in coordination with the Director of the Defense Advanced Re-
search Projects Agency and the Chief of Space Operations, to brief
the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of
Representatives, not later than March 1, 2027, on the Depart-
ment’s plan to develop and field operational nuclear fission power
systems for in-space operations. The briefing shall include: (1)
Operational nuclear fission power requirements across anticipated
missions, including in low earth orbit, mid-earth orbit, geosynchro-
nous orbit, cislunar space, and other deep-space environments; (2)
An assessment of barriers and capability gaps that have prevented
JETSON or other nuclear fission efforts from conducting in-space
deployment and testing; (3) An overview of previous congressional
funding and Department expenditure related to in-space nuclear
fission capabilities since fiscal year 2017; (4) A proposed architec-
ture and acquisition pathway for operational in-space nuclear fis-
sion power capabilities, including technology maturation mile-
stones, test and evaluation plans, and integration with Space Force
programs; and (5) A funding and resource plan identifying required
investments through fiscal year 2035, including opportunities for
interagency and commercial collaboration.

ical evacuation and other high-risk operational tasks

ments, which have complicated the execution of medical evacu-
ation, mine detection, and emergency response operations. Tradi-

to both wounded servicemembers and responding forces while po-
tentially delaying life-saving care. Autonomous and semi-autono-
mous robotic systems, including unmanned ground vehicles, hybrid
platforms, and humanoid or semi-humanoid systems, have the po-

To ensure the quick integration of robotics and other autonomous
and semi-autonomous systems into the hands of warfighting units

(4) Specifically for medical missions, an assessment of the

operational resilience, and the availability of bioindustrial mate-

ards. The committee encourages a review of military specifications
(MIL–SPEC), which establish standardized technical requirements

provisions.heading: Environmental Security Technology Certification Program
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the significant success of the Environ-
mental Security Technology Certification Program (ESTCP) in
identifying, demonstrating, and transitioning innovative tech-
nologies that improve military capability, installation resilience,
energy security, and environmental performance. The committee
notes that ESTCP has proven effective in validating emerging tech-
nologies in operational environments, accelerating technology adop-
tion, reducing lifecycle costs, strengthening mission assurance, and
enhancing military readiness across the Armed Forces.
The committee further recognizes the value of ESTCP-supported
projects focused on energy resilience and infrastructure moderniza-
tion at National Guard facilities operating in harsh cold-weather
environments. The committee notes that these projects are helping
evaluate and demonstrate resilient energy technologies, advanced
microgrid capabilities, distributed energy resources, and high-effi-
ciency heating and energy systems designed to improve reliability,
reduce operational energy costs, and support continued mission op-
erations during severe weather events and grid disruptions. The
committee believes these demonstrations provide scalable models
that can strengthen energy security and installation resilience
across other Department of Defense facilities facing similar envi-
ronmental and infrastructure challenges. The committee encour-
ages the Department of Defense to continue investing in ESTCP
projects as a mechanism for improving operational effectiveness
and enhancing installation resilience across the military depart-
ments. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment, the Vice Chairman of
the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Direct Reporting Program Manager
for Golden Dome for America, and the Director of the Missile De-

In preparing this briefing, the Under Secretary should evaluate,

The viability of unmanned systems to simulate adversarial missile
