High-altitude warfare strategy
The committee recognizes the stratosphere as an emerging, com-
petitive, and largely unclaimed operational domain with significant
potential to provide resilient, near-space capability across sensing,
communications, positioning, navigation, command and control,
and effects delivery in contested environments. The committee
views high-altitude capabilities as a critical layer in a diversified
and survivable architecture aligned with the National Defense
Strategy’s emphasis on mass, scale, and deterrence through denial
using low-cost, attritable systems.
While the Department of Defense has made sustained invest-
ments in stratospheric platforms, including high-altitude balloons,
pseudo-satellites, and other unmanned systems, the committee is
concerned that fragmented funding, limited coordination, and the
absence of a unified acquisition strategy have slowed the transition
of these capabilities from experimentation to operational, scalable
use. The committee further notes that high-altitude balloon sys-
tems, in particular, offer a cost-effective, persistent capability, but
the Department has not fielded any of them at scale or adequately
integrated them into operational planning.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Under Secretary of De-
fense for Research and Engineering, in coordination with the
Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment and
with inputs from the geographic combatant commands, to provide
a briefing to the congressional defense committees, not later than
March 31, 2027, on a comprehensive concept for sustained high-al-
titude and stratospheric operations.

support

sociated with sustaining distributed maritime forces across the vast
distances of the Indo-Pacific theater. In particular, the ability to
move critical supplies, equipment, and mission payloads between
forward locations while minimizing risk to crewed platforms will be
essential to maintaining operational resilience in a contested envi-
ronment. The committee believes that long-range unmanned under-
water vehicles (UUVs) offer significant potential to augment exist-

Use of non-destructive inspection and automated defect rec-
ognition techniques in the Department of Defense
The committee is concerned that current U.S. Marine Corps body
armor inspection systems rely on two-dimensional x-ray scans and
manual testing, which often miss defects and structural issues, are
slow and laborious, and involve inefficient life-cycle management
processes. Modern computed tomography technology, supported by
artificial intelligence, can enable rapid and comprehensive three-di-
mensional scanning of body armor and increase the detection of de-
fects, delamination, and other structural issues through non-de-
structive inspection (NDI) and automated defect recognition (ADR).
These capabilities have the potential to enhance warfighter protec-
tion and military readiness, avoid unnecessary replacement costs,
and support faster, data-driven decisions. The committee notes
modern NDI and ADR capabilities have been successfully dem-
onstrated through academic partners.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to pro-
vide a briefing to the congressional defense committees, not later
than December 1, 2026, on the feasibility of expanding the use of
these capabilities across the Department. The briefing shall include
the following: (1) The readiness risk of outdated armor inspection
systems in the military departments; (2) Potential avenues to adopt
NDI and ADR for body armor in the military departments; (3) An
assessment of using NDI and ADR in inspecting other forms of
military materiel; (4) The feasibility and advisability of estab-
lishing multi-site pilot programs for automated or high-throughput
armor NDI and ADR; and (5) An assessment of the feasibility and
advisability of creating an NDI/ADR Center of Excellence to de-
velop standard operating procedures, training, and regular per-
formance reporting with key performance parameters related to
NDI and ADR approaches.

provisions.heading: Items of Special Interest
provisions.text:
Arctic domain awareness
The committee notes that the rapid strategic emergence of the
Arctic region presents an urgent multi-domain national security
challenge, demanding enhanced domain awareness to ensure navi-
gational safety and strategic deterrence against peer adversaries.
The Department of Defense’s 2024 Arctic Strategy explicitly ac-
knowledges that the Joint Force’s primary operational barrier is
the environment itself, which is further hampered by a lack of lo-
calized sensors and data needed to accurately forecast and adapt
to longer-term climate projections. This deficit creates dangerous
intelligence gaps and operational security vulnerabilities, as dem-
onstrated during recent drone trials in Alaska and exercise Arctic
Edge 2025, where sub-zero temperatures down to ¥20°C and se-
vere magnetic distortions caused rapid battery degradation, instru-
mentation failures, and navigation disruptions, limiting the endur-
ance of autonomous systems and potentially masking adversary
submarine or research vessel incursions.
To mitigate these gaps, the committee believes the Department
must transition from isolated test cycles to a scalable network of
resilient monitoring infrastructure by leveraging existing facility,
human, and technological resources already established. Creating
an integrated ‘‘Arctic Watchtower’’ network framework will allow
the Department to collaboratively gather continuous data sets,
field-test cold-resistant unmanned aerial vehicles and autonomous
underwater vehicles, and rapidly insert mature sensing tech-
nologies into remote frontier sites. This persistent, place-based re-
search and monitoring footprint is vital to providing the Joint
Force with the close-to-real-time environmental intelligence and
multi-domain awareness required to maintain an uncontested stra-
tegic posture in the polar regions. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to pro-
vide a briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate
and the House of Representatives, not later than February 28,
2027, on the Department’s strategy to field resilient monitoring
networks and overcome domain awareness gaps in the Arctic. The
briefing shall include: (1) Current and future requirements to en-
sure Arctic domain awareness; (2) Current and planned autono-
mous detection and tracking systems; (3) An assessment of current
capability gaps regarding material fatigue, battery life, communica-
tions, data integration and processing, and navigation disruptions
in polar environments; (4) A plan to expand layered sensing net-
works by utilizing geographically remote frontier sites and existing
gateway research infrastructure; (5) A framework for scaling inter-
agency, academic, and tribal collaborations, including the Arctic
Watchtower network concept; and (6) Recommendations on miti-
gating existing capability gaps and improving Arctic domain aware-
ness.

provisions.heading: Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast services for
provisions.text:
Air Force flying installations
The committee is concerned by reports that Automatic Depend-
ent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS–B) service contracts at Air Force
installations within the United States, including Luke Air Force
Base, Arizona, are approaching renewal and that the Air Force
may shift responsibility for funding these services to individual in-
stallations. The committee notes that ADS–B capabilities are crit-
ical to the safe integration of military and civilian aircraft oper-
ating within the National Airspace System and provide enhanced
situational awareness, aircraft identification, and air traffic
deconfliction capabilities for military air traffic controllers and air-
crews.
The committee further notes that ADS–B capabilities support the
safe and efficient flow of military and civilian air traffic operating
in the region, including aircraft utilizing multiple civilian airports.
The committee believes that access to ADS–B services should be
sustained through a deliberate, enterprise-wide strategy that en-
sures continued aviation safety, operational readiness, and training
effectiveness across Air Force flying installations.
Therefore, the committee urges the Secretary of the Air Force to
assure multi-year, funded access to ADS–B services by all U.S. Air
Force flying units to ensure deconfliction of civilian and military
aircraft operating in the United States.
Autonomous or remote-controlled self-propelled railcars
The committee notes that the Army operates and maintains more
than 1,000 miles of railroad track across 60 installations and up-
ward of 140 diesel locomotives to support heavy equipment, muni-
tions, and materiel movements, primarily for switching operations
on base. Significant reductions in U88 rail specialists since 2015
have resulted in delays and cancellations of equipment for training
and rehearsals. According to the Government Accountability Office
report, published August 23, 2021, titled ‘‘Defense Transportation:

Briefing on defense reactor spent fuel management
Given the Department of Defense’s stated plans to deploy nuclear
reactors on military installations, the committee believes that the
Department of Defense should fully assess and share with the Con-
gress its plans for managing used nuclear fuel.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in
coordination with the Secretary of Energy and the Chair of the Nu-
clear Regulatory Commission, to submit a briefing to the Commit-
tees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representa-
tives, not later than March 1, 2027, on the Department of Defense’s
framework for managing spent nuclear fuel associated with its de-
ployment of nuclear power systems, including the expected quan-
tities, characteristics, and lifecycle profiles of spent fuel and associ-
ated high-level waste streams. The briefing shall include: (1) An as-
sessment of the expected quantities, characteristics, and lifecycle
profiles of used nuclear fuel and associated high-level waste
streams, including advanced fuel forms, generated by projected De-
partment of Defense deployments of small modular reactors or
other advanced nuclear systems at installations and potential for-
ward or remote locations; (2) A description of current Department
of Defense and Department of Energy authorities, policies, and in-
frastructure applicable to the handling, transportation, storage, re-
cycling, reuse, or disposition of used nuclear fuel generated by such
systems; (3) An evaluation of logistical, sustainment, and security
considerations associated with used nuclear fuel management, in-
cluding challenges unique to forward or austere environments; (4)
An assessment of options to recycle, reuse, or otherwise extract
value from used nuclear fuel, including pathways such as material
recovery, fuel recycling, and waste minimization approaches to re-
duce long-term waste volumes, recover usable materials, or enable
future energy, industrial, or national security applications, con-
sistent with applicable law and safety requirements; (5) Identifica-
tion of potential future uses of used nuclear fuel that could support
Department of Defense missions, energy resilience, or broader na-
tional security objectives, including a discussion of technical, regu-
latory, and policy barriers to such uses; (6) Identification of oppor-
tunities to align Department of Defense initiatives, as appropriate
and consistent with applicable law, with Department of Energy Nu-
clear Lifecycle Innovation Campus efforts to strengthen domestic
fuel-cycle, advanced manufacturing, and waste-management capa-
bilities supporting defense requirements; and (7) Identification of
gaps in policy, planning, interagency coordination, or statutory au-
thority that could impede responsible deployment of nuclear power
systems or the effective management, recycling, or reuse of used
nuclear fuel by the Department of Defense.

multiple domains and echelons, including through live, virtual, and
constructive training environments supporting combat training cen-

Comptroller General recommendation on prepositioned as-
sets in Indo-Pacific Region
The Indo-Pacific region is of critical strategic importance to the
Department of Defense (DOD), and ensuring that the United States
has combat-ready and well-equipped forces with capabilities to pre-
vail against peer and near-peer competitors in the region is vital
to defense planning. The committee recognizes significant chal-
lenges inherent in operating in the Indo-Pacific region, including
management of prepositioned assets. However, the committee is
concerned about the lack of a comprehensive plan to address chal-
lenges and risks in managing prepositioned materiel in the Indo-
Pacific region.
The committee notes that the Government Accountability Office
(GAO) issued a report in June 2025, titled, ‘‘Defense
Prepositioning: DOD Should Develop a Plan to Address Challenges
in the Indo-Pacific Region and Report to Congress’’ (GAO–25–
106991C), that recommended the Secretary of Defense, in coordina-
tion with the Secretaries of the Army, Navy, and Air Force, the
Commandant of the Marine Corps, and the Commander, U.S. Indo-
Pacific Command, assess the extent of ongoing challenges in man-
aging prepositioned materiel in the Indo-Pacific region and develop
a comprehensive plan to address those challenges and risks related
to storage, maintenance, personnel shortages, and contractor sup-
port. The plan should include an estimate of the costs and expected
timeline for implementation.
The committee believes it will be important for the DOD to im-
plement the GAO’s recommendation in an expeditious manner to
bolster deterrence, enable rapid crisis response, and reduce reliance
on strategic sealift and airlift. Accordingly, the committee directs
the Secretaries of the military departments to submit any relevant
plans and implementation reports regarding the GAO recommenda-
tion to the congressional defense committees and the Comptroller
General of the United States, not later than March 1, 2027. Such
plans shall address the actions the military departments have
taken or plan to take to implement the GAO’s recommendation. If

provisions.heading: Fort Polk modernization
provisions.text:
The committee commends the Secretary of the Army for advanc-
ing the Army Transformation Initiative (ATI) to posture the force
for emerging and future threats, including peer and near-peer com-
petition across all domains. The committee recognizes that modern-
izing Combat Training Centers (CTCs), including Fort Polk, is a
critical enabler of this transformation and supports the Secretary’s
objective of ensuring formations are prepared to operate in com-
plex, contested environments. The committee further recognizes
that the evolving character of warfare—including contested com-
munications, cyber and electronic warfare, unmanned systems
threats, and degraded sustainment environments—underscores the
strategic importance of CTCs in generating readiness for large-
scale combat operations. Accordingly, the committee strongly en-
courages the Secretary to appropriately modernize Fort Polk’s
multi-domain capabilities in order to support training for large-
scale combat operations against near-peer adversaries.
Consistent with ATI objectives and Army manning guidance, the
committee also encourages the Army to prioritize CTCs for senior-
grade and high-experience personnel fills, ensuring the most quali-
fied leaders are assigned to Observer/Controller-Trainer, opposing
force, and enabling roles essential to high-fidelity training. The
committee further encourages the Army to prioritize available
endstrength growth to maximize adversary force, sustainment, and
enabling unit manning at CTCs and the Army’s highest-tempo and
deploying brigade combat teams.
Lastly, not later than March 1, 2027, the Secretary shall brief
the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of
Representatives on: (1) The progress of Fort Polk modernization;
(2) Force structure adjustments; (3) Adversary force and
sustainment manning improvements; (4) Required resources; (5)
Alignment with ATI objectives; and (6) Measurable impacts on

Ground fuel distribution system
The committee recognizes that both the Army and the Marine
Corps rely on ground fuel distribution systems that were largely
designed for permissive operating environments and are increas-
ingly challenged by contested logistics conditions.
The committee notes that the Marine Corps does not operate
heavy expanded mobility tactical truck fueler variants and instead
relies on medium tactical vehicle replacement fuel trucks and logis-
tics vehicle system replacement-towed legacy fuel tank trailers, pri-
marily the M970 family, for bulk fuel transport. The committee is
concerned that these trailer-based systems present survivability,
mobility, and operational risks in distributed and expeditionary op-
erations.
The committee further recognizes the Army’s Tactical Fuel Dis-
tribution System (TFDS) as a modular capability typically config-
ured to store and dispense approximately 3,000 to 5,000 gallons of
fuel per site, enabling more distributed and survivable fuel oper-
ations when compared to legacy bulk fuel tankers. The committee
believes TFDS-like capabilities are increasingly relevant to Marine
Corps operational concepts, including Expeditionary Advanced
Base Operations and Littoral Operations in a Contested Environ-
ment.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Secretary of Defense,
in coordination with the Secretary of the Army and the Secretary
of the Navy, to assess opportunities to expand the application of
modular and distributed fuel distribution capabilities, including
TFDS, to Marine Corps operations. Such an assessment should in-
clude consideration of integration with existing Marine Corps vehi-
cle fleets, expeditionary shelter and protection systems, and train-
ing at Combat Training Centers and Marine Corps training instal-
lations.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to pro-
vide a report to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate
and the House of Representatives, not later than February 1, 2027,
on efforts to modernize ground fuel distribution across the Joint
Force. The report shall address: (1) Current Army and Marine
Corps fuel distribution capabilities; (2) Survivability and mobility
challenges associated with legacy fuel tank trailers; (3) The appli-
cability of TFDS and similar modular systems to Marine Corps op-
erations; (4) Funding requirements and legal authorities needed to
expand such capabilities; and (5) A recommended path to transition
these systems into enduring programs of record where appropriate.

Intermittent fault detection and isolation technology
One of the major cost drivers for the Department of Defense
(DOD) is the maintenance of electronics and electrical systems that
control and operate a wide-ranging inventory of weapons and weap-
on systems. Related to this cost driver, the Department’s most re-
cent estimate (April 2022) is that nearly $5.5 billion in non-value-
added costs and over 383,254 non-mission capable days annually
were incurred as the result of operationally induced intermittent
electronic faults that could not be identified and isolated. When a
failed system is tested with legacy equipment the Services have
been using for nearly 20 years, the result is almost always ‘‘No
Fault Found,’’ ‘‘Cannot Duplicate,’’ or ‘‘No Trouble Found’’—essen-
tially false readings to the effect that there is no problem even for
a non-functioning weapon system.
A DOD report to Congress, dated October 5, 2021, titled, ‘‘Assess-
ment of Electronics Maintenance as a Leading Driver of Weapon
Systems Non-Availability,’’ stated that ‘‘there is an available test
technology that could detect and reverse the intermittent fault
problem across the spectrum of DoD weapons systems,’’ with the
initial targets being various aircraft, including the F–35, F–16, and
F/A–18. Additionally, a January 2020 Government Accountability
Office (GAO) report, ‘‘Military Depots: DoD Can Benefit from Fur-
ther Sharing of Best Practices and Lessons Learned’’ (GAO–20–
116), highlighted the major improvements in flight hours, repair
times, and cost savings that resulted from the use of this tech-
nology. The GAO report specifically describes the Intermittent
Fault Detection and Isolation System (IFDIS) produced by a single
vendor. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

The committee commends the DOD for attempting to address
this issue by implementing and funding a related component of the
Rapid Sustainment Improvement Program (RSIP), which was in-
tended to pull readily available commercial solutions, such as
IFDIS, into the sustainment enterprise to reduce costs and improve
readiness. However, the Services, with the exception of the Air
Force, effectively ignored the direction of the DOD and this com-
mittee to acquire the technology (IFDIS) that has been proven to
successfully address this issue and either: (1) In the case of the
Navy, used the RSIP funding to acquire equipment that does not
successfully address the problem; or (2) In the case of the Army,
simply used the funds to ‘‘study’’ the problem, as opposed to solving
it. The committee strongly believes that meaningful funding for
RSIP should be restored with aggressive oversight, by the Sec-

Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, not

of RSIP, specifically identifying the programs and technologies for
inclusion in RSIP and a specific plan for oversight of the Services
for implementation of RSIP components within their enterprise. In
the event that RSIP is not reestablished, the committee directs the
Secretary to allocate sufficient funds to materially address the seri-
ous issue of ‘‘No Fault Found’’ as specified in the DOD’s October
2021 report and in the GAO’s 2020 report as described above. The
committee believes this issue is solvable with readily available
technology and that its resolution is long overdue to alleviate high-

Photovoltaic modules and inverters report
The committee is concerned that the Department of Defense has
issued Buy America waivers to purchase photovoltaic modules from
foreign sources when domestic supplies exist. The committee con-

Report on use of unmanned, autonomous systems for main-
tenance and logistics
The committee recognizes how the extensive use and integration
of unmanned systems for resupply, precision delivery and maritime
logistics in the Ukraine War and Operation Epic Fury have dem-
onstrated how uncrewed systems can enhance resilience, reduce
risk to personnel, and sustain distributed forces in contested envi-
ronments where traditional resupply methods are vulnerable or im-
practical. The committee is especially concerned that the Depart-
ment of Defense (DOD) lacks a clearly defined and resourced path-
way for using unmanned aerial systems for ship-to-shore and ship-
to-ship logistics across the naval and Joint Force. As the United
States prepares for potential crises in the Indo-Pacific—an oper-
ating environment characterized by vast distances and increased
threats to manned logistics platforms—the committee believes that
the development and fielding of cheap, attritable, autonomous lo-
gistics capabilities is essential.
To ensure the continued experimentation of uncrewed logistics
capabilities in contested environments, the committee directs the
Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the Secretaries of the
Army, Navy, and Air Force, to provide a report and a briefing to
the congressional defense committees, not later than February 1,
2027, on gaps and opportunities related to uncrewed aerial, sur-
face, and undersea systems capable of supporting logistics and
maintenance missions, including overland delivery, ship-to-shore
transfer, and ship-to-ship resupply of critical parts, tools, repair
materials, and maintenance consumables. The report and briefing
should include, but not be limited to, the following:
(1) An assessment of the performance of currently fielded
uncrewed systems capable of supporting logistics and mainte-
nance missions, an assessment that should include a capability E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: United States Marine Forces Special Operations Command
provisions.text:
The committee is concerned that existing manning for U.S. Ma-
rine Forces Special Operations Command (MARSOC) is well below
its authorized end strength. The committee is concerned that this
shortfall in manning, particularly in high-demand, low-density
Military Occupational Specialties, challenges the ability of
MARSOC to meet growing demands from the geographic combatant
commanders. The committee notes that MARSOC, and the broader
special operations enterprise, plays an increasingly key role in De-
partment of Defense operations around the world, across the spec-
trum of competition and conflict, and believes that addressing the
shortfall in MARSOC manning should be addressed.
Therefore, not later than February 1, 2027, the committee directs
the Secretary of the Navy, in coordination with the Assistant Sec-
retary of Defense for Special Operations and Low Intensity Con-
flict, to provide the congressional defense committees with a brief-
ing on the plan to address unfilled military manning for MARSOC,
including a detailed description of any ongoing or planned actions
by the U.S. Marine Corps to increase manning allocated to
MARSOC, and identify any challenges to filling MARSOC man-
ning. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.text:
Assessment of Department of Defense space law require-
ments
The committee recognizes that operational demands in the space
domain have grown, including reliance on commercial integration,
allied and partner cooperation, and dual-use technologies. Strategic
competition increasingly includes efforts to shape legal and nor-
mative frameworks. The committee is concerned that current legal,
policy, and institutional structures within the Department of De-
fense may not have kept pace with the complexity of space oper-
ations.
The Department currently relies primarily on the office of the Air

provisions.heading: Force General Counsel and the Air Force Judge Advocate General’s
provisions.text:
Corps for legal support to space operations. The U.S. Space Force
lacks its own legal corps, formalized training pipeline, or enduring
mechanism to develop a specialized space law expertise. The grow-
ing complexity of international space law, civil-military partner-
ships, commercial integration, dual-use technologies, and industrial
base considerations require enhanced, domain-specific legal capac-
ity.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force,
in coordination with the Chief of Space Operations, the Com- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

and other relevant components, to conduct a comprehensive assess-

CATCH a Serial Offender program expansion
The committee remains committed to eradicating sexual harass-
ment across the Armed Forces, their adult dependents, Department
of Defense civilians, and veterans. Anonymous reports are an im-
portant tool in bringing forward voices that may otherwise feel
they may not be able to safely publicly report an incident, but in
some cases they may allow repeat offenders to avoid accountability.
In the context of sexual assault, the Department sought to address
this challenge through the Catch a Serial Offender (CATCH) pro-
gram. However, the committee notes that integrating sexual har-
assment complaints into the current architecture may present sig-
nificant structural challenges, as sexual harassment is not univer-
sally categorized as a criminal offense under broader State and
Federal law.
Therefore, the Committee directs the Secretary of Defense to sub-
mit a briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate
and the House of Representatives, not later than January 15, 2027,
on the feasibility of expanding the CATCH program to include sex-
ual harassment. The briefing shall include, at minimum, the fol-
lowing:
(1) An assessment of the feasibility of adding confidential or
informal reports of sexual harassment into the CATCH pro-
gram architecture;
(2) A detailed technical analysis of the changes that would
need to be made to the CATCH system to facilitate the inclu-
sion of sexual harassment reports;
(3) A detailed analysis of the specific statutory, regulatory,
or policy changes required to grant Military Criminal Inves-
tigative Organization agents or appropriate investigative bod-
ies access to the necessary databases to track sexual harass-
ment offenders; and
(4) Recommendations for alternative interagency procedures,
processes, or framework modifications that would yield the in-
tended result of tracking and identifying serial sexual harass-
ment offenders.

The committee recognizes that basic allowance for housing (BAH)

provisions.heading: The committee believes Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations
provisions.text:
(EMSO) are coordinated military actions to exploit, attack, protect,
and manage the electromagnetic environment (JP 3–85). EMSO is
a core competency of the Department of Defense (DOD), which re-
quires a trained cadre of competent warfighters and federal work-
force to achieve superiority across the Electromagnetic Spectrum
(EMS) enterprise. Modern military operations require that every
warfighter and DOD civilian serving in a mission support role
across each of the services should be required to learn about the
EMS in the same foundational way before specializing first by com-
petency, then by each military service, as Joint personnel, and fi-
nally as senior leaders.
The committee notes that modern military operations require
every warfighter to learn about the EMS in the same foundational
way. The committee recognizes the value of EMSO education and
encourages the military service academies to consider opportunities
to incorporate both core competency fundamentals and service-spe-
cific fundamentals into their curricula. Therefore, the committee di-
rects the Secretary of Defense to:
(1) Conduct a comprehensive survey of existing EMSO
courseware in service academies, Senior Service Colleges, and
the Joint Forces Staff College to determine alignment with re-
quirements for both core competency fundamentals and serv-
ice-specific fundamentals, including Joint Force EMSO and
Senior Leaders EMSO; and
(2) Provide a report to the congressional defense committees,
not later than December 31, 2027. The report shall include:
(a) Findings from the survey, specifically how/if existing
courseware aligns with Goal 3 of the Department of De-
fense Electromagnetic Spectrum Superiority Strategy
(2020), which emphasizes advancing EMSO education and
training to strengthen operational readiness;
(b) Recommendations for curriculum integration; and
(c) An assessment of associated costs required to imple-
ment EMSO curriculum across military educational insti-
tutions.
Duty status modernization
The committee recognizes ongoing efforts by the Department of
Defense, in coordination with the Congress, to streamline and mod-
ernize the wide range of duty statuses across the reserve compo- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

numerous duty statuses can create unnecessary complexity, limit
transparency, and result in inconsistent access to pay and benefits
for servicemembers.
The committee acknowledges that the Department is actively
working to develop proposals to consolidate and standardize duty
statuses in a manner that improves administrative efficiency while
maintaining appropriate distinctions in authorities and benefits.
The committee supports these efforts and expects continued en-
gagement with the Congress as proposals are refined. The com-
mittee notes that, despite the Department’s ongoing work, formal

due to delays in review by the Office of Management and Budget

The committee intends to continue working closely with the De-
partment to advance duty status modernization and emphasizes
the importance of timely, consistent communication to ensure legis-

shared objectives.
Expanding opportunities for veterans in emerging tech-
nologies
The committee directs the Secretary of Defense to submit to the
Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of
Representatives, not later than April 1, 2027, a report on expand-
ing training and career pathway opportunities in emerging tech-
nologies for separating servicemembers.
The report should include a feasibility assessment of creating an
Emerging Technologies Program to fund graduate, trade, or voca-
tional training for members of the Armed Forces who are sepa-
rating from active duty. The report should also assess how the De-
partment of Defense leverages programs such as the SkillBridge
Program and the Transition Assistance Program to expand infor-
mation, opportunities, and career pathways for separating
servicemembers in emerging technology and high-demand technical
fields, including but not limited to biotechnology and the geospatial
field.
The report should further examine opportunities to support
workforce development in biotechnology and the geospatial commu-
nity, including pathways for servicemembers to apply relevant mili-
tary skills toward civilian employment and further education. This
examination should include potential partnerships with industry
and the feasibility of pilot programs within the Transition Assist-
ance Program to highlight such careers for separating
servicemembers with relevant skills, training, and experience.

Military to civilian credentialing
The committee recognizes that over 150,000 service members
transition from active duty each year, many with highly technical,
operationally validated skills in fields such as aviation mainte-
nance, aviation operations, cybersecurity, logistics, medical serv-
ices, and the skilled trades. Despite extensive training and years
of demonstrated proficiency, transitioning servicemembers rou-
tinely face unnecessary barriers in obtaining civilian occupational E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

The committee notes that while existing federal programs, in-
cluding the Credentialing Opportunities On-Line program, the

useful support to transitioning service members, these programs
are mostly voluntary and go underutilized during the chaotic last
several months a servicemember spends on active duty. No broad
government-wide framework exists that requires civilian licensing
boards, federal regulatory agencies, or private credentialing bodies
to recognize military qualifications as satisfying baseline civilian
occupational requirements, although certain occupation-specific
pathways, such as the military competency pathway for pilot cer-
tification under 14 CFR 61.73, demonstrate feasibility.
The committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in consultation
with the Secretary of Labor, the Secretary of Transportation, the
Secretary of Homeland Security, the Secretary of Health and
Human Services, and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, to conduct
a comprehensive review of military-to-civilian occupational
credentialing and to submit a report to the congressional defense
committees and the Committees on Veterans’ Affairs of the Senate
and the House of Representatives, not later than June 1, 2027. The
report shall contain the following:
(1) An assessment of not fewer than five and not more than
ten military occupational specialties, qualifications, or
credentialing pathways across the Armed Forces where mili-
tary training, operational qualification, and experience most di-
rectly correspond to civilian occupational credentials, including
at a minimum one specialty from each of the following do-
mains: aviation, cybersecurity and information technology, lo-
gistics and transportation, medical and emergency services,
and the skilled trades, and any additional specialties the Sec-
retary determines appropriate;
(2) With respect to each military specialty identified in ac-
cordance with paragraph (1):
(a) identify the corresponding civilian credential, certifi-
cation, or license that is most directly equivalent;
(b) conduct a comparison of military training, qualifica-
tion standards, and operational experience requirements
with corresponding civilian credentialing requirements;
(c) assess the substantive gaps between military and ci-
vilian qualification standards, distinguishing differences in
scope of practice from administrative or procedural bar-
riers; and
(d) offer recommendations identifying any additional ci-
vilian-specific content genuinely necessary to satisfy regu-
latory, safety, or scope-of-practice requirements; and
(3) For each occupational domain, identify opportunities and
barriers to broader recognition of military qualifications as sat-
isfying baseline civilian occupational requirements and provide
recommendations for actions within the authorities of the De-
partment of Defense, other Federal agencies, and Congress.

In conducting this review, the committee expects the Secretary

major private-sector credentialing bodies, state licensing authori-

heads of the departments and agencies identified herein to fully

expects the review to reflect the following considerations:
(1) Equivalency determinations should focus on the qualifica-

on the completion of initial military schoolhouse training. A
servicemember who has completed advanced qualifications, ac-
cumulated meaningful operational experience, and dem-

appropriately compared to civilian credentialing standards
than a recent schoolhouse graduate;
(2) Equivalency mechanisms should establish clear, objective
thresholds, such as specific qualification levels combined with
minimum time in rating or specialty, that trigger presumptive
equivalency, rather than relying on a case-by-case review;
(3) Any remaining civilian-specific requirements imposed on
service members who meet established military equivalency
thresholds should be narrowly tailored to address genuine dif-

or scope of practice, and should not function as barriers to

(4) Medical and emergency medical services credentialing
may require distinct treatment given the role of state licensing

provisions.heading: Navy Reserve Supply Corps Force Structure and Readiness
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the critical role of the Navy Reserve
Supply Corps in providing expeditionary logistics, contracting sup-
port, and specialized expertise to fleet and joint operations. The
committee is concerned that increasing demands associated with
distributed maritime operations and the growing reliance on Re-
serve personnel for logistics support may be outpacing the current
force structure, resourcing, and integration of the Navy Reserve
Supply Corps. The committee is further concerned that any mis-
alignment in these areas could create avoidable risk to operational
readiness and sustainment in a contested environment.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of the Navy to
submit a report to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate
and the House of Representatives, not later than February 1, 2027,
on the force structure, resourcing, and readiness of the Navy Re-
serve Supply Corps. The report shall include the following:
(1) An assessment of current Navy Reserve Supply Corps
end strength, rank structure, and billet distribution. This as-
sessment shall include quantitative data on manning levels
comparing manpower requirements to overall manning;
(2) An assessment of recruiting, accession, and retention
trends for the Navy Reserve Supply Corps over the previous 5
years, including the identification of critical skill shortfalls,
prior-service accessions, and possible impacts from promotion E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

opportunity and career progression on retention, as well as
identification of barriers to recruitment and retention; and
(3) An assessment of the extent to which Navy Reserve Sup-
ply Corps units and individuals are fully integrated into Navy
logistics planning, exercises, and operational deployments, in-
cluding the frequency and nature of such participation, roles
performed, and any limitations that reduce their effective em-
ployment in operational plans and exercises.
Personnel life cycle and workforce management software
The committee recognizes the importance of modern, secure soft-
ware platforms to support Department of Defense personnel func-
tions across recruiting, accession, and in-service career manage-
ment. The committee notes that fragmented and legacy systems
limit visibility, coordination, and decision-making for
servicemembers, commanders, recruiters, and career counselors.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Department of De-
fense to evaluate secure, interoperable personnel software and
workforce management technologies that improve continuity of in-
formation across recruiting and in-service functions. Such capabili-
ties may include advanced data analytics, automation, and respon-
sible artificial intelligence-enabled decision support tools to en-
hance recruiter effectiveness, career pathway guidance, workforce
planning, and servicemember engagement.
The committee further encourages the Department to assess op-
portunities to leverage modern software platforms to reduce admin-
istrative burden, improve data accuracy, and enhance coordination
across the military services, while ensuring appropriate safeguards
for data security, privacy, and service-specific requirements.

provisions.heading: Purple Heart review
provisions.text:
The committee notes the importance of recognition in regard to
servicemember receipt of the Purple Heart. The nature of warfare
has evolved over time, and the regulations surrounding awards
have changed with it.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in co-
ordination with the Secretaries of the military departments, to
brief the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the
House of Representatives, not later than April 1, 2027, on the cur-
rent guidelines and regulations for the award of the Purple Heart.
The briefing shall include but not be limited to: (1) Current data
being collected on ongoing military operations on the award of the
Purple Heart for mild traumatic brain injury; (2) Data from the
award of the Purple Heart for mild traumatic brain injury from the
last 5 years; (3) An assessment of the current regulations, includ-
ing whether a medical officer determination for mild traumatic
brain injury is feasible; and (4) Any other matters relevant to the
review.

Report on conflicts of interest in Department of Defense fi-
nancial literacy program
The committee is concerned about the challenges associated with
new members of the Armed Forces being enrolled into direct de-
posit programs offered by financial institutions without sufficient
financial literacy education to highlight potential conflicts of inter-
est associated with financial product offerings by those same insti-
tutions.
The Department of Defense’s financial management regulations
mandate participation in the Direct Deposit Program for all newly
enlisted and appointed military personnel. Enrollment in direct de-
posit programs can involve military service partnerships with fi-
nancial institutions and typically occurs during initial entry train-
ing. These new recruits may be vulnerable to coercive practices,
with many recruits managing their finances for the first time and
simultaneously being trained to trust authority figures. The com-
mittee seeks to ensure that new recruits are provided with a mean-
ingful opportunity to make the most informed decisions regarding
their finances, as financial security is an important element of mili-
tary readiness. The committee directs the Secretary of Defense to
submit to the congressional defense committees, not later than Feb-
ruary 1, 2027, a report outlining the financial literacy training and
direct deposit process for new recruits. The report shall include the
following information:
(1) An assessment of the process for enrolling new members
of the Armed Forces into the direct deposit programs of finan-
cial institutions; whether that process differs for new members
who have a bank account before joining the Armed Forces; and
whether the information and paperwork provided to new mem-
bers includes any information about account fees or penalties—
including overdraft fees—charged by financial institutions.
(2) A description of the terms and requirements for a finan-
cial institution to operate on a military installation and the
process by which installation leadership solicits potential fi-
nancial institutions, reviews the bids, and selects institutions
for the provision of direct deposit services, financial literacy
training under section 992 of title 10, United States Code, and
any other services under the Department of Defense Financial
Management Regulation.
(3) A description of how the Department of Defense ensures
that the financial institutions operating on military installa-
tions, employees of such institutions, and financial literacy in-
structors and counselors do not have any conflicts of interest
related to the advice they provide or the products they discuss. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

demonstration program
The committee recommends a provision that would amend sec-
tion 604 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization
Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (Public Law 117–263) to enhance the Air
Force rated officer retention demonstration program by increasing

mission and assess whether targeted career intermissions improve

provisions.heading: Items of Special Interest
provisions.text:
Combat-related special compensation review
The committee recognizes the Department of Defense’s ongoing
review of the Combat-Related Special Compensation (CRSC) pro-
gram, as directed in the March 2, 2026, memorandum from the
Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness, and com-
mends the Under Secretary for undertaking a comprehensive as-
sessment of how the program is administered.
The committee affirms the importance of appropriately recog-
nizing combat-related disabilities incurred by servicemembers and
ensuring that eligible retirees receive the benefits they have earned
in a timely and efficient manner. The committee believes the bur-
den of navigating the CRSC process should not fall disproportion-
ately on the individual retiree and expects the military depart-
ments to ensure timely and efficient adjudication of claims.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Under Secretary of De-
fense for Personnel and Readiness to provide a briefing to the Com-
mittees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Rep-
resentatives, not later than October 1, 2026, and every 90 days
thereafter until the review is complete, on the status of the review,
any preliminary findings, and planned actions to improve the pro-
gram. Upon completion of the review, the Under Secretary shall
provide a final briefing that includes the findings of the review,
planned improvements, and any recommended legislative pro-
posals.
Cyber incentive pay standardization
The committee recognizes the importance of attracting, devel-
oping, and retaining a highly skilled cyber workforce in support of
the Cyber Force Generation Model and U.S. Cyber Command. The
committee notes that the military departments currently apply dif-
fering approaches to incentive pay for members performing similar E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

for comparable qualifications and responsibilities.
The committee directs the Secretary of Defense to provide a

the House of Representatives, not later than April 1, 2027, that in-
cludes:
(1) An assessment of the feasibility and advisability of estab-

across the military departments under existing authorities;
(2) A description of current incentive pay programs for cyber

personnel;
(4) Any challenges or limitations associated with standard-
izing such incentive pay, including impacts on a Service’s flexi-
bility and budgetary considerations; and
(5) Any recommendations for legislative or policy changes to
improve the effectiveness and consistency of cyber incentive
pay across the Department of Defense.
Government travel charge card use and servicemember fi-
nancial risk
The committee is concerned that servicemembers executing per-
manent change of station (PCS) or temporary duty (TDY) orders
may be exposed to financial and credit risk as a result of Depart-
ment of Defense travel policies and processes, particularly where
delays in voucher processing, reimbursement, or split disbursement
contribute to Government Travel Charge Card (GTCC) delin-
quency. While the committee recognizes the GTCC as an important
tool for official travel, the committee is concerned that administra-
tive and reimbursement challenges within the defense travel sys-
tem may be placing servicemembers at avoidable financial risk.
The committee seeks to better understand the extent to which De-
partment processes contribute to delinquency and adverse credit
outcomes.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Chief of Staff of the Army,
the Chief of Naval Operations, the Chief of Staff of the Air Force,
the Commandant of the Marine Corps, and the Chief of Space Op-
erations to provide a briefing to the Committees on Armed Services
of the Senate and the House of Representatives, not later than Jan-
uary 1, 2027, on GTCC policies, usage, and associated financial
readiness impacts within their respective Services.
The briefing should include, for each Service:
(1) Current policies governing mandatory or directed use of
the GTCC for PCS and TDY travel, including any cir-
cumstances under which use is waived or alternatives are pro-
vided;
(2) An assessment of the primary drivers of GTCC delin-
quency, including the extent to which delayed voucher proc-
essing, delayed reimbursement, split disbursement errors, or
PCS-related expenses contribute to such delinquency; E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: National Guard Travel-in-Kind program
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the essential contributions of National
Guard personnel to national security, homeland defense, domestic
response, counterdrug operations, and support to civil authorities.
The committee remains concerned that certain categories of Na-
tional Guard personnel may not receive benefits comparable to
similarly situated members of the reserve components despite per-
forming equivalent duties and meeting similar service obligations.
In particular, the committee notes concerns regarding the admin-
istration of Basic Allowance for Housing (BAH) for members serv-
ing on Full-Time National Guard Duty—Counterdrug (FTNGD–
CD) orders and the availability of travel and lodging support for
Army National Guard members required to travel significant dis-
tances to perform Inactive Duty Training (IDT). The committee un-
derstands that statutory and policy differences affecting these pro-
grams may result in inconsistent treatment among
servicemembers, create barriers to recruitment and retention, and
adversely affect readiness and force management.
The committee further notes that FTNGD–CD personnel and Ac-
tive Guard and Reserve personnel both serve in full-time National
Guard duty statuses that provide long-term career opportunities
and perform critical missions in support of national security and
public safety objectives. The committee is also aware of concerns
that Army National Guard members may incur significant out-of-
pocket expenses associated with travel and lodging for IDT that are
not borne by similarly situated members of the Army Reserve.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in
coordination with the Chief of the National Guard Bureau, to pro-
vide a briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate
and the House of Representatives, not later than March 1, 2027,
on options to improve parity in benefits and support provided to
National Guard personnel. The briefing shall include:
(1) An assessment of current statutory, regulatory, and pol-
icy authorities governing:
(a) BAH determinations for FTNGD–CD personnel; and
(b) Travel and lodging support for Army National Guard
members performing IDT;
(2) An assessment of the scope of each issue, including: E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

(a) How BAH is currently administered for FTNGD–CD
personnel across the States and Territories, including the
extent of variation among jurisdictions; and
(b) The current out-of-pocket costs incurred by Army Na-
tional Guard members for travel and lodging associated
with IDT requirements;
(3) An evaluation of the feasibility and advisability of:
(a) Amending section 403(g)(6)(A) of title 37, United
States Code, to include FTNGD–CD personnel and align
BAH determinations with duty location; and
(b) Establishing a comprehensive Lodging-in-Kind and
travel support program for Army National Guard members
that achieves parity with comparable Army Reserve pro-
grams;
(4) An assessment of the effects that such changes would
have on recruitment, retention, readiness, force management,
and mission effectiveness within the National Guard;
(5) Legislative, regulatory, administrative, and policy options
to address each issue, including the advantages and disadvan-
tages of each option;
(6) Detailed cost estimates associated with each proposed op-

(a) Estimated costs of extending duty-location-based
BAH treatment to FTNGD–CD personnel; and
(b) Estimated costs of providing Lodging-in-Kind for
Army National Guard members residing more than 50
miles from their assigned drill location and travel reim-

more than 150 miles from their assigned unit or serving
in critically short specialties; and
(7) Recommendations from the Department of Defense re-
garding any legislative changes necessary to ensure equitable
treatment of National Guard personnel performing comparable
duties or meeting comparable training requirements.
Review of credentialing assistance programs
The committee recognizes the value of credentialing assistance
programs in enabling servicemembers to obtain industry-recognized
certifications and postsecondary credentials that translate into ci-
vilian career opportunities. The committee notes that credentialing
assistance is currently administered inconsistently across the mili-
tary departments, with significant variation in eligibility criteria,
funding limits, approved credential lists, cost controls, and vendor
oversight mechanisms. The committee is concerned that this frag-
mentation limits equitable access for servicemembers across the
force and has contributed to cost management challenges in recent
years.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in co-
ordination with the Secretaries of the military departments, to con-
duct a comprehensive review of credentialing assistance programs
across the Armed Forces and submit a report to the congressional
defense committees, not later than June 1, 2027.

provisions.heading: Access to Military OneSource
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the continued need for confidential,
non-medical, prevention-focused behavioral health and wellness re-
sources that support the readiness and well-being of
servicemembers and their families across the total force.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Secretary of Defense
to assess opportunities to pilot, integrate, or otherwise leverage
commercial, off-the-shelf behavioral health and wellness tech-
nologies as part of Military OneSource’s non-medical support eco-
system. These efforts should focus on expanding access to self-di-
rected and peer-enabled resources that support relationship skills,
stress management, coping strategies, adjustment challenges, and
other life skills consistent with the authorized scope of non-medical
counseling. The committee further encourages the Secretary to con-
sider how validated commercial solutions may improve coordina-
tion, continuity, and cost-effective delivery of non-medical support
services across the force, and to use lessons learned to inform fu-
ture program design and resource allocation decisions. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Advancing non-opioid alternatives for chronic pain
The committee recognizes the significant impact of chronic pain
on thousands of servicemembers and the over-reliance on opioids to
manage chronic pain conditions. The committee is concerned that,
despite advances in expanding access to non-opioid alternatives for
acute pain, significant barriers remain for chronic pain that limit
servicemembers’ and TRICARE beneficiaries’ treatment options.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to pro-
vide a briefing, not later than March 1, 2027, on: (1) The avail-
ability of non-opioid treatment options approved by the Food and
Drug Administration to manage chronic pain conditions; (2) The
number of patients that are utilizing these therapies; (3) The iden-
tification of incentives to improve access to non-opioid alternatives
for chronic pain; and (4) Recommendations that would further al-
leviate chronic pain issues for TRICARE beneficiaries.
All-hazards military medical response
The committee is aware of the Department’s policy for emergency
management related to medical emergencies caused by blast, burn,
and/or penetrating injuries. However, given the current and more
complex ‘‘All Hazards’’’ threat environment in both Contiguous
United States and Outside the Contiguous United States scenarios,
the committee believes that the Department’s medical response
plans related to exposure to chemical, biological, and radiological
weapons, potentially in addition to more traditional injuries, should
be reviewed and updated. Therefore, the committee directs the Sec-
retary of Defense to provide a briefing to the Committees on Armed
Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives, not later
than February 1, 2027, on the following:
(1) A description of current capabilities to detect, treat, and
safely transport patients with injuries related to chemical, bio-
logical, and radiological exposure, both in isolation and when
combined with blast, burn, and penetrating injuries;
(2) An assessment of gaps in current capabilities to detect,
treat, and safely transport patients with injuries related to
chemical, biological, and radiological exposure, both in isolation
and when combined with blast, burn, and penetrating injuries;
and
(3) A summary of policy, technology, manpower, and other
resource requirements needed to resolve these capability gaps.

Comptroller General review of TRICARE pharmacy pro-
gram
The committee remains concerned about the ability of the De-
partment of Defense’s (DOD) TRICARE pharmacy program to meet
the needs of its beneficiaries. The program is administered by a
contractor who has administered the program since 2009. The con-
tractor has responsibilities that include developing and maintain-
ing a network of retail pharmacies and operating a mail order
pharmacy. Information on the current management of the
TRICARE pharmacy program, including the adequacy of the net-
works and the DOD’s oversight of the program, will help to ensure
the program is delivering the benefit in the most effective and cost
effective manner.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Comptroller General of
the United States to conduct a series of studies on the TRICARE
Pharmacy program that include:
(1) A review of beneficiary access and network adequacy, in-
cluding:
(a) any geographic disparities in access, especially for
rural and underserved areas;
(b) differences in access to in-person pharmacies by
pharmacy type;
(c) reliance on mail-order pharmacy services;
(d) the timeliness of prescription fulfillment, including
home delivery and specialty pharmacy services;
(e) adequacy of access to care; and
(f) any associated impacts on patient care;
(2) A review of prescription drug costs under the program
and the extent to which the contractor’s practices affect those
costs, including whether the Department achieves cost savings
and receives the full value of negotiated discounts;
(3) An assessment of the Defense Health Agency’s (DHA)
management and oversight of the program, including:
(a) an assessment of whether the contract, and its re-
quirements and performance metrics, is structured in a
way to enable the DHA to effectively oversee the program
and minimize program integrity risks, such as those re-
lated to fraud, waste, and abuse, including improper pay-
ments and the effectiveness of safeguards to prevent inap-

Accelerate report on perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl sub-
stance-free chemical, biological, radiological, and nu-
clear protective garments
The committee understands that perfluoroalkyl and
polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)-free textile technologies can pro-
vide new performance capabilities for individual Chemical, Biologi-
cal, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) protective equipment. Indi-
vidual CBRN protection is a key part of strategic deterrence
against our adversaries. The committee is concerned that the De-
partment of Defense may not be able to provide the
servicemembers with advanced individual CBRN protection equip-
ment unless it accelerates efforts to acquire and field PFAS-free
textile technologies. In the Senate report accompanying S. 2296 (S.
Rept. 119–39) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal
Year 2026, the committee requested a briefing on ongoing efforts
and a strategy to acquire PFAS-free textile technologies for indi-
vidual CBRN protective equipment but has yet to receive the re-
quired briefing.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to pro-
vide a briefing to the congressional defense committees, not later
than February 1, 2027, on the Department’s assessment to acquire
PFAS-free textile technologies for individual CBRN protective
equipment as soon as feasible. The briefing should include:
(1) Current efforts to secure the industrial base for PFAS-
free textile technologies for individual CBRN protective equip-
ment;
(2) A description of how advanced performance may enable
new CBRN doctrines that enhance survivability and lethality
in contested environments; and
(3) Any resources or legislative authorities necessary or ben-
eficial to ensure these new technologies can be fielded by fiscal
year 2028.

The committee is aware of strategic adversaries’ rapid adoption
of scalable ground autonomous systems and the operational chal-
lenges this presents to U.S. forces. Existing investments and re-
sources supporting ground autonomy initiatives present opportuni-
ties to accelerate the deployment of small autonomous ground vehi-
cle (AGV) systems. The committee encourages the Army to
prioritize existing resources and modernization investments to en-
able rapid acquisition pathways.

briefing, not later than February 26, 2027, to the Committees on
Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives on
the Army’s efforts to accelerate adoption of ground autonomous ca-
pabilities. The briefing shall include:
(1) A capability investment strategy and modernization road-
map to scale AGV and swarming autonomy and transition
emerging AGV technologies into programs of record;
(2) An evaluation framework for attritable ground systems,
including small, medium, and large classification standards E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Acquisition workforce metrics
The committee believes that strengthening accountability for the
Department of Defense acquisition workforce, including program
managers and contracting officers, is essential to improving acqui-
sition program performance, ensuring timely deliveries, and safe-
guarding taxpayer resources. The committee notes that an empow-
ered acquisition workforce is necessary to fully utilize the many ac-
quisition authorities the Department has been provided, and that
high performing acquisition professionals should be rewarded pro-
fessionally.
However, the committee notes that oversight failures have con-
tributed to delays in sustainment, maintenance, and modernization
programs that directly affect operational readiness. Audit findings
frequently occur years after oversight deficiencies take place, at
which point responsible personnel may have rotated to new assign-
ments or separated from service, limiting meaningful account-
ability.
The committee believes that as the Secretary of Defense imple-
ments key performance objectives established under section 826 of
the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Pub-
lic Law 60–119) for the acquisition workforce, the Department of
Defense should create and maintain a formal process for tracking
the performance of individuals within the acquisition workforce
and assessing their performance against the key performance objec-
tives.
The committee directs the Secretary of Defense to provide a
briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and
the House of Representatives, not later than March 1, 2027, on the
implementation of section 826 of the National Defense Authoriza-
tion Act for Fiscal Year 2026 including the development of a per-
formance tracking system for members of the acquisition workforce.
This briefing should also include an update on implementing rel-
evant findings and recommendations from the Inspector General of
the Department of Defense, the Government Accountability Office,
and contract administration and audit agencies. If the Portfolio Ac-
quisition Executive validates any deficiencies identified through

cerned.

vulnerabilities in the domestic and global supply chains for carbon
black that are relevant to the defense industrial base. The briefing
shall include but not be limited to: (1) A comprehensive assessment
of current and projected defense demand for carbon black across
defense platforms, systems, and sustainment activities; (2) An
analysis of the risks associated with reliance on foreign sources of
carbon black, including sources located in countries of concern; (3)
An analysis of the risks associated with supply disruptions, aging
production facilities, or limited domestic production capacity of car-
bon black; and (4) Recommendations to strengthen domestic pro-
duction capacity and supply chain resilience for carbon black.

support contested logistics
The committee commends the Department of Defense for its

provisions.heading: Defense Civilian Training Corps
provisions.text:
The committee continues to support the Defense Civilian Train-
ing Corps (DCTC) as a talent development program that aligns E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

with the Department’s acquisition transformation agenda and pro-
vides an important pathway to attract top talent to the Depart-
ment of Defense (DOD). The committee appreciates the effort by
the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition &
Sustainment (OUSD(A&S)) and the Acquisition Innovation Re-
search Center (AIRC) to experiment, adapt, and iterate over the
past 3 years to build a DCTC talent development prototype that
can be scaled.
The committee notes a key lesson learned during the DCTC
prototyping phase. The universities that produce talent operate
largely independently from the DOD organizations that recruit,
hire, and employ talent, with different cycle times, resources, and
incentives. This disconnect reveals a talent valley of death, which
requires sponsorship between promising talent on the one side and
the integration and application of that talent, at scale, to imple-
ment DOD priorities.
The committee intends for the DCTC to bridge this talent gap,
by extending talent development into post-secondary education to
meet specific Department needs and connecting that talent with
those in the DOD that need it. The OUSD(A&S) alone cannot scale
a talent development pipeline into the robust factory needed to con-
tinuously produce new talent through experiential and project-
based learning. Pursuant to the authority in section 2200g of title
10, United States Code, the committee intends for the services to
identify specific universities as talent partners and for the AIRC to
provide the necessary talent development needed by specific DOD
organizations. Pursuant to the amendments made by section 823 of
the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Pub-
lic Law 119–60), the services have the hiring authority needed to
bring on students as term employees during the development phase
and transition to full-time employees upon graduation, if they meet
expectations. The committee encourages full use of this authority
in partnership with the services to develop new talent with critical
thinking, digital fluency, and a transformational mindset and to
smoothly transition that talent into the civilian workforce of the
Department.
The committee directs the Secretary of Defense and the Director
of the AIRC to provide a briefing to the Committees on Armed
Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives, not later
than March 1, 2027, on efforts by the OUSD(A&S), the AIRC, and
the services to bridge the talent valley of death using the DCTC.
The briefings shall include: (1) An explanation of how the services
use DCTC authority; (2) How the OUSD(A&S) measures success;
and (3) The annual Defense Acquisition Workforce Development
Account funding needed for the services to conduct strategic plan-
ning and expansion of the DCTC talent development program.
Design for manufacturing for munitions and energetics
The committee is pleased to note the Department of Defense’s
(DOD) increased focus on munitions and energetics production.
However, the committee believes that as the Department of De-
fense takes steps to increase munitions and energetics production,
the DOD should focus on incorporating modern manufacturing
processes to speed production and reduce waste. This is particu- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

larly important as the Department of the Army continues to mod-
ernize and expand the usage of the arsenals, ammunition plants,
and depots in the organic industrial base. Modern manufacturing
processes—such as design simplification to minimize part counts
and reduce reliance on bespoke tooling, testing components at the
lowest value state to minimize scrap rates, prioritizing automation
from the beginning of the manufacturing design process, focusing
on building production lines that can be scaled to meet demand, de-
veloping testing points along the manufacturing process to prevent
revisions, and others—have the potential to significantly reduce
both the cost and schedule of producing munitions and energetic
materials.
The committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in coordination
with the Secretaries of the military departments and the Joint
Energetics Transition Office, to provide a briefing to the Commit-
tees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representa-
tives, not later than March 31, 2027, on the automation and effi-
ciency of munitions production, including:
(1) An assessment of the efficiency and effectiveness of cur-
rent munitions and energetics manufacturing processes, with a
focus on enumerating the manual processes that exist and the
justification for why automation is not technically or economi-
cally feasible. This assessment should delineate any roadblocks
to expanding the production lines if required;
(2) Recommendations to improve the efficiency and effective-
ness of current munitions and energetics manufacturing proc-
esses;
(3) An assessment of how automation and streamlined proc-
esses are being incorporated into the Army’s organic industrial
base;
(4) An update on the Joint Energetics Transition Office’s ef-
forts to identify raw material waste during the explosives man-
ufacturing process and opportunities for implementation; and
(5) Any other areas the Secretary identifies to improve effi-
ciency or capacity in munitions and energetics production.
Digital modernization of the organic industrial base
The committee commends the military departments for ongoing
efforts to modernize the organic industrial base in collaboration
with the Nation’s digital manufacturing institute. The committee
believes that sustained progress toward a digitally enabled organic
industrial base is essential to improving readiness, expediting pro-
duction and maintenance timelines, and ensuring the Department
of Def

provisions.heading: Manufacturing USA network
provisions.text:
The committee appreciates the importance of the Department of
Defense (DOD) Manufacturing Technology Office, the Manufac-
turing Innovation Institutes, and the broader Manufacturing USA
network for revitalizing the domestic defense industrial base
through supporting manufacturing ecosystems, workforce develop-
ment, and manufacturing technology development and implementa-
tion.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to
provide a briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Sen-
ate and the House of Representatives, not later than March 1,
2027, detailing the work of the DOD Manufacturing Technology Of-
fice, the Manufacturing Innovation Institutes, and the broader
Manufacturing USA network in supporting the U.S. defense indus-
trial base. The briefing shall: (1) Describe the relevant metrics and
milestones by which the Department of Defense measures their im-
pact; (2) Lay out any barriers they have confronted in achieving
their mission; and (3) Note ways in which the Congress can help
support their work in strengthening American manufacturing.
Materials workforce for munitions
The committee recognizes the indispensable role of advanced ma-
terials, including composites, in munitions programs and is con-
cerned that current workforce pipelines are not producing enough
candidates with the requisite technical skills and experience to sat-
isfy munitions production staffing requirements for modern com-
posite fabrication. As munitions demand continues to increase for
long range precision fires, counter unmanned aircraft systems, mis-
sile defense, and other applications, shortfalls in a skilled work-
force could hinder production of these urgently required systems.
Therefore, the committee directs the Under Secretary of Defense
for Acquisition and Sustainment to provide a briefing to the Com-
mittees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Rep-
resentatives, not later than March 1, 2027, on programs to support
the development, training, and retention of the munitions indus-
trial base workforce to support increased production demand. This
briefing shall include the Department’s use of existing authorities,
such as those within the Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Support program, to close composite materials skills gaps and
maintain a sufficient pipeline of qualified technicians to meet mod-
ern composite fabrication requirements for the munitions industrial
base.
Medium caliber munitions industrial base
The committee recognizes that allowing new entrants into the
medium caliber portfolio could foster increased competition and im-
prove the long-term resilience of the industrial base.
Accordingly, the committee expects the Army to implement the
Medium Caliber Family Buy 4 (MCFB4) acquisition strategy in a
manner that enables new contractors to participate across the full
medium caliber portfolio, rather than through segmented competi-
tion that limits scale and investment. The committee emphasizes
that MCFB4 should be executed in a way that preserves the viabil-
ity of new entrants, incentivizes private capital investment, in-
creases competition, reduces supply chain risks, and strengthens
surge readiness.
Pharmaceutical supply chains of Department of Defense
The committee remains concerned about the strength and secu-
rity of the Department of Defense’s (DOD) supply chains for phar-
maceutical materials based on findings from the report required by
section 860(a) of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authoriza-
tion Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (Public Law 117–263). Additionally,
a DOD Inspector General report (Report No. DODIG–2021–126)
evaluated the Department’s mitigation of foreign suppliers in the
pharmaceutical supply chain. The Inspector General report con-
cluded that:
(1) The Department did not mitigate the risks of disruptions
to its pharmaceutical supply chain, which is reliant upon for-
eign suppliers;
(2) The Department did not have implementing guidance on
supply chain risk management for Department material; and
(3) The Department’s reliance on foreign suppliers for phar-
maceuticals is a public health, readiness, and national security
risk.
The resiliency of the pharmaceutical supply chain is imperative
for the health, well-being, and operational advantage of the
warfighter.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Under Secretary of De-
fense for Personnel and Readiness, in coordination with the Under
Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment, to provide a
briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and
the House of Representatives, not later than March 1, 2027, on the
Department’s implementation of the findings described in the re-
port published pursuant to section 860(a). Specifically, the briefing
shall include:
(1) Short-term risk mitigation efforts for pharmaceuticals
whose active pharmaceutical ingredients are sourced from for-
eign entities of concern or have been subject to supply chain
disruptions;
(2) Ongoing Department efforts to work with relevant stake-
holders to encourage investment in domestic, allied, and part- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

ner research and manufacturing in the pharmaceutical space;
and
(3) Department plans to partner with other federal stake-
holders on leveraging existing medical countermeasure stock-
