provisions.heading: Portfolio Acquisition Executive scorecards
provisions.text:
The committee notes that the effectiveness of the Department of
Defense’s acquisition enterprise depends on the performance and
accountability of its Program Acquisition Executives (PAEs). The
committee notes the Department’s utilization of performance score-
cards as a tool to assess these executive-level roles and the pro-
grams they oversee.
The committee is interested in how these scorecards provide visi-
bility into the defense acquisition lifecycle and ensure rigorous
oversight. Specifically, the committee emphasizes that these eval-
uations should maintain a standardized focus on the number and
quality of technology transitions and insertions, measurable im-
provements in user outcomes, and the timely divestment of re-
sources from non-performing efforts.
Therefore, the committee directs the Under Secretary of Defense
for Acquisition and Sustainment to provide an annual report to the
Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of
Representatives, not later than March 1, 2027, and continuing
through March 1, 2030, on the results of these scorecards. Each re-
port shall include, at a minimum:
(1) Aggregated data on the number and quality of successful
technology transitions and insertions achieved;
(2) Metrics detailing measurable improvements in user out-
comes, including warfighter feedback, capability effectiveness,
and mission performance enhancements, directly attributable
to PAE-managed programs;
(3) Data on the identification, assessment, and divestment of
non-performing efforts, including resources reallocated as a re-
sult of such divestments and the resulting improvements in
portfolio efficiency; and
(4) Recommended improvements to the scorecard process to
better capture technology transition performance, user outcome
results, and divestment effectiveness while enhancing data ac-
curacy and executive accountability.
Requirements for concurrent and rapid detection of biologi-
cal and chemical agents
The threat of aerosolized biological and chemical attacks on our
military’s operational readiness and continuity of operations is in-
creasing. Aerosol biological and chemical agents are both easy and
inexpensive to produce and provide adversaries with new ways to
target critical U.S. infrastructure. China continues to engage in bi-
ological and chemical activities, and Russia continues to research
and deploy biological and chemical weapons capabilities—as seen
in Ukraine—in violation of the Biological and Chemical Weapons E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Conventions. Renewed attention to this threat is vital, especially
for combatant commands.
Therefore, the committee directs the Assistant Secretary of De-
fense for Nuclear Deterrence, Chemical, and Biological Defense,
Policy and Programs to brief the congressional defense committees,
not later than March 31, 2027, on the current and future require-
ments for the procurement, deployment, and maintenance of sen-
sors capable of detecting biological and chemical agents in oper-
ational environments rapidly and concurrently.
Technologies for modernization of logistic yard operations
The committee recognizes the importance of improving the effi-
ciency, throughput, and resiliency of Department of Defense logis-
tics yard operations. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, com-
puter vision, sensor integration, and data analytics have enabled
commercial solutions capable of providing real-time visibility of ve-
hicles, equipment, cargo, and material flow across complex logistics
environments.
The committee notes that commercial technologies have dem-
onstrated the potential to improve asset utilization, reduce conges-
tion and delays, enhance safety, and support more efficient logistics
operations while minimizing infrastructure requirements and im-
plementation timelines.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Department of De-
fense, including the Defense Logistics Agency and military depart-
ments, to evaluate commercially available smart technologies and
identify opportunities to improve logistics yard operations through
the adoption of artificial intelligence-enabled, software-defined ca-
pabilities.
The committee directs the Under Secretary of Defense for Acqui-
sition and Sustainment, in coordination with the Director of the
Defense Logistics Agency and the Secretaries of the military de-
partments, to provide a briefing to the Committees on Armed Serv-
ices of the Senate and the House of Representatives, not later than
March 1, 2027, on the Department’s efforts to evaluate and deploy
commercial smart technologies to enhance and modernize logistics
yard operations. The briefing shall include an assessment of oper-
ational benefits, implementation challenges, interoperability con-
siderations, potential applications across defense logistics installa-
tions, and recommendations for broader adoption where appro-
priate.

existing code of conduct to apply to those positions, to ensure that

The committee is concerned that the use of new tools, such as
loans, loan guarantees, or equity stakes, may be leaving some am-

help employees avoid any appearance of impropriety or conflict of
interest. With the high possibility for distorting markets or corrup-

to be above reproach and should go above and beyond when it
comes to professional and ethical standards of behavior. The com-

infractions can result in legal ramifications as well as the loss of
professional certifications and standing. The committee believes
that the adoption of similar practices could be beneficial for this
nascent community of practice in the Department.

provisions.heading: Crane Army Ammunition Activity
provisions.text:
The committee notes that the Department of Defense should con-
tinue to look at more effective methods to transport munitions.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of Army to pro-
vide a report, not later than April 16, 2027, to the Committees on
Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives, on
the feasibility and advisability of developing alternative transpor-
tation methods for munitions supplied by Crane Army Ammunition
Activity. The report should include:
(1) Current transportation methods used to support the
movement of munitions, materiel, and related items to and
from Crane Army Ammunition Activity;
(2) Existing transportation constraints, vulnerabilities, and
infrastructure deficiencies affecting the efficiency of the trans-
portation of munitions, materiel, and related items to and from
Crane Army Ammunition Activity;
(3) The feasibility of alternative transportation methods, in-
cluding the improvement of existing airfield infrastructure at
Jefferson Proving Ground, the use of military aircraft to trans-
port munitions from Crane Army Ammunition Activity, and
any other transportation method the Secretary determines ap-
propriate;
(4) The costs and benefits associated with each alternative
transportation method identified under paragraph three, in-
cluding maintenance costs, operational benefits, scalability, re-
silience, and impacts on readiness;
(5) Any effects of such alternative transportation methods on
ammunition transport safety, explosive safety requirements,
security, and environmental compliance;
(6) The extent to which such alternative transportation
methods could reduce delivery time for munitions being trans-
ported from Crane Army Ammunition Activity and could en-
hance the ability of the Crane Army Ammunition Activity to
meet current and projected mission requirements;
(7) Any infrastructure investments, Federal or state approv-
als, or intergovernmental agreements that may be necessary to
implement such alternative transportation methods; and
(8) Any legislative, regulatory, or budgetary barriers to the
implementation of such alternative transportation methods.
High-power microwave technologies for airfield and instal-
lation defense
The committee recognizes the growing threat posed by unmanned
aircraft systems (UAS), including coordinated drone attacks against
military installations and airfields with concentrated aircraft as-
sets. The committee believes that high-power microwave (HPM)
technologies offer significant potential to provide non-kinetic, scal-
able, and cost-effective protection against massed UAS threats
while reducing reliance on expensive interceptor-based defenses.
The committee remains concerned that the Army has not
transitioned promising HPM capabilities into operational use de- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127
GNIRAEH
htiw
DORP3RG1076PAL
no
kcirederfr
207
spite continued congressional support and the demonstrated need
to protect critical facilities and high-value aircraft from emerging
aerial threats. The committee further believes that installations
with dense concentrations of fixed-wing, rotary-wing, and un-
manned aircraft represent attractive targets for adversaries and re-
quire layered counter-UAS defenses that include directed energy
capabilities.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Army, in
coordination with the Joint Interagency Task Force 401, to provide
a briefing, not later than April 5, 2027, to the congressional defense
committees on the feasibility and operational utility of employing
high-power microwave technologies to defend airfields and other fa-
cilities with high concentrations of aircraft. The briefing shall in-
clude at a minimum:
(1) An assessment of current and projected UAS threats to
aviation facilities and other high-value installations;
(2) The potential role of HPM systems within layered air and
missile defense architectures;
(3) Any operational lessons learned from demonstrations, ex-
ercises, or experimentation involving HPM technologies; and
(4) Planned investments, resourcing requirements, and ac-
quisition timelines for fielding HPM capabilities to protect crit-
ical installations.
Plan for identification and adoption of cutting-edge global
technologies
The committee is encouraged by the efforts undertaken by the
Department of Defense to foster the growth of the defense indus-
trial base and to leverage the U.S. technology industry for real-
world battlefield advantage. Given the pace of global innovation in
dual-use and defense technologies, especially related to ongoing
global conflicts, there exists an opportunity to strengthen the De-
partment’s capabilities by identifying and leveraging technological
innovations developed by early-stage technology companies around
the world while also preventing such innovations and related intel-
lectual property from being co-opted by adversary nations. The
committee acknowledges that the Department has several different
offices and authorities that could be leveraged for partnership, in-
vestment, and adoption of novel technologies and capabilities with
allies and partners. However, this approach does not appear to be
sufficiently coordinated nor aligned with other activities of the De-
partment and the broader interagency.
The committee directs the Secretary of Defense to brief the Com-
mittees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Rep-
resentatives, not later than March 1, 2027, on: (1) The Depart-
ment’s existing authorities, activities, and offices engaged in moni-
toring developments and making investments or partnerships in

provisions.heading: Items of Special Interest
provisions.text:
Base defense modernization
The committee recognizes the critical and growing need for the
protection of military installations from full-spectrum, all-domain
threats. The committee notes that the proliferation of low-altitude,
small unmanned aerial systems (sUAS) presents an immediate,
asymmetric risk to defense critical infrastructure. Industrial base
installations present a unique security challenge: they possess vast
physical footprints that are highly vulnerable to intrusion, infiltra-
tion, and aerial surveillance, yet they are typically secured by rel-
atively small, manned security forces. To mitigate these
vulnerabilities, the Department of Defense should transition from
a reliance on outdated surveillance systems toward integrated secu-
rity architectures.
The committee notes that recent advancements in commercial
technology have demonstrated the immediate availability and effi- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

cacy of various platforms and enhanced capabilities such as
leveraging existing infrastructure to integrate wide-area surveil-
lance tools, including radar, Light Detection and Ranging, unat-
tended ground sensors, and non-lethal deterrents.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of the Army to
provide a briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Sen-
ate and the House of Representatives, not later than April 1, 2027,
on the Army’s plans to address the full spectrum of all-domain
threats to its military installations. The briefing shall include:
(1) An operational assessment and after action review of the
Lake City Army Ammunition Plant pilot program conducted in
April 2026;
(2) A prioritized list of high-value Army installations, ammu-
nition plants, and depots designated where this capability
could be fielded; and
(3) A technical evaluation of incorporating prioritized follow-
on capability updates, including acoustic UAS detection, open-
source intelligence feed integration, and advanced seismic sen-
sors.
Comptroller General assessment of antisemitism training
within Department of Defense
The committee notes that a professional military workplace free
from antisemitism strengthens trust, morale, and mission effective-
ness, and that antisemitism threatens unit cohesion, undermines
command authority, and erodes military readiness.
Therefore, the committee directs the Comptroller General of the
United States to conduct a review of the Department of Defense’s
antisemitism training applicable to members of the Armed Forces
and civilian employees of the Department. The review should as-
sesses the status and efficiency of antisemitism training within the
Department, including:
(1) An identification of actions taken by the Department to
create an environment free of antisemitism;
(2) An accounting of any antisemitism training in the pre-
vious 5 years that has been provided to members of the Armed
Forces and civilian employees of the Department; and
(3) Any other items the Comptroller General deems appro-
priate.
The committee further directs the Comptroller General to pro-
vide a report on their findings to the Committees on Armed Serv-
ices of the Senate and the House of Representatives, not later than
March 1, 2027.
Comptroller General review of security clearance due proc-
ess and transparency
The committee believes that a robust and efficient security clear-
ance process is vital to maintaining a high-quality national security
workforce and enabling the mobility of that workforce across the
defense and intelligence enterprises. However, the committee is
concerned about impediments to that mobility. In particular, the
committee is concerned about the transparency and consistency of
due process protections, including rights to an appeal following
clearance revocation or suspension, in the security clearance proc- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

ess, particularly for government personnel with eligibility to access
Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) within the intelligence
community (IC).
The committee is also concerned by descriptions of instances in
which outstanding adjudicative issues are not resolved and the re-
lated effects they can have on the careers of government personnel
attempting to transfer between or within the IC and the Depart-
ment of Defense (DOD), particularly for personnel with eligibility
to access SCI. The committee further notes inconsistencies in the
due process protections and rights to an appeal following clearance
revocation or suspension available to government personnel at
some agencies compared to contractor and other personnel at the
Defense Office of Hearings and Appeals, as well as a lack of trans-
parency regarding when personnel are informed of outstanding ad-
judicative issues with their clearances.
Finally, the committee would like to better understand the due
process protections for government personnel who receive an ad-
verse determination with respect to their eligibility to access SCI.
Therefore, the committee directs the Comptroller General of the
United States to conduct an assessment of the processes, policies,
and transparency of SCI determinations within the DOD and the
IC. The assessment should include: (1) An evaluation of the effect
of unresolved adjudicative issues on personnel mobility; (2) The
consistency of due process protections for personnel who experience
unresolved adjudications or clearance revocations or suspensions
across the government; (3) The timelines for resolving issues; and
(4) Any additional matters the Comptroller General deems rel-
evant.
The committee further directs the Comptroller General to pro-
vide a briefing, not later than March 31, 2027, to the Committees
on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives
and the congressional intelligence committees, with the results of
the review to follow in a mutually agreed upon format and time-
frame.

Improvements to aviation safety
The committee is dedicated to improving aviation safety, espe-
cially the interactions between military and civilian aircraft in
light of the crash involving American Airlines flight 5342 and a
Blackhawk helicopter in January of 2025. The National Transpor-
tation Safety Board (NTSB) released its analysis into causal factors
of the crash in January 2026, including specific recommendations
for the Department of Defense and the Department of the Army.
The committee believes it is necessary for the safety of all pas-
sengers in American airspace that the Department of Defense im-
plement these recommendations to the broadest extent possible.
For any recommendation that the Department believes it cannot
implement as written, it must brief the committee about all imple-
mentation challenges and develop solutions to address the risks
identified in that recommendation. Recognizing that this effort may
take significant resources, but cognizant of the gravity of ensuring
the American airspace is safe for commercial and military aircraft,
the committee requests close collaboration with the Department
throughout this process.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to pro-
vide a briefing, not later than January 15, 2027, and every 90 days
thereafter, to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and
the House of Representatives on the implementation of the rec-
ommendations from the NTSB Aviation Investigation Report AIR–
26–02, including:
(1) Progress on implementation of each recommendation di-
rected to the Department of Defense;
(2) Progress on implementation of each recommendation di-
rected to the Department of the Army and implementation of
those recommendations by the Department of the Navy and
the Department of the Air Force;
(3) Description of barriers to any recommendation by the De-
partment of Defense or any military department;
(4) Proposed solutions to any identified barriers that address
the risk identified in the NTSB recommendations;
(5) Any other relevant information as determined by the Sec-
retary.

Increasing shipbuilding and repair capacity
The committee recognizes the strategic importance of a robust
domestic maritime industrial base to the national security and eco-
nomic resilience of the United States. The committee is concerned
that existing domestic shipbuilding, ship repair, dry dock avail-
ability, and associated waterfront infrastructure is at times inac-
cessible to the full range of military, government-owned, and U.S.-
flag commercial vessels and therefore poses a risk to strategic sea-
lift readiness, force projection capabilities, and sustainment oper-
ations.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Secretary of Defense,
in consultation with the Secretary of Transportation and the Mari-
time Administration, to identify opportunities to strengthen domes-
tic shipbuilding and repair capacity through investments in infra-
structure, industrial modernization, and workforce development.
Such efforts may include the expansion or rehabilitation of dry
docks; modernization of ship repair facilities and waterfront infra-
structure; upgrades to heavy-lift and crane capacity; dredging and
navigation improvements necessary to accommodate larger vessels
and increased throughput; and other capital improvements that en-
hance the ability of the United States to construct, maintain, and
repair military and commercially useful sealift vessels. The com-
mittee further encourages the Department of Defense to prioritize
projects that demonstrate a clear nexus to national defense objec-
tives, including support for surge sealift readiness, contested logis-
tics operations, distributed maritime operations, maintenance and
sustainment of Navy and Military Sealift Command vessels, stra-
tegic commercial shipping capacity, and the operational readiness
of the U.S.-flag fleet. The committee also encourages consultation
with private industry, public shipyards, commercial repair facili-
ties, and relevant Federal agencies to ensure a comprehensive ap-
proach to strengthening the Nation’s mariti

Navy shipbuilding software and artificial intelligence appli-
cations for surface combatants
The committee recognizes the Navy’s successful deployment of
advanced software and artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities in
submarine construction and commends these efforts to modernize
shipbuilding processes. The integration of digital tools, including
AI-enabled design optimization, production planning systems, and
quality assurance platforms, has demonstrated meaningful im-
provements in construction efficiency, cost management, and sched-
ule adherence in the submarine industrial base. The committee be-
lieves these technological advances should not remain limited to
submarine programs. The same software and AI capabilities that
have proven effective for submarine construction hold significant
potential to enhance productivity and reduce costs across the
Navy’s entire shipbuilding portfolio, including surface combatants,
amphibious vessels, auxiliary ships, and unmanned platforms.
The committee notes that modern commercial shipbuilding oper-
ations worldwide increasingly rely on integrated software systems
to manage complex construction workflows, optimize material logis-
tics, and ensure quality control. The Navy’s surface ship and auxil-
iary vessel construction programs would benefit from similar tech-
nological modernization. Therefore, the committee encourages the
Secretary of the Navy to expand the application of software and ar-
tificial intelligence tools beyond submarine programs to all classes
of naval vessels. This expansion should include:
(1) Assessment of current software and AI applications in
submarine construction that could be adapted for surface ship
and auxiliary vessel programs;
(2) Development of a comprehensive plan to integrate ad-
vanced digital tools across all surface combatant shipbuilding
programs, including specific timelines and expected perform-
ance improvements;

barriers within the shipbuilding industrial base that may im-
pede adoption of these technologies; and

provisions.heading: Office of Net Assessment
provisions.text:
The committee commends the contributions of the Office of Net
Assessment (ONA) and reaffirms the value of its longstanding part-
nership with the Congress. The ONA provides long-term, strategic,
and independent analysis in service of the national defense, and
when properly resourced and supported by leadership, it has made
significant contributions to the strategic direction and under-
standing for senior Department of Defense decision-makers.
The committee believes that ONA’s work is crucial and of signifi-
cant interest to a broad range of policymakers and senior leaders
striving for deeper, strategic understanding of the future problems
facing the Department. The committee expects the Department to
preserve and reinforce the office’s analytical independence, institu-
tional standing, and sufficient funding level. The committee further
encourages the Department to provide the ONA with the resources,
access, and authorities necessary to fulfill its mission, particularly
as it produces assessments on the character of future warfare, geo-
economic competition, and the long-term balance of military power
between the United States and its adversaries.
Potable water purification systems for new surface combat-
ants
The committee remains concerned that, despite over a decade of
repeated congressional direction and dedicated funding, hazardous
bromine cartridge systems continue to be used for potable water
disinfection on certain Navy surface combatants. These systems un-
necessarily expose sailors to health hazards and impose significant
recurring costs related to the handling and disposal of hazardous
materials.
The committee notes that reliance on ‘‘inherited’’ baseline de-
signs—rather than deliberate, forward-looking requirements deci-
sions—has resulted in these outdated systems being incorporated
by default into new ship classes. This lack of modernization at the
design phase risks locking obsolete and hazardous technology into
platforms that will remain in the fleet for decades, ultimately re-
quiring far more expensive post-award retrofits or modernization
efforts.
Mixed-oxidant electrolytic disinfectant generator systems have
been successfully deployed on Navy aircraft carriers and amphib-
ious ships for more than 20 years, and more recently on the Arleigh
Burke-class destroyers (DDG–51) and littoral combat ship plat-
forms. These systems generate a disinfectant solution on demand
using only common salt and electricity, effectively eliminating the
need for bromine cartridges. The failure to transition smaller sur-
face combatants to this safer technology appears to be driven by ac-
quisition sequencing rather than technical limitations.
The committee expects potable water disinfection to be treated as
a class-specific design requirement for every new platform. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

and surge floor
The committee remains concerned by the increasingly complex
security environment in the Arctic, marked by growing strategic
competition and expanding military activity by near-peer adver-
saries. The committee recognizes that protecting U.S. national se-
curity interests and strengthening integrated deterrence across the
areas of responsibility of U.S. Northern Command (NORTHCOM),

Command (EUCOM) will require a sustained and adaptable mili-
tary presence capable of operating in the Arctic environment.
The committee also recognizes that force posture decisions in the
Arctic present unique operational, logistical, and infrastructure
challenges. While permanent stationing or homeporting of forces
may provide certain advantages, a flexible mix of forward presence,
rotational deployments, and surge capacity may offer greater re-
sponsiveness to evolving threats and operational requirements. Ac-
cordingly, the committee believes it is important for the Depart-
ment of Defense to assess the appropriate balance between endur-
ing Arctic capabilities and the ability to rapidly reinforce the region
when necessary.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in co-
ordination with the Secretaries of the military departments and the
Commander, NORTHCOM, the Commander, EUCOM, and the
Commander, INDOPACOM to submit a report to the congressional
defense committees, not later than June 1, 2027, assessing the fea-
sibility and advisability of maintaining a persistent and scalable
Department of Defense presence in the Arctic.
The report shall include:
(1) An assessment of the operational feasibility and strategic
value of maintaining a baseline level of Arctic-capable assets
across the maritime, aviation, ground, and multi-domain envi-
ronments;
(2) An identification of the capabilities, capacity, and force
structure required to sustain domain awareness, deterrence,
and rapid response capabilities across the Arctic regions rel-
evant to NORTHCOM, INDOPACOM, and EUCOM.
(3) An evaluation of options for maintaining a scalable surge
capability, including the personnel, platforms, logistics infra-
structure, and mobility requirements necessary to reinforce the
region during periods of increased tension or conflict;
(4) A description of any capability gaps, force structure limi-
tations, or infrastructure shortfalls that could affect the De-
partment’s ability to sustain operations in the Arctic; and E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Report on Navy’s use of synthetic oil
The committee notes that the Navy is working to meet major in-
creases in mission demand, operating tempo, and service life for its
limited number of ships. Measures need to be taken to extend ex-
isting fleets’ operating capability, decrease operational failures and
maintenance costs, improve safety, and widen performance bound-
aries. One cost-effective way to extend operating capability and
service life is to use synthetic oil to replace the Navy’s existing pe-
troleum-based oil. Synthetic technology improves systems perform-
ance at low temperatures, enables ship commanders to confidently
press performance limits in high tempo environments, and im-
proves overall motion control, propulsion, weapons, and acoustic
performance. Synthetic oils reduce onboard fire hazards, maintain
stability over large temperature ranges, and resist seawater con-
tamination, oxidation, and corrosion. Tests have shown that syn-
thetic lubricants significantly extend the duration between oil
changes by at least a factor of two and result in less corrective op-
erations and maintenance associated with carbon and varnish
build-up on critical components. Synthetic lubricants can also
greatly reduce signature levels, mitigating noise and improving
stealth and precision benefits and survivability of the platforms
they support.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of the Navy to
brief the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the
House of Representatives, not later than March 1, 2027, on the
Navy’s assessment of increased usage of synthetic lubricants. The
briefing shall include any current plans by the Navy to increase the
use of synthetic lubricants, an outline of its current use, costs and
benefits of increased usage, conversion costs, and any additional
funding required to realize the benefits of increased lifecycle sav-
ings and reduced corrective downtime.

The committee is aware that U.S. Special Operations Forces
have been assisting the Somali Armed Forces in countering al-
Shabaab in Somalia, but desires more information on constraints
limiting their effectiveness.
Therefore, the committee directs the Under Secretary of Defense

Zumwalt-class destroyer homeporting
The Navy has just notified the committee of a change of home
port for the USS Zumwalt (DDG–1000) from Pascagoula, Mis-

Study on improving civilian employee performance manage-
ment
The committee is grateful for the hard work and dedication of
the career civil servants who serve in the Department of Defense.
In particular, civil servants in managerial or supervisory roles are
vital to carrying out the Department’s many critical national secu-
rity missions, serving as an anchor for productivity, high stand-
ards, and a positive work environment. In any enterprise, super-
visors and managers are critical for ensuring a well-trained and
functioning workforce.
The committee notes that in order to continue to grow a strong,
more competitive, and efficient workforce, empowering supervisors
to have a greater say in shaping the force that they manage could
lead to better hiring decisions, stronger teams, and a more produc-
tive work environment. In recent years, the Department has car-
ried out attempts to shape the workforce through Department-wide
policies that sometimes lead to a one-size-fits-all approach, which
fails to provide the nuanced approach to employee performance
management that supervisors and managers are otherwise able to
provide.
In 2017, the Institute for Defense Analysis published a study ti-
tled, ‘‘Civilian Personnel Reform at the Department of Defense:
Lessons from the Failure of the National Security Personnel Sys-
tem.’’ Among other things, the study recommended amending the
2-year probationary period to require performance manager review
before an employee’s tenure became fixed. The committee notes
that civil servants in supervisory roles are already in an ideal posi-
tion to conduct such a performance review.

conduct a study on improving supervisor oversight, employee per- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Sec. 1270—Modification of requirements for Department of

provisions.heading: Countering Islamic State of Iraq and Syria
provisions.text:
The committee commends the deep partnership of the Kurdish
Peshmerga forces and Syrian Democratic forces with the United
States in degrading and defeating the threat from the Islamic State
of Iraq and Syria (ISIS).
The committee is deeply concerned that there is significant risk
in pivoting away from the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces,
which served as the primary United States partner in defeating the
ISIS caliphate in Syria, and relying instead on the Syrian govern-
ment to counter ISIS and other terrorist groups that could pose a
threat to the United States Homeland.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to pro-
vide a briefing, not later than October 1, 2026, on the performance
of the Syrian government in countering terrorist groups and actors
within Syria, including foreign terrorists.
Furthermore, the committee has concerns that the Department of
Defense did not request funding to train and equip the Kurdish
Peshmerga forces in its 2027 budget request for the Counter-ISIS
Train and Equip Fund.
Therefore, the committee further directs the Secretary of Defense
to provide a briefing, not later than October 1, 2026, to the Com-
mittees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Rep-
resentatives on: (1) The Department’s plans for the Counter-ISIS
Train and Equip Fund; (2) The rationale for not including such
funds in the budget request; and (3) Plans to improve the ability
of the Kurdish Peshmerga forces to support counterterrorism oper-
ations with the Iraqi Security Forces and the United States.
Assessment of Chinese Communist Party malign influence

provisions.heading: Assessment of Hezbollah
provisions.text:
To better understand the security environment in southern Leb-
anon, where Hezbollah’s de facto control has been virtually
uncontested by the legitimate Lebanese government for approxi-
mately 2 decades, the committee directs the Director of the Defense
Intelligence Agency to provide a briefing to the Senate Armed Serv-
ices Committee, not later than January 1, 2027, assessing changes
in the security environment in southern Lebanon from October 8,
2023, to the present day, including: (1) An assessment of the dam-
age to Hezbollah infrastructure, capabilities, and personnel due to
Israeli operations; (2) The extent to which the Lebanese Armed
Forces deployed to southern Lebanon consistent with the November
2024 ceasefire and January 2025 ceasefire extension; (3) The extent
to which the Lebanese Armed Forces has been willing to counter,
and/or has been effective in countering, Hezbollah at any point
since 2006, whether within southern Lebanon, northern Lebanon,
or Beirut; (4) An assessment of Hezbollah’s strength over the same
period, including its remaining power projection capabilities into
Israel; (5) An assessment of the means and financial networks used
and relied upon by Hezbollah to fund its reconstitution; (6) An
evaluation of efforts being made by the Lebanese Armed Forces to
plan for further disarmament of Hezbollah throughout other parts
of Lebanon, including in South Beirut and the Bekaa Valley; (7) An
assessment of actions taken by the Government of Lebanon to dem-
onstrate its willingness to exert authority over Lebanon, including
through political steps and military steps to disarm Hezbollah and
counter the abilities of Hezbollah to reconstitute; and (8) An assess-
ment of the steps that can be taken to undermine Hezbollah’s con-
trol in southern Lebanon, south Beirut, and the Bekaa Valley.

The committee notes that Taiwan imports the overwhelming ma-

that a disruption of such supplies through blockade or other means

The committee strongly supports efforts to build the combined

provisions.heading: States and India
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the strong bond between the United
States and India and the growing importance of the defense indus-
trial relationship within the broader bilateral relationship. The
committee notes the progress of the India-United States Defense
Acceleration Ecosystem (INDUS–X), which is intended to facilitate
partnerships among defense companies, investors, universities, and
accelerators in both countries, as well as the conclusion of a Secu-
rity of Supply Arrangement between the Department of Defense
and the Ministry of Defense of India in 2024.
The committee believes the Department should seek to identify
steps to further expand co-development, co-production, and recip-
rocal sourcing with India in areas of mutual strategic interest. The
committee further believes that legal, regulatory, acquisition, and
export-control barriers to deeper industrial cooperation should be
identified and, where appropriate, addressed.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Under Secretary of De-
fense for Acquisition and Sustainment, in coordination with the
Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, the Di-
rector of the Defense Security Cooperation Agency, and the Sec-
retary of State, to provide a briefing to the congressional defense
committees, not later than December 1, 2026, that:

India
The committee believes that the maturation of the military space
programs of our allies and partners in the Indo-Pacific region, spe-
cifically India, is in our national security interest given the growing
space threat posed by China.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Assistant Secretary of De-
fense for Space Policy and the Assistant Secretary of Defense for
Indo-Pacific Security Affairs to brief the congressional defense com-
mittees, not later than March 31, 2027, on efforts to expand and
deepen bilateral military exercises with India in the space domain.
This would include the potential integration of Indian commercial
space entities that could help mature the Indian military’s space
program while enabling the U.S. Space Force’s multi-domain oper-
ations with ally and partner nations. The exercises considered in
this matter include but are not limited to Cope India, Yudh
Abhyas, and Tiger Triumph.

United States national security interests related to the war
in Sudan
The committee remains deeply concerned by the ongoing conflict
in Sudan, the resulting mass displacement and atrocities, the de-
stabilizing effects of that conflict on the Horn of Africa and Red Sea
region, and the role of external actors in fueling the war.
The committee is concerned that the conflict in Sudan has impli-
cations not only for regional humanitarian conditions but also for
U.S. national security interests related to Red Sea maritime secu-
rity, strategic competition, illicit trafficking, regional partner sta-
bility, and the potential expansion of malign foreign influence.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in
coordination with the heads of relevant U.S. Government depart-
ments and agencies, to submit to the congressional defense commit-
tees, the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate, and the
Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives, not
later than March 1, 2027, a report on Sudan and the Red Sea cor-
ridor.
The report shall include:
(1) An assessment of United States national security inter-
ests affected by the conflict in Sudan, including implications
for Red Sea maritime security, regional force posture, access,
overflight, logistics, and partner engagement in the Horn of Af-
rica and adjoining theaters;
(2) An assessment of the roles of foreign state and non-state
actors in supporting, enabling, financing, arming, equipping,

Waste water surveillance
The committee notes waste water surveillance is an important
tool for pathogen outbreak and monitoring. The Cooperative Threat
Reduction program has a long and successful history in tracking
and securing weapons of mass destruction, which includes dan-
gerous pathogens, especially associated with laboratories securing
and handling these materials.
Therefore, the committee directs the Assistant Secretary of De-
fense for Nuclear Deterrence, Chemical, and Biological Defense Pol-
icy and Programs to provide a briefing to the congressional defense
committees, not later than March 31, 2027, on the feasibility and
advisability of developing partnering efforts to strengthen waste
water and other potential environmental and clinical sampling as
a means to track the spread of such pathogens as part of an overall
effort to secure these biological materials. Such a cooperative effort
will also serve as a deterrence function to the potential use of bio-
logical agents.

provisions.heading: Items of Special Interest
provisions.text:
Domestic antimony and copper recovery for defense appli-
cations
The committee remains concerned about the continued reliance
of the United States on foreign sources of antimony and copper,
both critical minerals essential to the defense industrial base. The
committee notes the potential opportunity to recover antimony and
copper as byproducts of domestic mineral production and the pos-
sible benefits such recovery could provide for supply chain resil-
ience and national security.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in
coordination with the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition
and Sustainment and the Defense Logistics Agency, to conduct a
feasibility and advisability study regarding the establishment of a E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

pilot program to support the recovery of antimony and copper as
byproducts of mineral production in the United States. The study
should assess: (1) The technical feasibility of recovering antimony
and copper from domestic mineral production streams using mul-
tiple recovery processes and techniques; (2) The potential for devel-
oping process design plans necessary to scale such recovery activi-
ties to demonstration-level production; (3) The feasibility of gener-
ating representative sample materials for independent testing and
validation of suitability for defense applications; (4) The ability of
domestic producers to manufacture antimony materials that meet
Defense Logistics Agency specifications; (5) The estimated costs,
schedule, and resource requirements associated with establishing
and executing such a pilot program; (6) The expected benefits to do-
mestic supply chain resilience and reductions in dependence on for-
eign sources of antimony and copper; and (7) Any legislative or ad-
ministrative actions needed to support the establishment of such a
pilot program. The committee further directs the Secretary to sub-
mit the feasibility and advisability study to the Senate Armed
Services Committee, not later than March 31, 2027.
Recovery of critical minerals from lithium-ion battery waste
The committee finds that the secure domestic recovery of critical
minerals is a matter of significant national security. When properly
recycled, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) yield several of the most stra-
tegically important minerals in the U.S. supply chain, including
those essential for national defense such as graphite, manganese,
nickel, cobalt, and lithium. As the volume of LIB scrap continues
to escalate, the Department of Defense should view its own waste
streams as a strategic source for these materials rather than a dis-
posal liability.
The committee notes that the Defense Logistics Agency Haz-
ardous Waste Disposition Services does not currently recycle LIBs
internally. Instead, it classifies them as hazardous or universal
waste, consolidates them at Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) sites,
and ships them under contract to certified recyclers or treatment
facilities—with some of those materials eventually being exported
to geopolitical rivals for further recovery. As the demand for U.S.-
sourced critical minerals and other metals increases, recycling can
prove a viable option based on changes in recovery technology and
methods and changes in the market. The committee is concerned
about the limited information regarding the composition of the
waste stream generated by DLA, making it difficult to ensure these
strategic minerals are being recovered.
Therefore, the committee directs the Director of the Defense Lo-
gistics Agency (DLA) to provide a briefing to the Committees on
Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives,
not later than March 1, 2027, on how the DLA tracks, character-
izes, and reports the composition of critical minerals present in
DLA-managed LIB waste streams. The briefing shall include the
following: (1) An assessment of current LIB data collection prac-
tices, including any existing tracking of mineral content and a plan
to improve systematic tracking of materials contained in LIB waste
streams; (2) Opportunities to integrate advanced sorting, sensing,
or analytical technologies to improve the characterization of waste E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

streams; (3) Identification of required changes to the DLA’s logis-
tics, contracting, or hazardous waste management systems to en-

utory authorities and specialized capabilities required to implement
a recovery program, including the ability of the domestic industrial
base to provide these services; (5) An assessment of the costs to

The committee notes that the Department of Defense is currently
developing strategic plans to strengthen domestic supply chains for

range of industrial and defense applications. Tungsten is a strategi-
cally important material, and the United States has the potential
to establish a robust domestic supply chain capable of reducing re-

fense needs.
The committee is concerned about the current reliance on foreign
sources of tungsten and the associated risks to national security,
supply chain resilience, and defense readiness. The lack of a fully
developed domestic tungsten supply chain presents challenges in
ensuring consistent access to materials necessary for critical de-
fense systems and industrial applications. The absence of a domes-

provisions.text:
Affordable dual-capable air-launched strike capabilities
The committee is concerned that the evolving security environ-
ment increasingly requires the United States to deter and, if nec-
essary, prevail in simultaneous or overlapping crises across mul-
tiple theaters. The committee notes that potential adversaries con-
tinue to expand and diversify their inventories of long-range con-
ventional and nuclear-capable strike systems, including cruise mis-
siles, ballistic missiles, and hypersonic weapons designed to hold
United States forces, allies, and partners at risk. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

The committee further recognizes that current and planned
United States air-launched strike capabilities often involve highly
specialized systems optimized for either conventional or nuclear
missions, are procured in relatively limited quantities, or may not
be affordable to produce at the scale required for sustained oper-
ations in a protracted conflict. As a result, the committee believes
the Department of the Air Force should evaluate opportunities to
leverage common technologies, production infrastructure, and mod-
ular designs to develop more affordable and scalable air-launched
weapons capable of supporting both conventional and strategic de-
terrence requirements.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force,
in coordination with the Commander, U.S. Strategic Command, the
Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment, and
the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, to
conduct an assessment of options for developing a family of afford-
able, dual-capable air-launched cruise missiles, air-launched bal-
listic missiles, and air-launched hypersonic glide vehicles to include
a conventional variant of the Long Range Stand-Off Weapon that
could be produced at scale and employed by both fighter and bomb-
er aircraft.
The assessment shall examine:
(1) Operational requirements for dual-capable air-launched
weapons across the Indo-Pacific, European, and other geo-
graphic combatant command theaters;
(2) Opportunities to employ common airframes, propulsion
systems, guidance packages, launch interfaces, and other sub-
systems across conventional and nuclear mission sets;
(3) Options for integrating such weapons onto current and
planned Air Force fighter and bomber aircraft;
(4) Anticipated acquisition, procurement, sustainment, and
lifecycle costs associated with alternative concepts;
(5) Production capacity, supply chain considerations, and op-
portunities to maximize surge manufacturing capability during
crisis or conflict;
(6) The extent to which commercially derived technologies,
digital engineering approaches, open-system architectures, and
nontraditional defense contractors could reduce development
timelines and program costs;
(7) The relative advantages, limitations, and operational
risks associated with cruise missile, ballistic missile, and
hypersonic glide vehicle approaches;
(8) Opportunities to increase magazine depth and provide
commanders with a broader range of survivable strike options
at short-, medium-, and long-range distances; and
(9) Any legislative, budgetary, policy, or infrastructure-re-
lated considerations relevant to the development, deployment,
and sustainment of such capabilities.
Not later than April 1, 2027, the Secretary of the Air Force shall
brief the congressional defense committees on the results of the as-
sessment, including recommendations for potential prototype ef-
forts, technology demonstrations, acquisition strategies, and invest-

provisions.heading: Edge Resilience
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes that the 2026 National Defense Strat-
egy identifies electromagnetic spectrum (EMS) superiority as a pre-
requisite for maintaining U.S. military advantage and deterring
adversaries in increasingly contested operational environments.
The committee acknowledges that the Army Research Laboratory’s
collaborative research efforts through Project Autonomous EMS
Dominance and Edge Resilience (AEDER) to develop leap-ahead ca-
pabilities in communications, sensing, data processing, and elec-
tronic warfare. By integrating artificial intelligence and machine
learning with cyber and electromagnetic operations, Project
AEDER seeks to accelerate the development of autonomous capa-
bilities capable of detecting, identifying, and responding to adver-
sary actions at machine speed while protecting friendly systems
from interference and attack.
The committee is particularly encouraged by research efforts fo-
cused on resilient communications and adaptive antenna tech-
nologies, autonomous swarm and counter-swarm operations, ad-
vanced multi-modal sensing and positioning capabilities, and AI-
driven tactical edge computing. These technologies have the poten-
tial to enhance situational awareness, strengthen resilient commu-
nications in contested environments, improve protection against
electronic attack, and accelerate decision-making at the tactical
edge.
Accordingly, the committee emphasizes that sustained funding
for Project AEDER is critical to maturing these technologies, accel-
erating their transition to the warfighter, and achieving and main-
taining dominance across the electromagnetic spectrum.

Briefing on acquisition of Hypersonic and Ballistic Tracking

provisions.heading: Space Sensor
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the critical importance of Golden Dome
for America and advancing our missile defense capabilities to
counter emerging and evolving threats posed by both ballistic and
maneuverable hypersonic missiles. The successful deployment of
advanced missile defense systems is paramount in maintaining na-
tional security and ensuring the defense of the Homeland. In this
regard, the committee strongly emphasizes the significance of the
Hypersonic and Ballistic Tracking Space Sensor (HBTSS) capa-
bility, which underwent exhaustive competition and deployment of
a successful prototype under the Missile Defense Agency. The
HBTSS provides real-time tracking and early detection of
hypersonic and ballistic missiles over an operationally relevant
range of threat trajectories, enabling timely and effective intercep-
tion. The space-based sensor network is essential for providing con-
tinuous global coverage, high-resolution tracking, and improved
discrimination of complex threat environments.
To this end, in the spirit of the Acquisition Transformation Strat-
egy’s focus on delivering capability and speed and scale, embracing
proven capabilities that are ready-now, the committee directs the
U.S. Space Force to prioritize acquisition and operational deploy-
ment of a full constellation of at least 45 space vehicles equipped
with proven HBTSS payloads within the anticipated Missile De-
fense Tranche 3 (MDT3) program. In consideration of the urgent
need for this capability, the committee recommends that the U.S.
Space Force expedite the MDT3 program by utilizing the flexibility
of other transaction authorities (OTA) to move already competed,
successful prototype demonstrations into production to streamline
the acquisition process. This approach will facilitate rapid develop-
ment and deployment while maintaining rigorous oversight and ac-

Accordingly, the committee directs the Assistant Secretary of the
Air Force for Space Acquisition and Integration and the Director of
the Missile Defense Agency to provide a detailed briefing to the

sive acquisition plan for the MDT3 HBTSS constellation, including
timelines, cost estimates, and the intended use of sole source con-
tracts and OTAs. The briefing shall also address risk mitigation
strategies and coordination efforts with other relevant defense pro-
grams to ensure seamless integration and functionality of the
HBTSS.

Briefing on continuity of operations for Space Development
Agency ground infrastructure
The committee recognizes the critical importance of resilient
ground infrastructure to support space-enabled command and con-
trol, including space domain awareness, custody, and fire control
integration functions associated with proliferated space architec-
tures. The committee further notes that future contested and de-
graded operational environments will require the ability to main-
tain uninterrupted ground operations and mission management
functions supporting space-based capabilities.
The committee is interested in ensuring that the Department of
Defense maintains continuity of operations for mission-critical
ground systems supporting space warfighting capabilities, includ-
ing geographically distributed resilience and the ability to operate
through disruption or attack.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force,
in coordination with the Director of the Space Development Agen-

not later than March 31, 2027, on the Department’s plan to ensure
continuity of operations for ground infrastructure supporting space
domain awareness, custody, and fire control missions associated
with proliferated space architectures. The briefing shall include: (1)
The Department’s approach to establishing geographically distrib-
uted continuity of operations capabilities to ensure resilient and
uninterrupted ground operations under degraded or contested con-
ditions; (2) How existing Space Operations Center infrastructure is
being leveraged or adapted to support continuity of operations re-
quirements; (3) The integration of mission management functions
within the broader ground infrastructure supporting space-enabled
command and control; (4) The resources, infrastructure, and per-
sonnel required to achieve and sustain continuous 24-hour, 7-day-
per-week operational capability; and (5) Key milestones, implemen-

ational capability for distributed continuity of operations functions.

U.S. forces overseas, and serve allied and partner nations. Recent

rates exceeding 90 percent in engagements against cruise missiles,

The committee recognizes that future space operations will re-

sustained operations in a contested space domain. The committee
further notes that U.S. Space Command has identified space mobil-

space architectures, and support sustained deterrence and

sparing and sustainment plan
The committee notes that the Lower Tier Air and Missile De-
fense Sensor (LTAMDS) is the Army’s primary radar for the Inte-
grated Air and Missile Defense used by the United States and its
allies and partners. Additionally, the committee notes that the
Army has been designated the lead to integrate the LTAMDS into
the existing Phased Array Tracking Radar to Intercept on Target
(PATRIOT) weapon system architecture for the United States and
its 19 PATRIOT partner nations across the globe.
The committee understands that global missile defense posture
will rely heavily on LTAMDS capabilities to meet growing demand
for defense against advancing tactical ballistic missile and air
breathing threats and to withstand increased requirements for ra-
diation or ‘‘burn time’’ necessary to prevent threat leaks through
the layered defense architecture.
However, the committee is concerned that the Army has not ade-
quately defined the sparing package required for each LTAMDS
radar to ensure the system stays fully mission capable to meet de-
manding unified combatant commands’ commander requirements
for air defense of forward-deployed forces. The lack of a dedicated
sparing risks undermining billions of dollars in LTAMDS procure-
ment over the Department of Defense’s future years defense pro- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

quate sustainment planning is seen in the extreme case of the
Army’s current usage of a second LTAMDS radar in Guam solely
for cannibalization of parts for the other radar in testing.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Army to
brief the congressional defense committees, not later than March 1,
2027, on the sustainment and sparing plan for LTAMDS. The brief-

(5) Identification of near-term mission support gaps and

Briefing on options for development of low-cost space-based
interceptors in support of Golden Dome for America
The committee is concerned about emerging threats to the Home-
land as near-peer adversaries build and diversify their missile in-
ventories. The drastic increase in the volume and capability of
cruise, ballistic, hypersonic, and space-based missile threats over
the last several years requires a transformational response. The air
and missile defense system proposed by Executive Order 14186,
commonly known as Golden Dome for America, may provide the ar-
chitecture necessary to provide a lasting, modern defense against
these emerging threats. The architecture’s effectiveness is reliant
on the successful development and deployment of a proliferated
space-based interceptor (SBI) network of constellations to defeat in-
coming threats. In addition to a proliferated SBI network, the De-
partment of Defense must deploy an all-inclusive mesh command
and control solution that connects all capabilities into a single do-
main to provide theater-level insights for all potential threats.
The committee is aware of commercially available terminals able
to combine electronic warfare for terrestrial and space domain
awareness, artificial intelligence for electronic warfare and sensor
fusion applications, and secure tactical communications with a soft-
ware-defined radio and on-orbit software programmable crypto de-
veloped specifically to address these challenges. Commercially
available space terminal providers offer qualified low earth orbit
(LEO) space payloads and relevant application experience to meet
Golden Dome and Space Force needs and may aid in driving down
costs for an SBI constellation.
The committee encourages the U.S. Space Force to procure, test,
and evaluate commercial terminals launched and qualified in LEO
for integration into the future Golden Dome architecture that can

Briefing on proliferated space architectures
The committee notes the importance of proliferated space archi-
tectures for enabling resilience and mission assurance for national
security needs derived from space-based capabilities. The com-
mittee observes that proliferated space architectures in low earth
orbit (LEO) and geosynchronous earth orbit (GEO) for communica-

tionately benefit from the resilience provided by proliferation.
The committee further notes that proliferated architectures for
these mission areas provide an asymmetric advantage to the U.S.
national security community and deny first-mover advantage to ad-
versaries targeting space-based capabilities. Furthermore, the com-
mittee expresses interest in the potential for the Department of the
Air Force to leverage ‘‘productized,’’ domestically produced commer-

Briefing on radiation source testing capacity
The committee is concerned that existing radiation source testing

The committee recognizes that, in 2012, the Department of De-

(UARC) at the University of Nebraska, sponsored by the U.S. Stra-

among the United States, Russia, and China

among the United States, Russia, and China is occurring alongside
increasing reliance on space-based capabilities and the continued

sence of sufficient transparency, predictability, and risk reduction
mechanisms in both the nuclear and space domains increases the
potential for miscalculation, escalation, and unintended conflict. In
the absence of treaty-based mechanisms, measures for consistent
analytical reporting and transparency between the executive

sists of numerous legacy and fragmented systems that may not
adequately support the operational, workforce management,
auditability, and readiness requirements associated with imple-
mentation of the Personnel Management Act. Space Force has
identified the need for a unified and scalable human resources
management capability capable of integrating personnel data, auto-

force readiness requirements across sustained-duty and non-sus-
tained-duty Guardian populations. The committee believes that the
modernization of Space Force personnel systems is important to
supporting operational agility, talent management, readiness visi-
bility, and enterprise data management in support of the service’s
evolving warfighting mission. The committee further recognizes
that modern enterprise systems may improve accountability, trans-
parency, and interoperability in support of the Department of De-
fense’s objective of achieving a clean audit by 2028.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force,
in coordination with the Chief of Space Operations, to provide a

March 1, 2027, on the status of Space Force human resources infor-
mation technology modernization efforts. The briefing shall include:
(1) An assessment of projected cost savings and operational
efficiencies associated with modernization efforts;
(2) An explanation of how modernization efforts will support
audit readiness and enterprise data management objectives;
(3) A description of commercial technologies, cloud-based ar-
chitectures, automation capabilities, and data integration tools
being evaluated or implemented; and
(4) Any additional resources, authorities, or legislative ac-
tions required to achieve full operational capability by fiscal
year 2028.
Electromagnetic pulse capabilities of China
The committee remains concerned that advances in China’s elec-
tromagnetic pulse (EMP) research, development, and acquisition
activities could pose a significant threat to Taiwan. Given Taiwan’s
threat environment and geographic positioning, a successful EMP
or high-altitude electromagnetic pulse (HEMP) strike could rapidly
degrade the island’s ability to sustain its civilian population and
mount an effective defense. Given Taiwan’s unique vulnerabilities,
the committee is concerned that China may view such an attack as
an attractive first strike in a conflict with the island because the
effects can be catastrophic while remaining below the threshold of
conventional armed attack.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in con-
sultation with the Secretary of State, the Director of National In-
telligence, and the Secretary of Energy, to brief the congressional
defense committees, not later than March 31, 2027, on the fol-
lowing:

Electronic warfare workforce at Fort Huachuca Electronic

provisions.heading: Proving Ground
provisions.text:
The committee notes that the workforce for electronic warfare
and testing is a small and highly skilled workforce sometimes tak-
ing decades to train and typically having an outsized impact on De-
partment of Defense electronic warfare programs. The committee is
concerned about staffing at the Electronic Proving Ground (EPG),
given recent actions on force reduction in the Department.
Therefore, not later than March 1, 2027, and annually thereafter
through March 1, 2030, the Secretary of the Army shall brief the
congressional defense committees on staffing levels at the EPG.
The briefing shall include: (1) The number of full-time employees
as of the end of the preceding fiscal year; (2) Efforts to ensure the
EPG staffing is capable of performing its necessary testing mission;
and (3) A description of any actions and the reason for force reduc-
tions of such skilled staff at the EPG.
Enhancing adversarial testing for United States space assets
The committee notes that space systems, supporting terrestrial
infrastructure, and commercial space services integrated into De-
partment of Defense (DOD) operations face sophisticated, evolving
cyber threats, and that emerging acquisition requirements for an-
nual government-led adversarial cybersecurity testing require a
scalable execution model. The committee directs the Secretary of
the Air Force, acting through the Chief of Space Operations and in
coordination with the Office of the Assistant Secretary of the Air
Force for Space Acquisition and Integration, to assess and brief the
congressional defense committees, not later than March 31, 2027,
on the development of a repeatable framework for government-led
adversarial cybersecurity testing of DOD space Programs of Record,
associated ground segments, supporting commercial space services,
and relevant launch infrastructure.
This briefing shall address: (1) A framework description: govern-
ance, roles, authorities, and a methodology for persistent adver-
sarial engagement; (2) A method to emulate nation-state tactics,
techniques, and procedures and produce mission impact findings
assessing operational consequences; (3) The ability to conduct test-
ing on not fewer than two major space programs, including ground
infrastructure, with prioritized remediation actions and assigned
timelines; and (4) The capability to extend testing to ground sta-
tions, launch infrastructure, critical supporting utilities, and com-
mercial space services upon which DOD operations depend.
Expanding electronic warfare and counter-electronic war-
fare integration and testing facilities
The committee notes that the Department of Defense (DOD)
must prioritize developing and implementing robust, integrated
counter-electronic warfare (EW) systems and hardware quickly and
at scale across all components. Counter-EW capabilities are a crit- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

ical gap for the DOD, and recent battlefield experiences in Ukraine,
Gaza, and other conflict zones demonstrate the vulnerability of un-
manned systems and munitions to EW attack and interference. If
DOD unmanned systems and munitions lack counter-EW systems
and hardware, they will be ineffective at deterring peer competitors
or prevailing in peer-to-peer conflict. Most current and future DOD
unmanned systems and munitions should include integrated
counter-EW systems that harden them against EW attack and in-
terference, including communications, signal, multi-spectrum, and
global positioning system jamming and spoofing.
The committee believes that this hardware should be integrated,
because without an integrated counter-EW hardware, unmanned
systems are functionally ineffective under real-world contested con-
ditions. Accordingly, the DOD will accelerate development, procure-
ment, adoption, and implementation of robust counter-EW systems
and hardware, prioritizing capabilities that protect command and
control and the precision, navigation, and timing of any unmanned
systems and munitions. This hardware must be integrated into
new contracts, systems, and munitions and must also be integrated
into existing contracts, systems, and munitions.
Facility damage at Space Force launch ranges due to launch
The committee notes that recent launch and landing activities at

caused damage to government facilities. This damage is primarily
attributed to shock waves generated during reentry, commonly re-

to brief the congressional defense committees, not later than March

damaged from the shock waves caused by launch and landing, how

can expedite restitution or other such preventive actions, if so re-
quired.
Feasibility and advisability of expanding Operation Olympic

The committee recognizes that Multinational Force Operation
Olympic Defender (MNF–OOD), which reached initial operating ca-

demonstrated successful on-orbit operations and interoperability, is
a key framework for strengthening deterrence, resilience, and re-
sponsible behavior in space. Expanding participation to additional
Indo-Pacific allies, including Japan and the Republic of Korea,
would further reinforce burden sharing and enhance collective
space domain awareness in a strategically contested region.
Therefore, the committee directs the Chief of Space Operations
to submit to the congressional defense committees a report, not
later than March 31, 2027, on the feasibility and advisability of ex- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: Feasibility of establishing Joint Commercial Operations
provisions.text:
cells in the Indo-Pacific region
The committee notes that the development of joint partner na-
tions’ commercial space operations is an important mechanism for
sharing space domain awareness information and expanding the
capability for beyond-line-of-sight communications. In particular,
given the large area encompassing the Indo-Pacific region, there
are advantages to developing such joint commercial space oper-
ations cells with regard to Department of Defense operations.
Therefore, not later than May 1, 2027, the Commander, U.S.
Space Command, shall brief the congressional defense committees
on the feasibility and advisability of establishing additional Joint
Commercial Operations cells in the Indo-Pacific region to com-
plement existing such joint commercial cells in Australia and New
Zealand.
The briefing shall include the following: (1) An assessment of the
feasibility and advisability of establishing Joint Commercial Oper-
ations cells in Japan, the Republic of Korea, India, and any other
jurisdiction in the Indo-Pacific region the Commander considers ap-
propriate; and (2) An identification of any funding or policy change
necessary to feasibly establish Joint Commercial Operations cells
in Japan, the Republic of Korea, India, and any other jurisdiction
in the Indo-Pacific region the Commander considers appropriate.
Fort Huachuca electronic proving ground assessment
The committee recognizes the critical role of the Electronic Prov-
ing Ground (EPG) at Fort Huachuca, Arizona, in supporting testing E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

committee also recognizes that the EPG operates the only National

and their personnel are level II certified. The committee further
recognizes the increasing importance of these capabilities to the
missions of the Space Force, particularly in contested electro-

Therefore, given these unique attributes, the committee directs
the Secretary of the Air Force, in coordination with the Chief of

Not later than May 1, 2027, the Secretary of the Air Force shall

the assessment, along with any recommendations for legislative or
administrative action.
Future space launch capacity
The committee remains concerned about the Nation’s ability to
maintain sufficient, resilient, and geographically diverse launch ca-
pacity to meet current and projected national security space re-
quirements and has consistently emphasized the importance of as-
sured access to space, launch infrastructure resilience, and the
availability of multiple launch providers capable of supporting De-
partment of Defense missions. The committee is aware of the re-
cent New Glenn launch vehicle anomaly at Space Launch Complex
36 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. Given the importance
of resilient launch infrastructure and sufficient launch capacity to
support national security space requirements, the committee di-
rects the Secretary of the Air Force to submit a report and provide
a briefing to the congressional defense committees, not later than
December 1, 2026.
The report shall include:
(1) A summary of the known facts regarding the anomaly
and the status of any ongoing investigations;
(2) An assessment of the impact of the anomaly and any re-
sulting infrastructure damage on the availability of launch ca-
pacity and launch infrastructure supporting national security
space missions;
(3) An assessment of any resulting impacts to National Secu-
rity Space Launch program requirements, mission assurance,
launch resiliency, and assured access to space objectives;
(4) An evaluation of the extent to which the anomaly affects
the assumptions, findings, conclusions, and recommendations
developed pursuant to section 1608 of the National Defense
Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Public Law 119–60), ti-
tled, ‘‘Spaceport of the Future Initiative and Study on Future
Space Launch Capacity’’;

radation, or temporary unavailability of a major launch vehicle E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

from the anomaly.
The report shall also identify any additional actions the Depart-

The committee notes that the Golden Dome for America (GDA)

GDA architecture is a ‘‘system of systems’’ comprising space-,
air-, ground-, and sea-based sensors, kinetic and non-kinetic inter-
ceptors, and an integrated battle management, command, and con-
trol system intended to operate at machine speed. The verification
and validation of such an architecture against the full spectrum of
mixed-raid threa

Launch operations at Kodiak
The committee recognizes the growing importance of responsive
and resilient access to space for national security missions and the
strategic value of the Pacific Spaceport Complex Alaska as a
launch location capable of supporting polar and high-inclination
missions. The committee understands that additional infrastruc-
ture investments may be required to support current and future
national security space launch requirements at Kodiak.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force
to provide a report and associated briefing on the report to the con-
gressional defense committees, not later than April 1, 2027, assess-
ing the infrastructure, capability, funding, and authority require-
ments necessary to support current and future national security
space launch operations at Kodiak.
The report should identify the modifications, upgrades, and in-
vestments and feasibility thereof required to enable future and ex-
panded Space Force and national security launch activities; provide
estimated costs associated with such investments; and identify any E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

for:

cluding Sensitive Compartmented Information Facilities,
SIPRNET connectivity, JWICS connectivity, and other secure
communications capabilities;
(2) Climate-controlled vehicle integration facilities, payload

The committee further directs the Secretary to identify opportu-

that could accelerate infrastructure development at Kodiak and
provide recommendations regarding how such investments could be
leveraged to support future Department of Defense missions, in-
cluding investments supporting launch vehicle integration, payload
processing, and responsive space operations.
Initial Operational Capability of space control weapon sys-
tems
The committee notes that a key acquisition feature of Depart-
ment of Defense weapon systems is to spiral the acquisition devel-
opment so that the warfighter is given not a perfect solution but
one that works initially and is refined thereafter. The concept of a
weapon system for the U.S. Space Force and, in particular, a space
control weapon system is relatively new given the U.S. Space Force
itself is 6 years old. Issues such as test and training are essentially
new concepts for space warfighting systems. Yet in the other title
10 Services, spiral development and test and training are long-
standing objectives. Space Force Instruction 13–604, ‘‘System Ac-
ceptance,’’ is the first integrated approach to fielding space weap-
ons systems. The first step, however, is entry into the system ac-
ceptance process. The normal nomenclature would be Initial Oper-
ational Capability, which in effect drives down into the acquisition
process a date by which system development should be pressurized
to achieve. It is not a complete solution, but it does get the weapon E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

system into the warfighter’s use for additional test and training in
order to give feedback for material improvement.
This iterative process, starting with an Initial Operational Capa-
bility, is found in a Chief of Space Operations note to Guardians,
C–Note #38, April 24, 2026, ‘‘Space Acquisitions—A Warfighting
Imperative.’’ It states, ‘‘An 80 percent solution in the warfighters’
hands today is infinitely more valuable than a 100 percent solution
that arrives late. Well-intentioned setbacks are not failures, but
rather a means to learn and improve. In fact, taking more cal-
culated risk in capability delivery can decrease operational risk in
the end.’’
Therefore, the committee directs the Chief of Space Operations
to review all ongoing Space Control Weapons System acquisition
programs to determine if these programs are set with an Initial
Operational Capability date to pressurize the acquisition program
development not for a 100 percent solution but one that is 80 per-
cent. The Chief of Space Operations shall brief the congressional
defense committees on his findings, with recommendations, not
later than March 1, 2027.
Integration of space domain awareness in joint exercises
and training
The committee recognizes that space domain awareness (SDA) is
a foundational capability for the Joint Force. It underpins the abil-
ity to detect, track, characterize, and respond to threats in an in-
creasingly congested and contested space environment. Peer and
near-peer adversaries are expanding their on-orbit and
counterspace capabilities. Persistent and resilient space domain
awareness is therefore essential to protecting United States and al-
lied space assets and to maintaining freedom of operation in the
Indo-Pacific region.
The committee further recogn

provisions.heading: Positioning System (GPS) Satellite System III. This control system
