was to take full advantage of military grade encryption as well as
cyber hardness. The contract for production was awarded to
Raytheon at roughly $3.7 billion with work to be performed at its
Aurora, Colorado, facility and completed by 2016. A key tenet of
the acquisition acceleration was for the Government to accept the
product under a Department of Defense Form 250 (DD250) before
final operational acceptance. Normally, a DD250 acceptance is not
obtained until all defects or liens under the contract are resolved.
Due to poor performance with the Development, Security, and Op-
erations software production framework to incorporate cyber secu-
rity, the program was forced to undergo a critical Nunn-McCurdy
breach (section 4375 of title 10, United States Code) as per section
1610 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year
2017 (Public Law 114–328). The program was to be subsequently
re-baselined with a service cost position of $8.3 billion and was
ready to transition to operations (RTO) in the 3rd quarter of fiscal
year 2022. An independent cost position was $8.5 billion with an
RTO date of the 1st quarter of fiscal year 2023. Due to ongoing
delays and cost-overruns, the OCX was not transferred to the De-
partment until the summer of 2025.
On April 17, 2026, the congressional defense committees were in-
formed that the Undersecretary of Defense for Acquisition and
Sustainment cancelled the program, stating that, ‘‘The OCX pro-
gram has long been plagued by technical challenges, inadequate E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

has resulted in numerous schedule slips and associated cost
growth.’’ Further, the statement said that the existing GPS control
system built by Lockheed Martin would be modified to meet cyber
security requirements in order to control the GPS III and IIIF con-
stellation.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force
to conduct an Acquisition Incident Review (AIR) of the OCX pro-
gram and to brief the congressional defense committees, not later
than January 31, 2027. Sixty days after receipt of the AIR, the
committee directs the Comptroller General of the United States to

The committee and the Comptroller General have closely fol-
lowed the OCX program since its inception, pointing out problem-
atic decisions by both the Air Force and the prime contractor
Raytheon. It is important to perform an examination of the failed
effort to understand the root causes and avoid repeating them in

Launch ranges for medium and small lift capacity
The committee notes that the Public Law 119–21 provided sig-
nificant mandatory funding for National Security Space Launch
(NSSL) infrastructure to support assured access to space, launch
resiliency, and increased launch capacity in response to growing
NSSL demand. While the two existing Space Force ranges, the
Eastern Range and the Western Range, are capable of heavy and
super heavy launch capacity, a wide range of non-Space Force
ranges exist capable of NSSL medium and small lift capacity. They
can take the increasing launch rate burden from the two major
Space Force ranges. This is important given that the blast radius
of heavy and super-heavy launch pads is so large that adjacent
launch operations cannot proceed for long periods of time, affecting
other launch providers, including those that provide medium and
small lift capacity.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force
to brief the congressional defense committees, not later than March
31, 2027, on efforts to utilize these non-Space Force launch ranges
as a means to ease the launch burden on the Eastern Range and
the Western Range, and to list support given to these ranges for
their use.
Prioritization of commercial off-the-shelf tools at National

artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities across the defense intel-
ligence enterprise, particularly semantic search functionality ap-
plied to geospatial datasets. The committee encourages the Depart-

pecially the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA), to

(COTS) solutions where appropriate, rather than defaulting to cus-

Proliferated space architectures
The committee notes the importance of proliferated space archi-
tectures for enabling resilience and mission assurance for national
security needs derived from space-based capabilities. Proliferated
space architectures in low earth orbit (LEO) and geosynchronous
earth orbit (GEO) for fire control, communications, missile warn-
ing, and other space control missions disproportionately benefit
from the resilience provided by proliferation. Proliferated architec-
tures for these missions’ areas provide asymmetric advantage to
the U.S. national security community and deny first-mover advan-
tage to adversaries targeting space-based capabilities.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force
to provide a briefing to the congressional defense committees, not
later than March 31, 2027, on how the core mission areas of the
Space Force would benefit from transitioning to proliferated space
architectures in LEO and GEO through the acquisition of
productized, domestically produced commercial satellite buses. The
briefing shall include: (1) An assessment of how the core functions
of the Space Force would benefit from more proliferated space ar-
chitectures across all mission areas and orbital regimes; (2) An as-
sessment of the benefits of proliferated space architectures in en-
suring persistent mission availability that denies adversaries first-
mover advantage in times of conflict; (3) The cost, schedule, and
performance implications of transitioning to proliferated space ar-
chitectures while leveraging commoditized domestically produced
buses; and (4) The challenges of transitioning to such an architec-
ture within the next 2 years and a mitigation plan to address those
challenges.

an effort to improve cross-mission integration, align requirements

ance and program structure
The committee recognizes that accurate and timely environ-
mental monitoring and weather forecasting are foundational to
military success across space, air, missile warning, ground, naval,
and global strike missions. The committee notes with concern that
legacy space-based environmental monitoring systems, including
the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program, are projected to
cease operations in the near term, while replacement capabilities
such as the Weather System Follow-on-Microwave are not yet fully
operational or accessible. The committee is concerned that this
transition period may create gaps in environmental awareness that
could adversely impact operational effectiveness.
The committee further notes longstanding ambiguity regarding
responsibility within the Department of the Air Force for space-
based environmental monitoring capabilities, including the acquisi-
tion and integration of commercial weather data. While the Space
Force has been identified as the responsible Service, the committee

electro-optical space and ground capabilities in support of time-sen-

Review of National Security Space Launch Phase 3 acquisi-
tion strategy
The committee notes that the National Security Space Launch
(NSSL) Phase 3 construct is intended to ensure assured access to
space for the integrated space architecture at affordable prices
through a dual-lane approach, with Lane 1 designed to expand
competition and enable higher-risk missions and Lane 2 structured
as a block buy to provide stability, cadence assurance, and high
mission assurance for critical national security payloads. While this
framework was intended to balance innovation, resilience, competi-
tion, and predictability, the committee observes that rapid advance-
ments in commercial launch capabilities and evolving mission re-
quirements raise questions regarding whether both lanes are
achieving their intended outcomes in practice.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force,
in coordination with the Chief of Space Operations and the Assist-
ant Secretary of the Air Force for Space Acquisition and Integra-
tion, to provide a briefing to the congressional defense committees,
not later than March 31, 2027, on the performance and structure
of NSSL Phase 3 across both Lane 1 and Lane 2.
The briefing shall include: (1) An assessment of cost, schedule,
performance, mission assurance, and competition outcomes for both
lanes; (2) An evaluation of the extent to which Lane 1 has achieved
its objectives of expanding competition, enabling new entrants, and
driving affordability; (3) An assessment of whether the Lane 2
block buy construct continues to deliver intended benefits in cost
predictability, cadence stability, industrial base sustainment, and
mission assurance; (4) An analysis of how task order development,
requirements formulation, and contracting structures across both
lanes affect competition, pricing, and innovation; and (5) An exam-
ination of whether the current dual-lane construct remains opti-
mally aligned with evolving commercial launch capabilities and
mission needs, and what alternative structures or adjustments may
better achieve program objectives of affordability, resilience, and
assured access to space.

provisions.heading: Solar Observing Optical Network
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the importance of the Solar Observing
Optical Network (SOON) to provide critical solar observations
through monitoring sunspots to predict the occurrence of a flare or
coronal mass ejection. Along with other systems, SOON notifies the
military of solar events, enabling them to protect assets and per-
sonnel. However, the committee remains concerned about progress
transitioning from SOON to the Next-Generation Global Oscilla-
tions Network Group—Operational (ngGONG–O) which is set to re-
place it and will be shared between the Space Force, the National
Solar Observatory (NSO), and the National Oceanic and Atmos-
pheric Administration (NOAA). The committee expects to be kept
apprised of Space Force negotiations with NSO and NOAA to set
forth a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) detailing an acquisition
strategy, a cost-sharing agreement, and a sustainment strategy for
the future ngGONG–O system.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Space Force to work
expeditiously to complete the MOA with NSO and NOAA. Further- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

The committee is concerned that the U.S. Space Force has not

Space data network strategy and ground architecture

duplication, and misalignment with user terminal fielding.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force,
in coordination with the Chief of Space Operations, the Director of
the Space Development Agency, and the Commander, U.S. Space

Space domain awareness
The committee notes that the U.S. Space Force’s space domain
awareness (SDA) mission is a critical part of military operations.
It allows the U.S. Space Force and other space organizations to un-
derstand and monitor the space domain, ensure the safety of U.S.
space assets, and respond to potential threats. In recent years, nu-
merous space companies and organizations have increased the
number of satellites they operate in low earth orbit, increasing the
total number of space objects that the U.S. Space Force needs to
include in SDA efforts. In addition, adversary nations have dem-
onstrated increased capability to threaten U.S. space assets in re-
cent years. Taken together, there is increased need for specialized
SDA systems to monitor these threats. The U.S. Space Force uses
a variety of space and ground-based systems to monitor, charac-
terize, and track objects in space for the benefit of military, civil,
and commercial space organizations. Some of these systems are
operational, and the Space Force is developing a variety of others
to contribute to this mission. Additionally, SDA may be important
to support missile defense capabilities. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Space Training and Readiness Command resourcing and
other training capabilities
The committee recognizes the critical role of the Space Force’s
Space Training and Readiness Command (STARCOM) in training
Guardians, developing space warfighting doctrine; developing its
tactics, techniques, and procedures; and testing and evaluating
Space Force capabilities. The committee further recognizes the in-
creasing importance of realistic, on-orbit training environments to
prepare Guardians to recognize, characterize, and respond to in-
creasingly complex and aggressive behaviors by near-peer competi-
tors in the space domain.
The committee notes that commercially operated on-orbit sys-
tems now provide mature capabilities that may support operational
test, training, and exercise activities in ways that are not fully
achievable through ground-based or purely simulated systems.
These capabilities include, but are not limited to, rendezvous and
proximity operations, inspection, maneuver characterization, space
domain awareness, and other mission-relevant activities associated
with contested space operations. The committee encourages the De-
partment of the Air Force to leverage such commercial capabilities
to the maximum extent practicable in support of STARCOM-led
training and the Space Systems Command Operational Test and
Training Infrastructure (OTTI) construct.
Therefore, the committee directs the Commander of STARCOM,
in coordination with the Commander of Space Systems Command,
to provide a briefing to the congressional defense committees, not
later than March 31, 2027, on STARCOM resourcing and the inte-
gration of commercial on-orbit capabilities into Space Force train-
ing and test activities.
The briefing shall include:
(1) An assessment of how STARCOM is currently resourced
to execute its mission set, including the training of Guardians,
the development of doctrine and tactics, and the test and eval-
uation of Space Force capabilities;
(2) A plan to integrate commercially available on-orbit capa-
bilities into OTTI-supported training, test, and exercise activi-
ties;
(3) The funding strategy and contracting mechanism

The committee notes that vehicles used by the Air Force Global
Strike Command for missile field operations and maintenance rou-
tinely exceed 200,000 miles. However, these vehicles are not re-
placed in a timely fashion and in turn become increasingly harder
to maintain, affecting missile field wing readiness. For example, E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

trucks can exceed 140,000 miles, and 2010 F350 cargo trucks can
exceed 150,000 miles. The property accountability system used to
assess vehicle replacement versus continued maintenance is re-
ferred to as the Enterprise Logistics Management System (ELMS).
The committee notes that ELMS is designed for Department of De-
fense vehicles that do not receive such high mileage and wear as

fields, often under harsh weather. As a result, mission capable
rates may be skewed for vehicles not physically possessed by Mis-

ELMS may not capture other key metrics that would provide a
more complete picture of the health of the vehicle fleet used to sup-

Therefore, the committee directs the Comptroller General of the

vehicle; (2) Whether ELMS adequately captures break rates for ve-

The committee further directs the Comptroller General to assess

used in these large and remote missile field locations should be re-

The committee directs the Comptroller General to provide initial

Support for United States-Mexico intelligence sharing
The committee recognizes the persistent and evolving threat
posed by transnational criminal organizations, including drug car-
tels operating in Mexico, which continue to undermine regional sta-
bility and threaten the security of the United States. The com-
mittee notes that these organizations are responsible for significant
volumes of illicit narcotics trafficking, violence, and other nefarious
activity that impact communities on both sides of the United
States-Mexico border.
The committee supports continued and enhanced security co-
operation between the Armed Forces of the United States and the
Mexican government, particularly efforts focused on identifying
high-value cartel leaders and weakening cartel networks. The com-
mittee believes that bilateral cooperation—including intelligence
sharing and capacity building—remains essential to disrupting car-
tel command structures and degrading operational capabilities.
The committee encourages the Department of Defense, in con-
sultation with the Department of State, the intelligence commu-
nity, and other relevant agencies, to expand collaboration with vet-
ted Mexican security forces to support efforts to combat cartels.
The committee further encourages the Department of Defense to
assess opportunities to improve real-time intelligence sharing and
communications synchronization with Mexican counterparts to in- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

crease the effectiveness of joint efforts targeting cartel leadership
networks.
United States critical infrastructure resilience against elec-
tromagnetic pulse weapons
The committee remains concerned about the growing strategic
threat posed by electromagnetic pulse (EMP) and high-altitude
electromagnetic pulse (HEMP) weapons to the United States. The
United States’ ability to defend its critical infrastructure against
such attacks is critical, as a successful strike would deny civilian
populations access to life-critical services—including clean water,
healthcare, communications, and transportation—creating mass
panic and disruption. The committee recognizes that these weapons
could provide adversaries with an asymmetric means of coercion
that may be more attractive than conventional military force in a
conflict with the United States.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to pro-
vide a briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate
and the House of Representatives, not later than February 1, 2027,
on the following:
(1) An assessment of current U.S. vulnerabilities across mili-
tary and civilian critical infrastructure, including energy,
water, healthcare, communications, and transportation sys-
tems;
(2) The status and adequacy of hardening, mitigation, and
recovery efforts across Department of Defense systems and
platforms; and
(3) Recommendations to strengthen U.S. resilience against
EMP and HEMP threats.

provisions.heading: United States Telecommunications Training Institute
provisions.text:
The committee notes the importance of the United States Tele-
communications Training Institute (USTTI) to help the Depart-
ment of Defense work with allies and partners as they develop
high-risk communications infrastructure around the world. This is
particularly important in developing nations, in order to counter
China’s aggressive strategy with respect to proposals at the World
Radio Conference. The training courses the USTTI provides, many
times with the participation of the Department, forge long-term re-
lationships with the host nation, ensuring their future strategies
also align with United States national defense strategies, especially
with respect to spectrum allocations through the International
Telecommunications Union.
Vandenberg public-private partnership
The committee is encouraged by the launch of Space Vandenberg
as a new public-private partnership to support the Western Range.
Innovative public-private partnerships can play an important role
in accelerating spaceport development, leveraging state, local, and
private capital to advance infrastructure priorities, and maximizing
the innovation potential of the ranges through university partner-
ships and the creation of mission development zones for research-
ers and entrepreneurs to innovate new space technologies. We en-
courage the U.S. Space Force to continue these innovative collabo- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

rations to advance the Spaceport of the Future initiative and na-
tional space priorities.
Weather satellites
The U.S. Air Force and Navy have previously testified that over
90 percent of their weather forecasting data comes from satellites,
emphasizing the need for continued, secure, and modernized
weather data.
Yet, weather satellite funding is virtually non-existent in the an-
nual U.S. Space Force budget request. While demonstrations and
prototypes have been funded, nothing yet has transitioned into a
significant program of record, continuing the Space Force’s reliance
on the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for crit-
ical weather data. This lack of U.S. warfighter capability includes
potential threats to military readiness, as well as weakens support
for new initiatives such as Golden Dome, which relies on accurate
weather and atmospheric models to counter hypersonic, missile,
and space-borne threats.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Department of the Air
Force to provide a briefing to the Senate Armed Services Com-
mittee, not later than March 1, 2027. This briefing should include
steps the Space Force will take to ensure the Space Force is not
relying solely on non-military entities for future military weather
requirements. It will also assess the potential for the Space Force
to leverage the Golden Dome initiative and military modernizations
for the purposes of reinvigorating Department of Defense space-
based weather programs and capabilities.
Wireless intrusion detection
The committee directs the Under Secretary of Defense for Intel-
ligence and Security to provide a briefing to the congressional de-
fense committees, not later than February 1, 2027, providing a de-

TITLE XVI—CYBERSPACE RELATED MATTERS
Subtitle A—Matters Relating to Cyber Operations and Cyber
Forces
Sec. 1601—Independent study on the authorities and organi-
zational structure of the principal cyber advisors
The committee recommends a provision that would direct the
Secretary of Defense to enter into an agreement with a federally
funded research and development center or independent entity, not
later than March 1, 2027, to conduct a study on the roles, respon-
sibilities, authorities, and resourcing of the Principal Cyber Advi-
sors (PCA) of the military departments. The study shall assess
whether current authorities under section 392a(c) of title 10,
United States Code, are sufficient to enable PCAs to execute their
statutory responsibilities and examine the organizational relation-
ships between PCAs and other senior cyber and information tech-
nology officials within each military department. The conducting
entity shall submit a report to the Secretary of Defense and the
congressional defense committees, not later than January 1, 2028.
The Secretary of Defense shall provide a briefing on the findings
to the congressional defense committees, not later than January 15,
2028.
The committee notes that the PCA role has existed for over 6
years. Over that period, resourcing for PCA offices has evolved, and
the approach to organizing and employing the PCA varies consider-
ably across the military departments. The committee believes this
variation makes it an appropriate time to assess whether the PCA
construct has the authorities, organizational placement, and
resourcing necessary to provide effective civilian oversight and ad-
vocacy for service cyber forces. The committee further notes that as
the Department of Defense invests in the implementation of the
Department of Defense Revised Cyber Force Generation Model,
known more commonly as CYBERCOM 2.0, ensuring that the PCA
offices are well-positioned to support the Department’s evolving
cyber workforce needs is an important consideration.

peculiar operations

Sec. 1621—Improving reserve component network account
continuity
The committee recommends a provision that would require the
Department of Defense Chief Information Officer (CIO), in coordi-
nation with the CIOs of the military departments, to establish min-
imum standards for reserve component personnel accounts on un-
classified and classified networks, not later than March 1, 2027.
The provision also directs the Department of Defense Inspector
General to conduct an audit of implementation and provide find-
ings to the congressional defense committees, not later than Octo-
ber 1, 2028.
The committee is aware that members of the reserve components
frequently encounter avoidable network access issues when
transitioning between duty statuses, including repeated account re-
activation or credential resets. This persists despite policies in-
tended to maintain access for longer periods in recognition of the
intermittent nature of reserve service, creating unnecessary admin-
istrative burden and detracting from readiness.
Sec. 1622—Reducing administrative burden in the Depart-
ment of Defense risk management framework implemen-
tation
The committee recommends a provision that would direct the De-
partment of Defense (DOD) Chief Information Officer (CIO) to re-
duce administrative burden in the implementation of the Risk
Management Framework (RMF) across the Department. The provi-
sion requires the DOD CIO to issue standardized RMF policy guid-
ance, not later than October 1, 2027; directs each military depart-
ment’s CIO to publish consistent implementing guidance, not later
than December 1, 2027; and requires modernization of the enter-
prise platform supporting RMF approvals and documentation, not
later than October 1, 2028. Not later than April 1, 2027, and annu-
ally thereafter through April 1, 2032, the DOD CIO shall provide
a briefing to the congressional defense committees on the status of
the new policy guidance and implementation.
The committee recognizes that repeated congressional and DOD
efforts to address burdensome and inconsistent RMF implementa-
tion have yielded mixed results. The committee is concerned that
the accelerating pace of software delivery makes the cost of the cur-
rent process increasingly acute, creating compounding risk to
warfighter capability and security.
The committee believes that many of the root causes of these
challenges were surfaced in industry responses to the DOD’s Soft-
ware Fast Track Initiative. This provision reflects the continuation
of that effort by directing the establishment of a standardized, con-
sistent process across all DOD services and components, addressing
the friction that has prevented prior reciprocity provisions from
being fully realized, and correcting the inconsistent application of
control inheritance that has been a key barrier to progress. The

Sec. 1623—Science, Technology, and Innovation Board study
on software-as-a-service in classified networks
The committee recommends a provision that would direct the
Secretary of Defense to task the Science, Technology, and Innova-
tion Board (STIB), not later than February 1, 2027, to study the
enablement of commercial software-as-a-service (SaaS) offerings on
classified networks of the Department of Defense (DOD). The STIB
would deliver an interim briefing to the congressional defense com-
mittees, not later than August 1, 2027; a final report, not later
than January 15, 2028; and a briefing on the findings of such
study, not later than January 31, 2028.
The committee recognizes that commercial SaaS offerings could
deliver significant operational and innovation benefits to the DOD
on classified networks, but that no clear or transparent pathway
currently exists for vendors to bring such offerings to scale. The
committee is aware that while some vendors have obtained author-
izations and sponsorship, the process spanning technical, security,
and contractual requirements lacks consistency and transparency,
and the investments required are substantial, particularly for
small businesses and nontraditional defense contractors. The com-
mittee believes this study would provide industry a defined path to-
ward certification, authorization, and contract eligibility. The com-
mittee believes that without such clarity, the DOD risks forgoing
the innovation benefits a competitive classified SaaS marketplace
could provide.
Sec. 1624—Streamlining Department of Defense governance
process for cross-domain solution approvals
The committee recommends a provision directing the Department
of Defense (DOD) Chief Information Officer (CIO) to streamline
cross-domain solution (CDS) approval governance by eliminating
unnecessary procedural steps and governance body involvement
that does not contribute a meaningful security benefit. Not later
than December 15, 2027, the DOD CIO shall submit a report to the
congressional defense committees assessing current processes and
a plan to establish a risk-tiered review framework. Additionally,
the DOD CIO shall provide a briefing to the congressional defense
committees, not later than March 1, 2028, on the implementation
status of the findings of the report.
The committee recognizes that robust protections are essential
when moving data across classification boundaries, but finds that
the current CDS approval process has grown unnecessarily bureau-
cratic, introducing latency into a domain where the balance of
speed and security is paramount. Consensus-based decision re-
quirements, full board reviews regardless of risk level, and limited
use of reciprocity authorities risk imposing real operational costs
on warfighters, who require timely access to information across do-
mains. The committee believes that rigorous process review and

The committee recommends a provision that would direct the
Secretary of Defense to establish the Cybersecurity Maturity Model
Certification (CMMC) Assessment Grant Program, not later than
July 1, 2027, to award one-time grants of up to $100,000 to eligible
small businesses and nontraditional defense contractors seeking
CMMC Level 2 certification, with total grant funding not to exceed
$50.0 million. The provision also directs the Secretary of Defense
to submit annual reports to the congressional defense committees
beginning July 1, 2028, through December 31, 2031.
Sec. 1627—Harmonization of Department of Defense secu-
rity boundaries to enable reciprocity
The committee recommends a provision that would direct the
Secretary of Defense to standardize security boundaries across the
Department of Defense (DOD) to maximize security control inherit-
ance and reduce duplicative security assessments. The provision re-
quires the DOD Chief Information Officer (CIO) to update all appli-
cable policy and guidance, not later than October 1, 2027, and mili-
tary department CIOs to publish implementing guidance, not later
than December 1, 2027. All programs and systems must be brought
into compliance not later than October 1, 2030, and annual brief-
ings to the congressional defense committees are required, not later
than April 1, 2027, and continuing through April 1, 2031.
The committee is concerned that inconsistent security boundary
definitions have been a persistent barrier to effective reciprocity.
The committee notes that when authorizing officials attempt to
apply the DOD reciprocity handbook, inconsistent boundary con-
structs force them to decipher which documents apply to which por-
tions of their review. This introduces ambiguity that often under-
mines prior authorization work and negates the intent of existing
reciprocity policy. The committee views boundary standardization
as foundational to realizing the full potential of reciprocity and as
an essential complement to broader Risk Management Framework
reform efforts currently underway. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Sec. 1641—Establishing an ecosystem for use of artificial in-
telligence agents at scale and speed
The committee recommends a provision directing the Secretary of
Defense, acting through the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence
Officer (CDAO), to establish a Department of Defense (DOD)-wide
ecosystem for the deployment and enterprise use of agentic artifi-

The committee commends the Department for its investment in
agentic AI, particularly through the seven pace-setting projects.
However, the committee is concerned that the DOD is overlooking
the importance of translating the lessons from these projects into
a broader ecosystem that supports the speed and scale of develop-
ment and adoption and is, instead, treating it as an afterthought
to individual program success.
Effective commercial agentic ecosystems include governance, best
practice forums, agent discovery applications, and deployment plat-
forms. They are also designed for both technical developers and
non-technical end users, who have proven equally capable of
leveraging agents for daily tasks.
Without such an ecosystem, the Department risks not being able
to consistently replicate the success of the pace-setting projects at
speed and scale. Rather, each fast follow-on project and those after
will be forced to rebuild and relearn from scratch rather than
drawing on shared infrastructure, common standards, and reusable
agents.

The committee recommends a provision that would direct the

2027.
As the DOD continues to expand its use of AI agents, the com-
mittee believes appropriate security policies are essential. The com-
mittee cautions the Department, however, against creating a com-
pliance-focused process versus a security-focused, risk-informed
one. The former approach risks slowing adoption and technological
advancement rather than securing those activities.

Access to Department of Defense-unique data for commer-
cial development
The committee commends the Department of Defense (DOD) for
its efforts to reduce barriers to fielding commercial solutions but
believes acquisition reform alone is insufficient. For commercial so-
lutions to effectively support the warfighter, commercial companies,
particularly small businesses and nontraditional defense contrac-
tors, need access to DOD data, or appropriately representative
data, to develop and validate their solutions. Currently, obtaining
such access places a significant burden of time and financial invest-
ment on the commercial entity, slowing the pathway from solution
development to deployed capability.
The committee notes that early access to relevant data can more
quickly demonstrate the value of a commercial solution and, if
performant, can accelerate integration into deployed capabilities for
the warfighter. Much of the DOD’s data is unique to military oper-
ations and has no commercial equivalent, and the committee be-
lieves the Department should develop an open-source and unclassi-
fied data platform, to include synthetic data representative of clas-
sified datasets, organized around specific mission problem sets for
which the Department seeks commercial solutions.
Therefore, the committee directs the Chief Digital and Artificial
Intelligence Officer (CDAO), in coordination with the service and
Joint Staff Chief Data Officers (CDOs), to provide a briefing to the
Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of
Representatives, not later than January 15, 2027, on a roadmap for
such a platform. This briefing should address the following: (1)
Prioritization of mission problem sets for which open or synthetic
data should be developed; (2) A governance model defining the
roles of the CDAO, the service CDOs, and the Joint Staff CDO; and
(3) An assessment of investments required to build and sustain the
platform.

and operations centers

tegration of data products at the tactical level through the estab-
lishment of Operational Data Teams (ODTs) and the Army Data
Operations Center (ADOC). As the Army progresses in its mod-
ernization initiatives and develops low-code/no-code platforms for
agile software development in support of rapidly evolving battle-
field requirements, these teams and this capability will become in-
creasingly critical to operational effectiveness. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Comptroller General review of role of Chief Data Officers in

provisions.heading: Department of Defense
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes that artificial intelligence (AI) rep-
resents a transformative technology with the potential to fun-
damentally revolutionize the battlespace and sustain U.S. decision
advantage over adversaries. However, the committee is concerned
that the broad focus on AI development and adoption has had the
unintended consequence of deprioritizing investments and govern-
ance associated with the data upon which AI depends. The com-
mittee acknowledges the ongoing efforts of the Department of De-
fense (DOD) to consolidate data catalogs as a meaningful step for-
ward but believes substantially more sustained work is required to
achieve true data centricity across the enterprise.
Central to this concern is the committee’s uncertainty regarding
the current state of the Chief Data Officer (CDO) function across
the DOD. The committee is not confident that CDOs possess the
organizational prominence, authorities, or resources necessary to
drive the cultural and structural changes required to make data a
true warfighting asset.
Therefore, the committee directs the Comptroller General of the
United States to conduct a comprehensive assessment of the CDO
function across the DOD enterprise, including: (1) The organiza-
tional placement of each CDO and the degree to which that place-
ment enables or inhibits their ability to influence enterprise data
policy and practice; (2) The level of authority each CDO possesses
to direct his or her respective organization to implement data gov-
ernance guidance, and the degree to which that authority is actu-
ally exercised; (3) The degree to which each CDO’s perceived re-
sponsibilities align with statutory requirements, including any au-
thorities or responsibilities not currently being executed; (4) Each
CDO’s approach to advancing data centricity, including efforts to
make data discoverable, accessible, and interoperable across his or
her organization; (5) The effectiveness of existing forums and mech-
anisms for coordination and information sharing among CDOs
across the enterprise; (6) The adequacy of CDO office resourcing in
terms of personnel, funding, and tools; (7) The maturity and en-
forcement of data governance frameworks, policies, and standards
within each CDO’s organization; (8) The sufficiency of enterprise
data management practices—including data labeling, lineage, and E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Comptroller General review of software factories
The committee notes that over the past decade, the Department
of Defense (DOD) has made significant investments in software fac-
tories to develop and field software capabilities at the speed and
agility demanded by the modern battlefield. Under the DOD Soft-
ware Modernization Implementation Plan, software factories and
their broader ecosystem serve critical functions in scaling software
delivery. The rapid emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) capabili-
ties that can write code and build applications at scale presents
new opportunities to accelerate software development across the
force. These developments also demand a hard look at whether the
policies and directives governing software factories are being fol-
lowed and how these should be updated to seize the opportunity
this technology presents. The committee is concerned by the lack
of clarity, standardization, and data around the Department’s use
of software factories. The committee believes that without a clear
governance framework and standard that all software factories con-
sistently follow, the ecosystem will fail at the tasks of scaling those
solutions that provide benefit and discarding those that are either
duplicative or do not deliver value.
Therefore, the committee directs the Comptroller General of the
United States to conduct a comprehensive review of the Depart-
ment’s and the military services’ use of software factories, to in-
clude: (1) An assessment of existing policy and guidance governing
software factories, the degree to which such guidance is being fol-
lowed across the Department, and whether such guidance remains
adequate and appropriate in an AI-enabled environment; (2) An
analysis of current operating practices across the software factory
ecosystem to identify areas of compliance and non-compliance with
existing guidance; and (3) An analysis of the cumulative costs and
work product of the Department’s software factory ecosystem to
identify redundancies and assess overall return on investment.
Furthermore, the committee directs the Comptroller General to
complete the review and provide a briefing on its findings to the
Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of
Representatives, not later than February 15, 2027, with a final re-
port to be delivered at a mutually agreed time. The committee also
directs that such report be provided to the Science, Technology and
Innovation Board in support of a review they are tasked to conduct
under section 907 of the National Defense Authorization Act for
Fiscal Year 2026 (Public Law 119–60). E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of
Representatives on the results of its review, not later than April
15, 2027, with the final report on the results of the review to follow
in a mutually agreed upon format and timeframe.
Containerized commercial artificial intelligence
The committee is encouraged by the progress the Department of
Defense (DOD) has made in advancing enterprise artificial intel-
ligence (AI) capabilities but believes it is important not to lose
sight of AI at the tactical edge. Operations in air-gapped, discon-
nected, or contested environments preclude reliance on cloud-based
infrastructure and demand advanced on-premise compute and con-
tainerized AI models. The committee notes that a number of com-
mercial vendors have developed such capabilities for both commer-
cial and defense-specific use cases and that the DOD should be bet-
ter leveraging these solutions. The committee is further concerned
that commercial AI software acquired by the Department may
carry inherent dependencies on cloud-based application program-
ming interfaces for core functionality, creating unacceptable oper-
ational risk in denied or degraded network environments.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in co-
ordination with the DOD Chief Information Officer, the Under Sec-
retary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment, and the Chief
Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer, to submit to the Commit-
tees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representa-
tives, not later than March 1, 2027, a strategy and implementation
plan for accelerating the adoption of containerized commercial AI
capabilities for local, on-premise execution in air-gapped or discon-
nected operational environments. The strategy and implementation
plan shall include: (1) A plan to transition mission-critical AI appli-
cations to containerized architectures capable of local execution
across tactical-edge infrastructure; (2) A framework for the secure
transfer, validation, and updating of containerized models in air-
gapped environments; (3) An evaluation of current inventory and
future requirements for ruggedized, on-premise compute hardware E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

capable of hosting large-scale AI models at the tactical edge; (4) A
review to ensure commercial AI software acquired by the DOD is

provisions.heading: Coordination of Open Centralized Unit Distributed Unit
provisions.text:
Ecosystem
The committee is aware that the Department of Defense (DOD),
in partnership with industry and academia, has made progress in
advancing open architecture wireless infrastructure through the
Future G Office. The committee is also aware that partnership
with stakeholders, such as the Open Centralized Unit Distributed
Unit (OCUDU) Ecosystem Foundation, is critical to bringing next-
generation wireless technology to the Department. The intent of
OCUDU is to develop open-source software for the centralized unit
and distributed unit components of next-generation wireless net-
works, which represent a critical layer of secure, resilient, tactical,
and strategic telecommunications architecture.
Open source development provides significant operational advan-
tages for 5G, emerging 6G, and future iterations of advanced wire-
less infrastructure at the tactical edge. By establishing a shared
community-governed software foundation, the OCUDU Ecosystem
enables faster innovation, greater joint force interoperability, and
reduced duplication of effort across both government and industry.
Transparent and neutral governance ensures that no single vendor
controls critical national security network infrastructure while
broad participation strengthens supply chain diversity and resil-
ience against peer adversaries.
The committee directs the Under Secretary of Defense for Re-
search and Engineering and the DOD Chief Information Officer to
provide a briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Sen-
ate and the House of Representatives, not later than May 1, 2027,
on the progress of the OCUDU Ecosystem. The briefing shall in-
clude the following: (1) A description of technical progress, includ-
ing the development of centralized unit and distributed unit soft-
ware capabilities, including for tactical and enterprise operations;
(2) An assessment of industry and academic participation, includ-
ing contributions from non-traditional entities with a specific em-
phasis on U.S.-owned businesses and domestic manufacturing part-
ners; (3) A description of deployment activities and the transition
of capabilities into operational environments; (4) An evaluation of
the impact of the OCUDU ecosystem on interoperability security
and supply chain resilience; (5) A description of coordination with
other federal initiatives related to wireless communications and ad-
vanced network technologies; and (6) Any recommendations for fur-
ther actions to support continued adoption and scaling, particularly
across the military departments and combatant commands. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Cyber warfare engineering officer reserve component ca-
reer field
The committee recognizes the significant progress the Depart-
ment of the Navy has made in developing skilled cyber profes-
sionals, particularly within the Cyber Warfare Engineering (CWE)
officer community. CWE officers possess highly specialized tech-
nical skills in areas that have proven invaluable to cyber oper-
ations and are in exceptional demand across both government and
industry. The committee recognizes that retention of cyber profes-
sionals is a broader challenge facing the Department of Defense
and notes that efforts are underway to address it across the cyber
workforce. Nevertheless, the committee believes it is critical that
CWE officers who transition out of active duty have the option to
continue serving in a reserve capacity should they choose to do so.
Currently, the Navy does not maintain a CWE career field within
its reserve component, limiting the ability of separating active duty
CWE officers to continue contributing their unique skills in a part-
time uniformed capacity. The committee acknowledges the re-
sources required to establish and sustain career fields in the re-
serve component but believes the operational and strategic benefits
of retaining access to this specialized talent pool justify the invest-
ment.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of the Navy, in
consultation with the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Cyber Pol-
icy, and the Commander, U.S. Cyber Command, to conduct a feasi-
bility and advisability study on establishing a CWE career field in
the Navy Reserve. The study shall assess, at a minimum, the fol-
lowing: (1) The requirements necessary to support a CWE career
field in the Navy Reserve, including personnel, training, and infra-
structure needs; (2) Opportunities to share resources with the ac-
tive component, including matrixed options for career field manage-
ment; (3) The operational benefits of establishing such a career
field; (4) The risks associated with not establishing such a career
field; and (5) How the Navy would structure reserve billets at suffi-
cient grades to enable meaningful career progression for CWE offi-
cers within the reserve component, including pathways for ad-
vancement in rank.
The Secretary of the Navy shall provide a briefing on the find-
ings of this study, along with recommendations and proposed next
steps, to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the
House of Representatives, not later than March 15, 2027.

provisions.text:
The committee remains concerned about the increasing frequency
and sophistication of cyberattacks targeting the healthcare sector,
including entities that provide medical services, systems, and de-
vices in support of the Department of Defense (DOD). Recent cyber
incidents involving defense contractors underscore the potential
risk to military medical readiness, the security of sensitive health
data, and the integrity of network-connected medical devices used
by the Armed Forces. The committee notes that many defense con-
tractors and suppliers supporting military medical operations, in-
cluding those providing network-enabled medical devices, may be E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

other relevant Department of Defense medical components, to pro-
vide a briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate
and the House of Representatives, not later than February 1, 2027,

Options to modernize Department policies and acquisition require-

Data readiness and analytical modernization across Joint
Force
The committee recognizes that common operating picture appli-
cations, while critical for operational planning, represent only a
fraction of the analytical work combatant commands perform. The-
ater cooperation, assessments, policy development, and interagency
coordination generate substantial data demands that existing tools
currently available to the combatant commands do not address.
Many commercial solutions are capable, however, of filling these
gaps if procured, while also complementing operational applica-
tions.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Chairman of the Joint
Chiefs of Staff to provide a briefing to the Committees on Armed
Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives, not later
than February 1, 2027, on how the Joint Staff is consolidating and
building requirements for the combatant commands to support the
full range of data and analytical needs. The briefing shall address:
(1) The feasibility and advisability of establishing a unified, accred-
ited repository for publicly available information and information
environment operations; (2) The feasibility and advisability of de-
veloping a minimum fieldable artificial intelligence trust package
inclusive of data provenance standards, attribute-based access con-
trol, and continuous monitoring; (3) How automated workflows can
reduce the burden of manual database searches and accelerate ac-
tionable intelligence production; and (4) Current efforts to enable
small businesses and non-traditional providers to contribute to De-
partment of Defense analytical missions.

provisions.heading: Joint Cyber Warfighting Architecture
provisions.text:
As the Department of Defense continues to mature its cyber
operational capabilities, the committee reiterates the importance of
ensuring that defense investments result in operationally relevant
capabilities that enable offensive cyber operations at speed and
scale. The committee notes actions taken by U.S. Cyber Command
(CYBERCOM) to refactor the Joint Cyber Warfighting Architecture
pursuant to section 1545 of the Servicemember Quality of Life Im-
provement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year
2025 (Public Law 118–159). The committee further notes the im-
portance of continued progress in this effort in light of the evolving
cyber threat environment and the Department’s requirement to ef-
fectively integrate relevant advanced technologies such as artificial
intelligence (AI). The committee is aware of CYBERCOM’s use of
AI-enabled programs, such as the PATHFINDER platform, that le-
verage commercial technologies and capabilities to increase tar-
geting and access.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Commander, CYBERCOM
to submit a briefing to the Committees on Armed Services of the
Senate and the House of Representatives, not later than March 1,
2027, detailing the use of commercially developed AI platforms to
support targeting and access development, such as the PATH-
FINDER program, as well as planned resourcing across the future
years defense program.
Joint Force common operating picture scaling and fed-
erated ontology strategy
The committee recognizes that warfighters across multiple do-
mains require a common operating picture capable of rapidly in-
gesting and connecting data to support time-sensitive targeting, in-
telligence fusion, and operational data integration. Platforms such
as the Maven Smart System have demonstrated that a shared, ar-
tificial intelligence (AI)-backed data ontology can satisfy this re-
quirement and deliver meaningful decision advantage. Having vali-
dated this approach, the committee believes the Department of De-
fense (DOD) should evaluate whether and how scaling this capa-
bility across the Joint Force would further satisfy warfighter re-
quirements by ensuring that all service components operating with-
in and supporting combatant commands share a common under-
standing of the battlespace regardless of service or component.
Additionally, the committee recognizes that deployed platforms
are generating a valuable data ontology. This ontology includes the
structured, semantic relationships between entities, events, and
data across DOD operations, which represent a growing institu-
tional asset. Realizing its full value requires that DOD tools, appli-
cations, and data sources, including intelligence community hold-
ings, interagency partners, and allied and coalition partners, be E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

able to both contribute to, and benefit from, these semantic rela-
tionships. Without a strategy to federate this data into a shared
ontological framework, critical data sources will remain semanti-
cally isolated, limiting the common operating picture and con-
straining the broader DOD AI ecosystem.
Therefore, the committee directs the Chief Digital and Artificial
Intelligence Officer, in his or her capacity as Chief Data Officer of
the DOD and program manager for joint AI-enabled operational
platforms, to develop a strategy for scaling common operating pic-
ture capabilities across the Joint Force and federating their under-
lying data ontologies and to provide a briefing to the Committees
on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives,
not later than January 15, 2027.
The strategy shall include the following: (1) An evaluation of the
feasibility and advisability of expanding this capability to all serv-
ice components within the combatant commands, including an as-
sessment of the degree to which scaling would further satisfy
warfighter requirements for a common operating and intelligence
picture; (2) A governance framework for managing the Depart-
ment’s operational data ontology as a DOD enterprise asset extend-
able across the broader DOD AI ecosystem; (3) Technical ap-
proaches for enabling data and applications residing outside of ex-
isting platforms to integrate with and contribute to these ontolog-
ical relationships, including through open, vendor-neutral stand-
ards and federation mechanisms that do not require physical data
ingestion into any single platform; and (4) An assessment of oppor-
tunities to extend ontology-based data sharing to the intelligence
community, interagency partners, and allied and coalition partners,
and recommendations for addressing any legislative, policy, con-
tractual, or resource barriers to implementation.
Modernization plan for commercial solutions for classified
program
The committee notes that the Commercial Solutions for Classi-
fied (CSfC) program at the National Security Agency (NSA) has
been an important tool to find industry solutions to Department of
Defense (DOD) needs for classified systems, especially tactical sys-
tems. However, the committee believes that the program would
benefit from a comprehensive review of its processes to determine
if the changing state of technology and policy would offer an oppor-
tunity for modernization.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in co-
ordination with the Director of the NSA, to submit a report to the
congressional defense and intelligence committees, not later than
August 1, 2027, on a comprehensive roadmap that details the mod-
ernization of the CSfC program, as well as a plan to modernize the
DOD and the NSA’s policies and procedures associated with CSfC.
The roadmap shall include the following: (1) An assessment of
structural and operational limitations within the current CSfC
framework, including the responsiveness of Capability Packages
and Protection Profiles to evolving warfighter needs, cyber threats,
and technological advances; the impact of

mittee encourages prioritization of funding to the successful ‘‘train

intelligence, quantum, and cybersecurity, which are all critical na-

The committee supports the inclusion of new capabilities in the

synchronize, coordinate, and direct the activities of participating

designated research university that has participated in the pilot

Report on agile telecommunications technologies
Near-peer adversaries continue to advance signals intelligence
and electronic warfare capabilities designed to intercept and dis-
rupt Joint Force communications. The committee notes that while
the Department of Defense (DOD) has integrated commercial 4G
and 5G waveforms into tactical settings, these systems often rely
on static frequencies that can be vulnerable to detection in con-
tested environments.
The committee is aware of existing research and development ef-
forts into emerging technology that enable operators to apply anti-
jam capabilities such as frequency-hop communications through
randomized, alternative frequencies in contested and congested
multidomain environments, similar to other tactical communica-
tions systems.
The committee directs the Director of the DOD 5G Cross-Func-
tional Team and the Director of the FutureG Office to provide a
briefing on frequency and modality agile technologies to the Com-
mittees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Rep-
resentatives, not later than April 1, 2027. The report shall include:
(1) An assessment of how frequency- and modality-agile emergent
technologies could enable more secure and resilient communica-
tions in contested, congested, and constrained electromagnetic spec- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

frequency- and modality-agile technologies; (3) A description of how
such technologies could operate within the existing Joint All-Do-

ing with commercial providers, including Open Radio Access Net-

Review of Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification pro-
gram approach following release of cyber-focused gen-
erative artificial intelligence models
The committee recognizes that point-in-time security and compli-
ance frameworks present an inherent and growing vulnerability as
the interval between assessments increases. The recent emergence
of sophisticated cyber-focused generative artificial intelligence (AI)
models has materially accelerated this risk by providing adver-
saries with powerful new capabilities to identify and exploit secu-
rity gaps within the defense industrial base (DIB). The committee
believes this development warrants a critical examination of
whether the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC)
program, as currently structured, remains sufficient to protect DIB
contractors and subcontractors against this evolving threat envi-
ronment.
The committee acknowledges the considerable financial and ad-
ministrative investment that CMMC certification imposes on DIB
vendors and does not take lightly the burden that any pro-
grammatic evolution may present. Nevertheless, the committee be-
lieves the security of the DIB must remain paramount and that the
maturation of cyber-focused generative AI necessitates a serious
evaluation of whether a transition from periodic, point-in-time as-
sessments to a model of continuous evaluation is both necessary
and achievable within the existing CMMC framework.
Therefore, the committee directs the Department of Defense
(DOD) Chief Information Officer (CIO) to conduct a comprehensive
evaluation of the CMMC program and provide a briefing to the
Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of
Representatives, not later than March 15, 2027, on the outcomes
of that evaluation.
The evaluation and briefing shall address the following: (1) An
assessment of the ability of the current CMMC framework to pro-
tect the DIB against threats enabled by cyber-focused generative
AI, including the identification of any programmatic gaps or
vulnerabilities; (2) A determination of the CMMC certification level
or levels at which a transition to continuous evaluation would be
necessary to adequately mitigate the identified threat; (3) A pro-
posed timeline and implementation plan for transitioning from
point-in-time assessments to continuous evaluation, including any
required regulatory, contractual, or programmatic changes; (4) An
assessment of the impact such a transition would have on the
Third Party Assessment Organization (3PAO) evaluation model, in-
cluding any changes to 3PAO roles, responsibilities, accreditation
standards, or capacity; and (5) An assessment of how cyber-focused E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

Space domain awareness software
The committee is aware that the space domain is becoming in-
creasingly congested and contested, with rapid growth in resident
space objects, more frequent deployment events, and adversary be-
haviors designed to exploit ambiguity below the threshold of armed
conflict.
The committee further notes that adversaries are employing
Camouflage, Concealment, Deception, and Maneuver (CCDM) tac-
tics, including the introduction of unexpected objects, novel configu-
rations, and atypical behaviors that challenge existing space do-
main awareness (SDA) processes.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of the Air Force
to provide a briefing to the Senate Armed Services Committee, not
later than June 1, 2027, on how the Space Force and Air Force
plan to operationalize machine learning-enabled object classifica-
tion and anomaly detection tools that identify suspected CCDM,
flag unexpected object behaviors during deployment events, and in-
tegrate with existing SDA architectures. The briefing shall include:

Strategy for leveraging artificial intelligence tools for med-
ical countermeasures development
The committee notes that significant progress is being made in
the capabilities for advanced artificial intelligence (AI) systems,
and their application for a broad range of uses in the Department
of Defense continues to expand. The committee is aware that the
use of such systems with domain specific data is for focused tech-
nical needs. While the Department has invested in generalized
large language models for broad application, the committee believes
the Department needs to emphasize additional attention on these
domain specific needs.
Therefore, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense to de-
velop a strategy for leveraging AI tools for medical counter-
measures development and deliver a report to the Committees on
Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives,
not later than December 1, 2027. The strategy shall include: (1) An
assessment of the current and projected threat landscape for bio-
logical and chemical threats against which the Department re-
quires medical countermeasures; (2) A prioritized list of near-term
and long-term medical countermeasures platforms needed by the
Department; (3) Proposals to synchronize, coordinate, and integrate
relevant Department components to most effectively leverage AI
tools for medical countermeasures development; (4) Identification of
any issues, problems, or roadblocks that would impede progress; (5)
Opportunities to leverage support from non-Departmental entities;
(6) Resources required, including personnel, facilities, and funding;
(7) Implementation timeline over the next 5 years, including budg-
et estimates and key milestones; (8) Recommendations for improv-
ing or formalizing interagency coordination and support mecha-
nisms; and (9) Any required policy or legislative changes that
would enable implementation of the strategy.

TITLE XXVIII—MILITARY CONSTRUCTION

provisions.heading: GENERAL PROVISIONS
provisions.text:
Subtitle A—Military Construction Program
Sec. 2801—Modification of master plans for major military
installations
The committee recommends a provision that would amend sec-
tion 2864 of title 10, United States Code, to align major military
installation master plans to the new definition for military installa-
tion resilience requested last year by the Department of Defense
and adopted in the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal
Year 2026 (Public Law 119–60).
Sec. 2802—Prohibition on use of repair projects to expand
footprint of existing facilities or infrastructure
The committee recommends a provision that would amend sec-
tion 2811 of title 10, United States Code, to clarify that the expan-
sion of the footprint of existing facilities or infrastructure is not al-
lowed outside of very limited criteria.
Sec. 2803—Increase of authority for Indo-Pacific posture un-
specified military construction projects
The committee recommends a provision that would amend sec-
tion 2810(a) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal
Year 2024 (Public Law 118–31) by increasing the minor military
construction threshold from $30.0 million to $35.0 million.
Sec. 2804—Use of certain amounts for electrical or infra-
structure upgrades on Barbers Point, Hawaii
The committee recommends a provision that would amend
2814(i)(1) of title 10, United States Code, to authorize the Secretary
of Defense to use existing funding in the Ford Island Improvement
Account to make electrical upgrades on Barbers Point, Hawaii.
Sec. 2805—Temporary adjustment of unspecified minor mili-
tary construction requirements
The committee recommends a provision that would amend sec-
tion 2805 of title 10, United States Code, to increase the unspec-
ified minor military construction threshold from $9.0 million to
$15.0 million and relieve area cost factor adjustments for Alaska,
Hawaii, and other islands in the Indo-Pacific for a period of 5
years. The provision would also make additional conforming and
clarifying changes to the underlying statute to improve under-
standing within the Department of Defense.

Subtitle B—Military Housing
Sec. 2821—Exclusion of window opening control devices
from requirement for window fall prevention devices in
military family housing units
The committee recommends a provision that would amend sec-
tion 2857(a)(3) of title 10, United States Code, to clarify that a win-
dow fall prevention device in military family housing units does not
include a device that is solely a window opening control device.
Sec. 2822—Health and safety requirements for military
housing
The committee recommends a provision that would require the
Secretary of Defense to ensure that all housing project agreements
and renewals for privatized military housing are compliant with
the appropriate environmental health and safety standards and
that all maintenance personnel, contracted mold assessors, indoor
environmental professionals, and mold remediators responsible for
assessing or remediating mold and water damage in covered hous-
ing shall possess and maintain current certifications issued by a
nationally recognized, third-party, nonprofit certifying body.
Sec. 2823—Expansion of protection from reprisal or retalia-
tion against tenants of privatized military housing units
who report housing-related issues
The committee recommends a provision that would amend sec-
tion 2890(e) of title 10, United States Code, to expand protected
communications of tenants of privatized military housing who re-
port housing-related issues relative to the privatized housing.
Sec. 2824—Transparency and strategic planning for housing
The committee recommends a provision that would require the
Secretary of Defense to ensure that any enhanced-use lease exe-
cuted, extended, or renewed under section 2662 or 2667 of title 10,
United States Code, consider a range of more transparent and stra-
tegic planning considerations with respect to military housing.
Sec. 2825—Development and implementation of minimum
health and safety standards for military family housing
The committee recommends a provision that would require the
Secretary of Defense to mandate specific standards for housing and
environmental health and safety protections for members of the
Armed Forces and their families residing in military family hous-
ing. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: Items of Special Interest
provisions.text:
Accounting for force protection and weather concerns for
B–21 Bomber shelter budgeting
The committee continues to support the Air Force’s efforts to de-
fend air bases and recognizes that technology and tactics for un-
manned aerial systems (UAS) and first person view (FPV) drones,
demonstrated in Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb and Israel’s Oper-
ation Roaring Lion, challenge the suitability of open-sided environ-
mental protection shelters (EPS) in comparison to traditional hang-
ars for B–21 bomber aircraft, especially for priority alert missions.
Furthermore, the matter of operational security and information
control relating to strategic nuclear and stealth assets has been
underappreciated in discussions that originally focused on weather
conditions, which, prior to the rapid emergence of UAS and FPV
threats, determined that the current EPS design is inadequate for
blizzard conditions often experienced at the future Main Operating
Base for the B–21.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Department of the Air
Force to take these issues under consideration when programming
for aircraft sustainment as well as military construction and to co-
ordinate with both force protection and construction agents when
planning for design allocation funding over the future years de-
fense program.
Adoption and integration of additive construction tech-
nologies
The committee supports efforts by the Department of Defense
and the military services to accelerate the adoption of additive con-
struction technology for construction projects. The committee notes
additive construction’s potential to reduce the time and cost of
projects compared to traditional construction. The committee sup-
ports Department initiatives to pursue additive construction tech-
nology demonstration projects for rapid construction in contingency
environments as well as organic additive construction capabilities
within garrison engineering units such as the ongoing demonstra-
tions at Ellsworth Air Force Base and the U.S. Air Force Academy.
The committee further notes that recent updates to the Unified Fa-
cilities Criteria (UFC), UFC 3–301–01, specifically address addi-
tively constructed concrete (ACC) structures to allow for broader
adoption and further innovation. However, the committee is con-
cerned that some limitations in current regulations, such as lim-
iting ACC buildings to a height of no more than two stories, will
hinder broader adoption and thus require further research, dem-
onstration, and refinement of UFC and other Department regula-
tions or policies.
Accordingly, the committee strongly encourages the Secretary of
Defense, in coordination with the military services, to pursue fur-
ther research and demonstration of multi-story ACC structures, in-
cluding required seismic certification and compliance with other
safety requirements. The committee believes this research should
inform and enable revisions to current Department regulations and
policies to permit future additive construction of larger projects
such as barracks, schools, and office space, as well as garrison and E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

expeditionary structures to harden and defend high-value defense
assets such as aircraft hangers that will house the B–21 strategic
bomber and other exquisite platforms.
Additionally, the committee directs the Secretary of Defense, in
coordination with the military services, to provide a briefing to the
congressional defense committees, not later than January 31, 2027,
on the status of Department research and demonstration of multi-

of Department efforts to demonstrate and certify the use of ACC

fectively than the traditional military construction process.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Secretary of the Air

mittee on the status of the discussions, not later than January 15,

Army National Guard training center range improvement
The committee recognizes the Army National Guard’s critical role
as part of the Army’s Operational Reserve and its contributions to
the Joint Force. Army National Guard training sites across the
country, including Camp Navajo, Florence Military Reservation,
and the Buckeye Training Site (in partnership with the U.S. Army
Reserve), provide diverse and complementary training environ-
ments that are well-suited for realistic and effective readiness
training across a range of missions, terrain, and operating condi-
tions and are essential to sustaining the readiness of units that
must be prepared to respond to both federal and domestic missions.

Army Reserve component facilities joint use with Army Na-
tional Guard
The committee notes with concern the fiscal and operational
challenges facing the Army’s reserve components regarding facility
sustainment. The Army National Guard’s (ARNG) 2,200 Readiness
Centers have an average age of 48 years, with an estimated $60.0
billion required to remedy a 40 percent total space deficit. The com-
mittee is aware that despite the ARNG managing a significant por-
tion of the Army’s facility inventory, its share of military construc-
tion funding has been disproportionately low, leading to a projected
130-year modernization timeline that is unsustainable and de-
grades readiness.
The committee believes the current model of operating separate,
single-component facilities for the U.S. Army Reserve (USAR) and
the ARNG may be inefficient and fail to maximize the use of tax-
payer dollars. This model of facility management can lead to costly
redundancies and the deterioration of valuable federal assets when
units are realigned. The committee believes that the Army’s Total
Force Policy, which seeks to integrate the active and reserve com-
ponents into a unified operational force, should be reflected in how
the Army manages its real property.
Accordingly, the committee encourages the Secretary of the Army
to assess the feasibility and benefits of transferring sustainment
responsibility of USAR facilities to the ARNG. The committee notes
that USAR and ARNG are already planning such facility transfers
in Texas and Connecticut and commends those efforts.
The committee directs the Secretary of the Army to provide a re-
port to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the

ment of the operational benefits, including efficiencies in mainte-
nance and repair; (3) An evaluation of how this model can support
force structure changes resulting from the Army Transformation

provisions.heading: Cargo pier at United States Army Garrison Kwajalein Atoll
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the enduring strategic value of Kwaja-
lein Atoll to the Department of Defense. As the location of the Ron-
ald Reagan Space and Missile Test Range, Kwajalein provides irre-
placeable capabilities for ballistic missile defense developmental
and operational testing, long-range missile flight testing, space do-
main awareness, and space object tracking. Its position in the cen-
tral Pacific has taken on heightened importance as the Department
reorients toward strategic competition in the Indo-Pacific, and the
United States’ access to the atoll represents a significant national
security interest. The committee believes that sustained invest-
ment in the installation’s enabling infrastructure is essential to
preserving these capabilities over the long term.
The committee is concerned, however, that the extreme remote-
ness of Kwajalein Atoll and its near-total dependence on maritime
resupply place a premium on resilient and sufficient cargo-handling
infrastructure that current port facilities may not provide. The
committee understands that the atoll’s existing pier infrastructure
is aging and constrains cargo throughput and that these limitations
may complicate the timely delivery of sustainment cargo, military
construction materiel, and mission-critical equipment. The com-
mittee is particularly concerned that existing facilities lack roll-on/
roll-off capability, requiring that wheeled and tracked vehicles, roll-
ing stock, and outsized equipment be handled by lift-on/lift-off
methods that are slower, more labor- and equipment-intensive, and
ill-suited to the efficient movement of vehicular cargo. The com-
mittee is further concerned that the lack of redundant pier capacity
creates a potential single point of failure that could jeopardize in-
stallation readiness, particularly in the event of damage to existing
facilities or a contingency requiring surge logistics support.
Accordingly, the committee directs the Secretary of the Army to
provide a briefing to the Senate Armed Services Committee, not
later than February 1, 2027, on the feasibility and estimated cost
of constructing a new cargo pier at U.S. Army Garrison Kwajalein
Atoll. The briefing shall include, at a minimum: (1) An assessment
of current cargo handling capacity and identified deficiencies, in-
cluding the absence of roll-on/roll-off capability; (2) The projected
cargo throughput and resilience requirements needed to support
current and anticipated missions; (3) An evaluation of options for
new or expanded pier construction, including roll-on/roll-off capa-
bility, with a rough order of magnitude cost estimate and notional
construction schedule for each; (4) An assessment of associated
dredging, landside, staging, and supporting infrastructure require-
ments and costs; and (5) A discussion of relevant environmental,
regulatory, and host-nation considerations under applicable agree-
ments with the Republic of the Marshall Islands.
