Ensuring department budgets for plant replacement value
investment requirement
The committee notes that section 2841 of the Servicemember

provisions.heading: Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization
provisions.text:
Act for Fiscal Year 2025 (Public Law 118–159) established a bind-
ing statutory requirement that the Secretaries of the military de-
partments invest in the budget for facilities sustainment, restora-
tion, and modernization (FSRM) an amount equal to no less than
4 percent of the total plant replacement value (PRV) of all their re-
spective department facilities by fiscal year 2030 and sustain that
level in each subsequent fiscal year. The law further establishes a
structured schedule of interim statutory investment obligations:
1.75 percent of total PRV in fiscal year 2027; 2.5 percent in fiscal
year 2028; 3.25 percent in fiscal year 2029; and 4.0 percent in fiscal
year 2030 and each fiscal year thereafter.
The committee notes that the Department of Defense reported an
FSRM investment rate of 1.75 percent of total PRV in fiscal year
2027, nominally satisfying the first statutory milestone established
under Section 2841 of the Servicemember Quality of Life Improve-
ment and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025.
However, the committee finds that this result was achieved only
through the application of funds provided under the Public Law
119–21, a reconciliation measure constituting mandatory spending.
The committee notes that while satisfaction with the section 2841
statutory milestone through one-time mandatory spending does
comply with the intent of the law, it does not demonstrate the De-
partment’s resolve in fulfilling the statutory requirement by allo-
cating appropriate resources in its discretionary budget. The com-
mittee notes that reconciliation is a non-recurring budgetary mech- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

anism and cannot serve as the programmatic foundation for a sus-

The committee also believes it is important to note that the De-
partment requested a repeal of section 2841 even though the mili-

mittee is unambiguous in its direction: the Department must pro-

emergency, or mandatory spending.

provisions.heading: Gila Bend Air Force Auxiliary Field North Turnaround
provisions.text:
The committee recognizes the critical role of Gila Bend Air Force
Auxiliary Field (GBAFAF) in supporting pilot training and combat
readiness for aircraft operating from Luke Air Force Base and
throughout the Barry M. Goldwater Range complex. As a key train-
ing and emergency divert airfield, GBAFAF supports high-tempo
flight operations for Air Force, Air National Guard, and partner na-
tion aircraft.
The committee notes that the existing north turnaround does not
meet current Unified Facilities Criteria requirements and operates
under a waiver, creating operational and safety challenges. The
committee understands that replacing and expanding the north
turnaround would provide immediate compliance with applicable
standards, improve aircraft maneuverability and safety, and enable
parking for additional aircraft. The committee further notes that
the project would enhance airfield capacity and support continued
operations for current and future aircraft missions.
The committee is concerned that failure to modernize this infra-
structure could increase operational risk, constrain airfield oper-
ations, and degrade the airfield’s ability to support readiness re-
quirements and training activities. Therefore, the committee urges
the Secretary of the Air Force to prioritize funding for the north
turnaround replacement and expansion project at GBAFAF in fis-
cal year 2028.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning replacement at

provisions.heading: Luke Air Force Base
provisions.text:
The committee remains concerned by the condition of aging heat-
ing, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems across Luke
Air Force Base, Arizona, and notes that funding for necessary re-
placements was not included in the fiscal year 2027 budget request.
The committee understands that HVAC systems, including the
main cooling tower, at Luke Air Force Base have exceeded their ex- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

pected service lives, resulting in increased maintenance require-

The committee further notes that Luke Air Force Base is located
in one of the hottest regions of the United States, where summer
temperatures routinely approach 120 degrees Fahrenheit. Reliable
climate control is essential to maintaining safe working conditions
for airmen and civilian personnel, protecting mission-critical equip-
ment, and sustaining installation readiness. HVAC failures during
periods of extreme heat can adversely affect personnel health and
productivity while disrupting mission operations.
The committee emphasizes that continued reliance on aging
HVAC infrastructure is both a readiness concern and a fiscal ineffi-
ciency. Accordingly, the committee strongly urges the Secretary of
the Air Force to prioritize funding for HVAC replacement projects
at Luke Air Force Base and to ensure that future budget requests
adequately address facility sustainment requirements at installa-
tions operating in extreme climate conditions.

Therefore, the committee urges the Secretary of the Navy, acting

electronic monitoring of perimeter fence areas, improve early detec-

ture, and enable more rapid security force response to potential
threats. The committee directs the Secretary of the Navy to provide
a briefing to the Senate Armed Services Committee, not later than

Report on military construction in Freely Associated States
The military services are making large infrastructure invest-
ments in the Freely Associated States (FAS) for the first time in
generations, and local on-the-ground engagement with the national
and local governments in these countries will greatly reduce risks
of construction delay and cost increases.
To better understand what actions can be taken in the FAS to
address these risks, the committee directs the Indo-Pacific Com-
mand’s Joint Task Force-Micronesia, in consultation with the As-
sistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy, and Envi-

than February 1, 2027, summarizing:
(1) Action taken to date to improve the civilian-military rela-

(2) Potential options for and advisability of building an en-

military personnel stationed in the FAS, to improve coordina-

community relations issues.
Requirement for Camp Navajo entry bridge replacement

for recapitalizing Pantex Plant infrastructure and facili-
ties
The committee directs the Administrator for Nuclear Security to
provide a detailed briefing, not later than December 1, 2026, on
long-term recapitalization plans for the Pantex Plant, including
critical high explosives facilities and the materials staging capa-
bility. The briefing shall include a 10-year outlook focused on the
necessary assets and resources, including special tooling develop-
ment and supply chain requirements, as well as actions required,
to modernize the critical capabilities needed to deliver warheads on
schedule. The committee believes that a focused 10-year strategy
with steady state funding may yield cost savings while advancing
the mission.
Briefing on plutonium pit production and reuse planning
The committee notes that the expansion of plutonium pit produc-
tion capabilities and the revitalization of associated facilities and
infrastructure are critical in facilitating the modernization of the
U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile. The committee further notes that
consistent communication between the National Nuclear Security
Administration and the congressional defense committees is nec-
essary to ensure that emerging execution challenges are identified
and addressed in a timely manner.
Therefore, the committee directs the Administrator for Nuclear
Security to brief the congressional defense committees, not later
than December 1, 2026, on: (1) The progress of Los Alamos Na-
tional Laboratory’s (LANL) plutonium pit production capability ex-
pansion to enable the production of at least 100 pits by the end of
calendar year 2028; (2) Opportunities for the Savannah River Site
to facilitate expanded plutonium pit production at LANL; (3)
Progress on establishing a complementary production capability at
the Savannah River Plutonium Processing Facility (SRPPF); and
(4) Options where the reuse of existing plutonium pits may support
a bridging strategy for meeting Department of Defense stockpile re-
quirements until pit production targets are met at LANL and
SRPPF.
Briefing on procurement of United States-origin unobli-
gated enriched uranium
The committee is concerned about the adequacy of current and
future capacity to supply U.S.-origin, unobligated uranium, includ-
ing the mining and conversion needed to replenish defense inven-
tories on an enduring basis.The National Nuclear Security Admin-
istration (NNSA) made an initial round of purchases of natural
uranium from U.S. mining companies in 2022 to begin filling the
strategic uranium reserve managed by the NNSA. These purchases
illustrate that the necessary infrastructure, permits, and licenses
to transport and store the uranium in the reserve are in place.
However, longer-term contracts with uranium producers, refiners, E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: Assessments of National Nuclear Security Administration Major
provisions.text:
Projects,’’ (GAO–26–107777), that the National Nuclear Security
Administration (NNSA) and its management and operating (M&O)
contractors are carrying out nearly 30 major construction projects
estimated to cost a total of more than $30.0 billion. In addition,
M&O contractors carry out hundreds of smaller projects, which col-
lectively add billions of dollars in investment to the agency’s overall
construction portfolio.
Under M&O contracts, the contractor is responsible for nearly all
aspects of site operation, security, maintenance, and construction,
as well as mission-related work, including research and weapons
production. M&O contract terms are generally long, and new or
large-scale construction efforts may not have been contemplated at
the time of the NNSA’s initial awarding of the M&O contract. The
Department of Energy has used M&O contracts since the Manhat-
tan Project and remains the primary user of these unique contracts
to this day.
A feature of M&O contracts is that the contractor is responsible
for managing construction acquisition processes and applies its
overhead rates to these services. Especially for the major projects,
these costs can be considerable. Given M&O contractors’ poor
records of performance in delivering projects on budget and on
schedule, the committee is seeking to understand whether alter-
native management approaches could reduce cost and improve
project delivery.
Therefore, the committee directs the Comptroller General of the
United States to assess: (1) The benefits, costs, and challenges as-
sociated with using M&O contractors to manage construction
projects at their sites; and (2) The extent to which the NNSA has
used or considered alternatives to M&O contracts to manage con-
struction projects and the benefits, costs, and challenges of these
alternatives. E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: Comptroller General review of National Nuclear Security
provisions.text:
Administration approaches to incentivizing contractors’
performance
The committee notes that since its establishment in 2000, the
National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) has changed its
performance evaluation approach for management and operating
(M&O) contractors several times, and there has been frequent dis-
cussion of the benefits of different contract incentive structures to
incentivize desired performance outcomes. In the 2000s, the NNSA
used detailed performance criteria specific to each contract to make
decisions on awarding incentives. Since 2013, the NNSA has used
broad, more subjective NNSA-wide performance criteria to make
award fee decisions. In a 2019 report, the Government Account-
ability Office found that the NNSA generally awarded M&O con-
tractors high ratings and most available performance incentives,
except in cases of significant safety or security incidents. This pat-
tern has seemed to hold since then.
Throughout this period, while the NNSA’s modernization efforts
and program of record have changed and expanded significantly,
cost and schedule performance have continued to raise concerns,
particularly in areas such as large construction projects and infra-
structure recapitalization. Further, challenges in recruitment and
retention of contractors’ workforces are essential to address in
order to achieve modernization objectives. Several external reviews,
such as the Augustine-Mies report and the NNSA’s own Enhanced
Mission Delivery Initiative, have called for the NNSA to move
away from award fees to fixed fees as it is unclear that award fees
have been meaningful for performance. Further, as the NNSA
seeks to speed up its efforts and reduce project costs while also
evaluating how regulation can be streamlined, getting its contract
incentives right is essential.
The Federal Acquisition Regulation discusses various types of po-
tential contract incentives that establish realistic and achievable
targets that are clearly communicated to the contractor, that in-
clude appropriate incentive arrangements designed to motivate
contractor efforts that might not otherwise be emphasized, and
that discourage contractor inefficiency and waste. Different incen-
tives may be appropriate depending on the nature of the work.
NNSA sites conduct a variety of work, including research, produc-
tion, construction, maintenance, and site operations, but generally
only use award fees and fixed fees as incentives.
Therefore, the committee directs the Comptroller General of the
United States to assess: (1) The extent to which current incentives
align with the scope of the work the NNSA seeks to incentivize; (2)
Opportunities that alternative incentive structures could provide to
improve contractor motivation and performance; and (3) The views
of stakeholders and experts regarding what incentives drive and re- E:\HR\OC\SR127.XXX SR127

provisions.heading: Comptroller General review of National Nuclear Security
provisions.text:
Administration efforts to sustain science, technology,
and engineering facilities
The committee realizes that the National Nuclear Security Ad-
ministration (NNSA) relies on unique science, technology, and engi-
neering (ST&E) facilities across the U.S. nuclear security enter-
prise to assess and certify weapon performance and to research and
develop new materials, designs, technologies, and production proc-
esses for modernizing the nuclear deterrent. The NNSA has re-
ported that ongoing stockpile stewardship and modernizations are
placing greater demand on these facilities than at any time in the
past 30 years. Many of these facilities and supporting infrastruc-
ture are relatively new and well-maintained compared to the pro-
duction infrastructure in the nuclear security enterprise. However,
these facilities are still decades old and in need of substantial
sustainment and, in some cases, recapitalization to ensure that
they continue to support stockpile stewardship and modernization,
even as the NNSA plans replacement capabilities in the future for
some facilities. The NNSA funds its ST&E facility sustainment ac-
tivities through multiple programs’ operations budgets, rather than
as line-item projects, limiting visibility into the full scope and esti-
mated cost of these efforts, particularly in the agency’s budget ma-
terials.
Therefore, the committee directs the Comptroller General of the
United States to assess: (1) The NNSA’s ongoing and planned in-
ventory of ST&E sustainment efforts and any risk assessments of
these facilities; (2) The costs and schedules for the sustainment ef-
forts and the program budgets through which these efforts are car-
ried out; and (3) Any opportunities to improve the visibility of these
efforts in the NNSA’s budget materials to ensure budgetary needs
can be fully considered.
The committee directs the Comptroller General to brief the con-
gressional defense committees, not later than March 31, 2027, and
meet with the congressional defense committees to determine a
mutually agreeable time for a final report.

provisions.heading: ADDITIONAL VIEWS
provisions.text:
I’ve been a proud member of the Senate Armed Services Com-
mittee for more than 13 years. My work on the Committee is the
highlight of my Senate service because of my deep connection to
Virginia’s military families and my deep respect for my colleagues.
The process that our Committee uses to carefully craft the Na-
tional Defense Authorization Act—months of hearings to consider
all dimensions of our nation’s security challenges followed by a
markup in which all members have the opportunity to shape the
final product—is a model for how the Senate should operate. The
leadership of the Committee, Senators Wicker and Reed, have ably
carried out this long tradition whereby SASC is the only committee
to do an authorizing bill every year and they do so in a way that
guarantees significant bipartisan approval.
I’ve always voted for the NDAA in Committee and on the floor
of the Senate. The bill is never perfect—often omitting items I ad-
vocated or including items I opposed. But it is usually so full of
good provisions that a yes vote has always been an easy call. This
year, for the first time, I voted against the NDAA. I did so with
deep regret. I file this dissenting perspective to explain why.
This NDAA is much like earlier versions in containing solid pol-
icy, including many provisions I worked to include as the lead
Democrat on the Seapower Subcommittee. Just as in past years,
the Committee’s leadership and dedicated staff put together a proc-
ess that maximized inclusion of content from all members. In vir-
tually every particular, this NDAA represents ‘‘business as usual’’
from a Committee for whom that phrase is actually a high com-
pliment rather than a casual throwaway line.
But an exemplary process cannot obscure the fact that the times
are anything but usual. Since last year’s NDAA, our situation has
changed dramatically. The United States is in the middle of an ille-
gal and foolish war with Iran, initiated by the President for spu-
rious reasons, that is harming our troops and causing massive
damage to American families and the global economy. The United
States is bombing boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific and
killing those aboard in a campaign described as an ‘‘international
armed conflict’’ against narco-traffickers even though many of these
fatal strikes are carried out against boats containing no drugs. The
United States invaded Venezuela to topple the Maduro regime, but
has left the regime in place and thus far denied the legitimate po-
litical opposition the opportunity to build a Venezuela for Ven-
ezuelans. And the President has threatened military action against
other nations—Cuba, Colombia, Mexico, Denmark—with more such
threats likely to emerge at any given moment based on his whims
and personal grievances.
All these Presidential actions to initiate armed conflict here,
there, and everywhere have been unilateral decisions taken with-

out the consultation with Congress required by the Constitution.
The President has chosen to make Congress a bystander in matters
of war and, thus far, Congress has passively accepted that eviscera-
tion of its most solemn obligation.
This year’s NDAA shows no self-awareness of this growing power
grab by the executive branch and, in my view, even paves the way
for more unilateral executive control over matters of war. To begin,
the Administration proposes a massive increase in the Defense
budget—growing the topline from $850 billion to $1.14 trillion
while additionally seeking $350 billion more via reconciliation and
hinting at a future supplemental request likely to add an addi-
tional $200 billion to the defense budget. This is a staggering in-
crease of funding for Defense, particularly when counterposed with
the sizable cuts being made to Medicaid, Supplemental Nutrition
Assistance, and other programs relied upon by everyday Ameri-
cans—and the fact that Social Security’s trust fund is expected to
be depleted by the end of 2032.
Efforts to amend the bill to fence off funds for the Iran war—at
least until Congress authorizes it—failed, as did efforts to simply
get accurate information about the war’s costs. Efforts to provide
protection against other threatened abuses, such as the deployment
of the military to polling places during elections, failed. This NDAA
would swell the Defense budget at the very moment when Congress
shows a determined unwillingness to exercise any meaningful
check on how the President uses the nation’s military might.
The most telling single item in this year’s NDAA, even beyond
the dramatic increase in spending, is the provision ordering that
the Department of Defense be renamed the ‘‘Department of War.’’
The United States long had a Secretary of War, but President Tru-
man and Congress, reflecting on the devastation of World War II,
chose to embrace Defense rather than War as the descriptor of our
national security mission, a change that closely matches the oaths
still taken by all who wear the uniform of this country. The United
States shouldn’t prefer war. We must be committed to defense of
our nation, our people, our allies and our values and, if that re-
quires war, we must always be prepared and ready to succeed. But
war is not the goal and it never should be.
When the United States embraced the ‘‘Department of Defense’’
nomenclature in 1947, we inspired other nations to do the same.
Allies like the United Kingdom and France, former adversaries like
Japan and Germany, current adversaries like Russia, China, North
Korea, and Iran—they now all have Defense agencies rather than
War agencies. The word ‘‘war’’ in the title of a nation’s defense
ministry is essentially extinct in the modern world. If the NDAA
passes with this change intact, the United States will stand alone
as the sole nation advertising War as the mission of its military.
